text:
Letter

Here begins the letter of Saint Jerome to Paulinus the presbyter, concerning the books of divine history.
Chapter One

Brother Ambrose, bringing me your little gifts, delivered at the same time your most delightful letter, which from the beginning was seen to attest to a holy friendship and a longstanding affection. For that is true fellowship, bound together by the bond of Christ: it is fostered not by material advantage, not merely by bodily presence, not by flattery that is cunning and fawning, but by the fear of God and by the shared study of the divine scriptures. We read in ancient histories that certain men traveled through provinces, visited new peoples, crossed seas, so that they might see face to face those whom they had known only from books. Thus Pythagoras visited the prophets of Memphis; thus Plato visited Egypt and Archytas of Tarentum, and that coast of Italy which was once called Magna Graecia, with the greatest effort: and though he was a master at Athens and powerful, able to fill the halls of the academy with his voice, he went about as a stranger and a pupil, preferring to learn humbly from others rather than to impose his own views with arrogance. And when he pursued letters as if fleeing across the whole world, captured by pirates and sold, he submitted to a most cruel tyrant, led away as a captive, bound and enslaved: yet because he was a philosopher, he proved himself greater than the tyrant. We read that from the distant regions of Spain and Gaul certain noblemen came to see Livy, flowing from the fountain of eloquence, men whom the fame of Rome itself had not drawn, but the fame of one man brought there. That age had a wonder unheard of in all centuries, worthy of celebration: that men who entered the city sought something beyond the city.

Apollonius, whether he was a magician as the common people say, or a philosopher as the Pythagoreans hold, traveled beyond the Caucasus, among the Albanians, the Scythians, the Massagetae, and penetrated into the most opulent kingdoms of India: and crossing the broad river Physon at its furthest reach, he came to the Brahmans, so that he might hear Hiarcas seated on his golden throne, drinking from the spring of Tantalus, teaching a few disciples about nature, about customs, and about the course of the days and the stars. Then passing through the Elamites, the Babylonians, the Chaldeans, the Medes, the Assyrians, the Parthians, the Syrians, the Phoenicians, the Arabs, and the Palestinians, he returned to Alexandria, and went on to Ethiopia to see the Gymnosophists and the famous Table of the Sun. That man found everywhere something to learn, and ever making progress, he became always better. Philostratus described all this most fully in eight volumes. Chapter II.

What shall I say of men of this age, when the apostle Paul, vessel of election and teacher of the nations, who spoke of the consciousness of so great a guest dwelling within him, saying: Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me — after having traversed Damascus and Arabia, went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and stayed with him for fifteen days? For by the mystery of the week and the octave, the future preacher to the nations was there to be instructed. And again, after fourteen years, taking with him Barnabas and Titus, he laid before the apostles the gospel he preached, lest he should run or had run in vain. The living voice has a certain hidden power in its delivery, and resounding from the author's mouth into the ears of the disciple, it strikes with greater force. Thus even Aeschines, when he was in exile at Rhodes and read aloud those speeches of Demosthenes —

· Letter ·

the prayer he had delivered against him: while all marveled and praised him, he sighed and said, "What if you had heard the beast herself, resounding with her own words?"

I say this not because there is anything in me such that you could hear from me or would wish to learn from me, but so that your ardor and zeal for learning might be proved by itself even without us. A teachable mind is praiseworthy even without a teacher. But consider not what you may find, but what you should seek. Soft wax, pliable and easy to shape — even if the hand of the craftsman and modeler should cease — nonetheless everything that it can be is by virtue of the whole. The Apostle Paul boasts that he learned the law of Moses and the Pharisees at the feet of Gamaliel, so that, armed with spiritual weapons, he might afterward teach with confidence. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of fortifications and the tearing down of thoughts, and of every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God: and bringing into captivity every understanding to the obedience of Christ, and being ready to punish all disobedience. He writes to Timothy, who was educated from infancy in the sacred letters, and urges him to the study of reading, lest he neglect the grace given to him through the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. He commands the young man that among the other virtues of a bishop, which he described briefly, he should not neglect the scriptures, saying that he who holds fast to the faithful word that is according to sound doctrine is able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict.

Holy simplicity profits only itself, and however much it builds up the church by its own merit, it harms just as much if it does not resist those who destroy it. The prophet Malachi — or rather, the Lord through Malachi — questioned the priests about the law. It is the duty of the priestly office to answer when questioned about the law. And in Deuteronomy we read: Ask your father and he will tell you; your elders and they will say to you. In the Psalm which is the hundred and eighteenth: Your statutes were my songs in the place of my pilgrimage. And in the description of the just man, when he compared him to the tree of life of David which is in paradise, among other virtues he also introduced this: his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he meditates day and night. Daniel at the end of the most sacred vision says: That the just shall shine like the stars, and the learned — that is, the wise — like the firmament. You see how far apart simple righteousness and learned righteousness are from each other. Some aspire to the stars, others to the sky. Although according to the Hebrew truth both can be understood of the learned. For thus we read among them: And they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and they that turn many to righteousness, as the stars forever and ever. Why do you call Paul the apostle a vessel of election? Always because he was a vessel of the law and an archive of the holy scriptures. The Pharisees are astonished at the teaching of the Lord, and they marvel how Peter and John know the law, since they had not learned letters. For the daily exercises and daily meditation in the law that he was accustomed to give to others, the Holy Spirit supplied to them. And they were, as Scripture says, taught of God. The Savior spent twelve years and, sitting in the temple, questioned about matters of the law — he teaches all the more by questioning wisely. Unless perhaps you say that John was an uneducated rustic? Both could say the same thing, and even if impulse drove him, it was not mere knowledge. John a rustic? A fisherman, unlearned? And whence, I ask, that voice: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God? Logos in Greek — many things...

· Letter ·

For a word is reason and reckoning, and the cause of each individual thing by which singular things subsist, and all of which we correctly understand in Christ. Chapter 5.
This the learned Plato did not know; this the eloquent Demosthenes ignored. "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will reject." True wisdom destroys false wisdom, and although the foolishness of preaching the cross is what it is, Paul nevertheless speaks wisdom among the perfect. But not the wisdom of this age which passes away, nor of its rulers, but he speaks the wisdom of God in a mystery, hidden, which God predestined before the ages. The wisdom of God is Christ. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. This wisdom is hidden in mystery, concerning which the title of the ninth psalm makes note, "for the hidden things of the Son," in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge of God. And he who was hidden in mystery was predestined before the ages, and was predestined and prefigured in the law and the prophets. Hence the prophets were called seers, because they saw him whom the blind did not see. Abraham saw his day and rejoiced. The heavens were opened to Ezekiel, which had been shut before sinners. "Open my eyes," says David, "and I will consider the wonders of your law." For the Law is spiritual, and it needs revelation to be understood, so that with unveiled face they may contemplate the glory of God. The book in the Apocalypse, shown sealed with seven seals, if you give it to a learned man to read, he will answer you: "I cannot. For it is sealed." How many today think they know the scriptures, yet hold a sealed book they cannot open, unless he who holds the key of David — who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens — should unseal it. In the Acts of the Apostles, the holy eunuch — indeed a holy man, for sacred scripture so names him — when he was reading the prophet Isaiah and was questioned by Philip: "Do you understand what you are reading?" he answered: "How can I, unless someone teaches me?" I, to speak of myself, am less holy than this eunuch and no more diligent — he who came from Ethiopia, that is from the farthest ends of the world, to the Temple, left the royal court, and was so great a lover of the divine Law that he even read the sacred scriptures while riding in his chariot. And yet though he held the book, turned the words of the Lord in his mind, rolled them over his tongue, sounded them with his lips, he did not know him whom he unknowingly venerated in the book. Philip came, showed him Jesus, who lay hidden in the letter. Wondrous is the power of the teacher. That same hour the eunuch believed; baptized, he became a faithful and holy man — more effective in making a disciple at a desert spring for the Church than in the gilded temple of the synagogue. Chapter 6.
These things have been briefly sketched by me, and the narrow space of your letter did not permit a longer wandering, so that you might understand that without instruction and a shown path you cannot enter into the scriptures. I say nothing of grammarians, rhetoricians, philosophers, geometricians, dialecticians, musicians, astronomers, astrologers, physicians — whose knowledge is sufficiently useful or most useful to mortals, and is divided into three parts: doctrine, reason, and practice. To come to the lesser arts, those administered not so much by tongue as by hand: farmers, masons, smiths, woodcutters, wool-workers and fullers, and the rest who make various furnishings and humble small works — they cannot be what they wish to be without instruction. What belongs to physicians, physicians handle; what belongs to smiths, smiths handle. The art of the scriptures alone is one that...

He demonstrates further that in Zadok and David the mysteries of the new priesthood and new empire are attested. Malachim, that is, the third and fourth book of Kings, describes from Solomon to the time of the captivity, and from Jeroboam son of Nabat to Hosea who was led away to the Assyrians: the kingdom of Judah and the kingdom of Israel. If you look to the history, the words are simple; but if you examine the hidden meaning in the letters, it tells of the fewness of the church and of heretics waging war against the church. The twelve prophets, compressed into one volume, prefigure much more than the letters sound. Hosea frequently names Ephraim, Samaria, Joseph, Jezreel; and speaks of a wife of harlotry and the children of fornication, and of an adulteress in a bedchamber who is the cause of her husband's grief, sitting as a widow, and waiting in mourning garb for the return of her husband. Joel son of Pethuel describes the land of the twelve tribes laid waste by the caterpillar, the locust, the blight, having been consumed; and after the outpouring upon the earlier people, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the servants of God and the handmaids, that is, upon the acknowledged believers by name; and the outpouring into the renewal of Zion. These, counting from one up to fifteen, rising gradually and by degrees, make the number fifteen; and in the Psalter they are mystically signified. Amos, shepherd and farmer, marking the seasons of the ripening of mulberries, cannot be summarized in few words. For who can worthily reprove the three and four crimes of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and in the seventh and eighth degree those of Judah and Israel? He speaks to the fat cows that were in the mountain of Samaria, and foretells the ruin of both the greater and the lesser house. He himself received the sign of the locust and the burning, and the plumb line and the hook of fruits, declaring punishments upon sinners; and a famine in the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water:

but of hearing the word of God. Obadiah, whose name is interpreted as servant of the Lord, prophesies against Edom; and the bloody enemy who is always the rival brother of Jacob he strikes down with the spear in a special way. Jonah, fairest of doves, prefiguring the passion of the Lord through his own shipwreck, calls the world to repentance; and under the name of Nineveh announces salvation to the Gentiles. Micah of Moresheth, heir of the rustic estate, foretells the devastation of the daughter of the robbers, and lays siege against her; for the scepter of the judge of Israel shall be struck upon the cheek. Nahum, consoler of the world, rebukes the city of blood; and after its expulsion he says: behold upon the mountains the feet of one who brings good news and announces peace. Habakkuk, strong and steadfast wrestler, stands at his watch, and leaps over the step and completes the mystery of Christ upon the cross, and says: His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise; his brightness is as the light, he has horns coming out of his hand, and there is the hiding of his power. Zephaniah, watchman and knower of the secrets of the Lord, hears the cry from the fish gate, and the wailing from the second quarter, and the crashing from the hills. He calls the inhabitants of the mortar to lamentation, for all the Canaanite people are cut off; all those who were laden with silver are destroyed. Haggai, festive and joyful, who had sown in tears so that he might reap in joy, rebuilds the destroyed temple; and above he brings in the Father speaking: yet once more, a little while, and I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land, and I will shake all nations, and the Desire of all nations shall come. Zechariah, mindful of his Lord, manifold in visions, clothed in filthy garments and having the lampstand and the seven candelabra of gold with their seven lamps and eyes, and two olive trees standing to the left of the lampstand, seek and

on the right: so that after the red horses, the various black and white ones, and the scattered pitchers of Ephraim, and the colt from Jerusalem, he prophesies of a poor king, and proclaims a king sitting upon the foal of a she-ass. Malachi speaks openly, and at the end of all the prophets, concerning the rejection of Israel and the calling of the Gentiles: "I have no pleasure in you," says the Lord of hosts, "and I will not accept an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place sacrifice is offered and a pure offering is made to my name." As for Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel — who is able either to understand or to expound them? The first of them seems to me not a prophet but an evangelist. The second speaks of the almond rod and the boiling pot from the face of the north, and of the leopard stripped of its colors, and he renders a fourfold alphabet in different meters. The third has his beginning and end wrapped in such great obscurities that among the Hebrews these passages, along with the beginning of Genesis, are not read before the age of thirty. The fourth, who is also called the third among the four prophets, aware of his times and a philosophical historian of the whole world, speaks plainly of a stone cut from the mountain without hands, and of all kingdoms being overthrown. David is our Simonides, our Pindar and Alcaeus, our Flaccus and Catullus and Serenus — he sings to the lyre, and on the ten-stringed psaltery he calls back from below the one rising from the dead. Solomon, peaceful and beloved of God, corrects morals, teaches nature, joins the Church to Christ, and sweetly sings the holy nuptial hymn. Esther, as a type of the Church, frees the people from peril, and the wicked Haman, whose name is interpreted as iniquity, meets a day famous to posterity.

The book of Paralipomenon (Chronicles) is of such great importance to the instrument of the Old Testament that without it, whoever claims for himself knowledge of the Scriptures makes a mockery of himself. For through its individual names and words, it touches on things omitted in the books of Kings and unfolds countless questions of the Gospels. Ezra and Nehemiah — that is, Helper and Comforter of the Lord — are contained in one volume; they restore the temple, rebuild the walls of the city, and all that great crowd returning to their homeland, the list of priests, Levites, and Israelites, and the singers, and the various families assigned to building the walls and towers — some carry material on the outside, others retain it within the core. I confess that love of the Scriptures has swept me away and caused me to exceed the bounds of a letter, without having accomplished what I wished. We have heard enough to know what we ought to desire — so that we too may say: "My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times." The Socratic saying is fulfilled in us: "This only I know, that I know nothing." Let me also briefly touch on the New Testament. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John are the chariot of the Lord, and the true cherubim, which is interpreted as the fullness of knowledge — throughout their whole body they are full of eyes; sparks flash from them, lightnings run; their feet are straight, and stretching upward, their backs are winged, and flying everywhere, they hold one another and are intertwined: and like a wheel within a wheel, they roll along and go wherever the breath of the Holy Spirit drives them. Paul writes to seven churches; for the letter to the Hebrews is placed outside the number by most. He instructs Timothy, Titus, and pleads for Philemon on behalf of a runaway slave — on which matter I think it better to say nothing than to say too little. The Acts of the Apostles seem bare indeed.

Epistle.

...to recount the history and cover the infancy of the nascent church. But if we know that their writer Luke was a physician, whose praise is in the Gospel, we equally observe that all words were medicine for the languishing soul. James, Peter, John, Jude published seven epistles at once mystical and concise, brief in words yet long in meaning, so that few can resist returning to read them. The Apocalypse of John has as many mysteries as it has words. I have said too little: even the highest praise falls short of the merit of the work. In each single word lie multiple meanings. I beg you, dearest brother, to meditate among these things, to know nothing else and seek nothing else. Does it not seem to you that even here on earth this is the dwelling place of the heavenly kingdom? I do not want you to be offended by the simplicity and plainness of language in the holy scriptures, which have been set forth either through the fault of translators or deliberately, so that the unlearned congregation might more easily be instructed, and in the same passage the learned and unlearned might each draw different meaning. I am not so bold and dull as to promise that I know these things and can pluck their fruits on earth, whose roots are fixed in heaven. But I confess my willingness; I prefer a companion to a master, and though I decline the role of teacher, I offer myself as a fellow traveler. To him who asks it is given; to him who knocks it is opened; he who seeks finds. Let me learn also about earthly things, which knowledge will surpass for us in heaven. I will receive you with open arms, and however ineptly and with whatever confusion pours forth, I will try to learn together with you whatever you seek. Chapter 8.

You have here the most loving Eusebius, the grandfather, who doubled my gratitude for your letter by reporting the honorable character of your conduct, the steadfastness of friendship in these times, and the love of the spirit. For the elegance of his speech even without the letter itself commended it. Hasten, I beg you: when a boat is in the open sea, it is better to unfasten the rope than to make it fast. No one who is about to renounce the world can sell well what he despised in order to sell. Whatever you spend from your own means, count it as gain. The ancients said: the miser lacks as much as he has, and also what he does not have. For the believer the whole world is riches. But the unbeliever lacks even an obol. Let us live as having nothing yet possessing all things. Food and clothing are sufficient for the devout Christian. If you have property in your power, sell it; if you do not have it, cast it away. To him who takes your tunic, the cloak also must be left. Unless of course you are always procrastinating and selling off your little possessions cautiously and little by little, so that Christ has nothing with which to feed his poor. He gave all to God who offered himself. The apostles left only a boat and nets; the widow casts two mites into the treasury and surpasses the rich in heaven's eyes. He easily computes the day who always thinks of himself as dying.

Here begins the prologue to the Pentateuch of Moses.

I have received the longed-for letter of my longing friend, who bears a name chosen by lot together with Daniel as if by presage of things to come, entreating me to render the Pentateuch into Latin from the Hebrew tongue for the ears of our people. It is certainly a dangerous work and open to the attacks of my detractors, who bark that I am daring something new against the reputation of the Seventy translators. They test genius with wine in this way; though I most frequently testify that I offer what I am able for a lowly place in the tabernacle of God, and that I am not enriched by the poverty of others. That I might listen to Origen, who made me acquainted...

Prologue.

He stirred up controversy: he mixed his edition of the ancient translation of Theodotion with the asterisk and obelus — that is, the star and the spit — distinguishing the whole work, making clear what was previously obscure, and cutting down and destroying what was superfluous; and especially what the authority of the evangelists and apostles had proclaimed. Among these we read many things from the Old Testament that are not found in our codices: such as that saying, "Out of Egypt I have called my son," and "He shall be called a Nazarene," and "They shall look upon him whom they pierced," and "Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly," and "What eye has not seen nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what he has prepared for those who love him" — and many other things which the original text requires. Let us therefore ask them where these things are written: and when they cannot say, let them produce them from the Hebrew books. The first testimony is in Hosea, the second in Isaiah, the third in Zechariah, the fourth in Proverbs — which many, being ignorant, prefer to follow as apocryphal ravings, and prefer idle nonsense to authentic books. It is not my place to assign causes for the error. The Jews say it was done by the counsel of the wise, so that Ptolemy, a worshipper of one God, should not discover the duality of divinity among the Hebrews: and they did this especially because he seemed to be inclined toward the teaching of Plato. Finally, wherever the scriptures testify concerning the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, they either translated differently or kept entirely silent: so as to satisfy the king and not make public the mystery of the faith. And I do not know who was the first author to construct the seventy cells at Alexandria with his lie, in which the translators worked separately — since Aristeas, the bodyguard of that same Ptolemy, and Josephus not long afterward, report nothing of the sort: but write that they met together in one basilica and compared their translations, not that they prophesied separately. For it is one thing to be a prophet, another to be a translator. There the spirit foretells what is to come; here, learning and richness of expression transfers what one understands. Unless perhaps we should suppose that Cicero translated the Economics of Xenophon, the Timaeus of Plato, and the speeches of Demosthenes, inspired by rhetorical spirit. Or that the Holy Spirit received testimonies from the same books differently through the seventy translators and differently again through the apostles — so that what those kept silent about, these lied about as being written. What then? Do we condemn the ancients? By no means: but after the labors of those earlier scholars, we work in the house of the Lord as best we can. They translated before the coming of Christ, and what they did not know they expressed in ambiguous phrases; we write after his passion not so much a mystery as a history. For things heard are told differently from things seen. What we understand better, we also express better. Hear, then, O rival; listen, O detractor. I do not condemn or criticize the Seventy; but I confidently prefer the apostles over those unlearned men. Through these the Spirit speaks to my mouth — those whom I read were placed first among the spiritual gifts, among which translators hold nearly the last rank. Why do you twist with envy? Why do you rack the minds of the inexperienced with strange anxieties? If you think I am erring somewhere in the translation, ask the Hebrews; consult the Jews of various cities. What they have concerning Christ, your codices do not have. It is another matter if what was afterward adopted by the apostles has been demonstrated against them, and if the Latin copies are more correct than the Greek, and the Greek more than the Hebrew. This, this is what you should argue with the Jews. And now, most beloved, I ask you: since you have imposed so great a burden upon me, help me with your prayers, so that I may transfer these books into the Latin language in the same spirit in which they were written.

Genesis

Here begins the book of Bereshit, which we call Genesis.
In the beginning God created heaven and the earth. But the earth was without form and empty, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the spirit of God moved over the waters. And God said: Let there be light. And there was light. And God saw that the light was good, and he divided the light from the darkness, and he called the light Day and the darkness Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day. And God said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters. And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament, and it was so. And God called the firmament Heaven, and there was evening and there was morning, the second day. And God said: Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear. And it was so. And God called the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters he called Seas. And God saw that it was good, and said: Let the earth bring forth grass, and plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth. And it was so. And the earth brought forth grass and plants yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit whose seed was in itself after their kind. And God saw that it was good, and there was evening and there was morning, the third day. And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to divide the day from the night, and let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years, and let them give light in the firmament of heaven upon the earth. And it was so. And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night; and the stars also. And he set them in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth, and to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good, and there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day. And God said: Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creature that has life, and birds that may fly above the earth in the open firmament of heaven. And God created great sea creatures, and every living creature that moves, which the waters brought forth abundantly after their kind, and every winged bird after its kind. And God saw that it was good, and God blessed them, saying: Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters of the seas, and let birds multiply upon the earth. And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day. And God said: Let the earth bring forth living creatures after their kind: cattle and creeping things and beasts of the earth after their kind. And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth after their kind, and cattle and every creeping thing of the earth after its kind. And God saw that it was good, and said: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said: Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the air and over every living thing that moves upon the earth. And God said: Behold, I have given you every plant bearing seed that is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree in which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for food, and to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the air and to everything that moves upon the earth in which there is life. And it was so. And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.

· Genesis ·

And there was evening and morning, the sixth day. Chapter 2.
So the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their adornment. And on the seventh day God completed his work which he had done: and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it: because in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made. These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that the Lord God made the earth and the heavens: and every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground. But there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground. And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul. And the Lord God had planted a garden eastward in Eden: and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground made the Lord God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil. And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads. The name of the first is Pison: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold; and the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone. And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia. And the name of the third river is Tigris: that is it which goeth toward Assyria. And the fourth river is Euphrates. And the Lord God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it. And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof

thou shalt surely die. And the Lord God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him. And out of the ground the Lord God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof. And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him. And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof. And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man. And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh. And they were both naked, Adam and his wife, and were not ashamed.

Now the serpent was more subtle. Chapter 3.
than any beast of the field which the Lord God had made. And he said unto the woman, Why has God commanded you that you should not eat of every tree of the garden? And the woman said to the serpent, We may eat of the fruit of the trees of the garden: but of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God has said, You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die. And the serpent said unto the woman, You shall not surely die. For God knows that in the day you eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened: and you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil. And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and ate, and gave also

Genesis

that I might obtain mercy. Behold, you drive me out this day from the face of the earth, and from your face I shall be hidden; and I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth. Everyone who finds me will kill me. And the Lord said to him: Not so; whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold. And the Lord set a mark on Cain, so that none who found him should kill him. And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and dwelt as a fugitive in the land east of Eden. And Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. And he built a city, and called the name of the city after the name of his son Enoch. To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech. And Lamech took two wives. The name of one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah. Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and raise livestock, and his brother's name was Jubal. He was the father of those who play the harp and flute. Zillah also bore Tubal-cain, who was a forger and craftsman in every work of bronze and iron. And the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah. And Lamech said to his wives Adah and Zillah: Hear my voice, wives of Lamech, listen to my speech. For I have killed a man for wounding me, and a young man for striking me. If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold. And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, saying: God has appointed for me another offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed. And Seth also had a son, and he called his name Enosh. He began to call upon the name of the Lord. Chapter 5.

This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and called their name Adam in the day they were created.

Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and called his name Seth. And the days of Adam after he fathered Seth were eight hundred years, and he had sons and daughters. And all the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years, and he died. Seth lived one hundred and five years and fathered Enosh. And Seth lived after he fathered Enosh eight hundred and seven years and had sons and daughters. And all the days of Seth were nine hundred and twelve years, and he died. Enosh lived ninety years and fathered Kenan. After he fathered Kenan, he lived eight hundred and fifteen years and had sons and daughters. And all the days of Enosh were nine hundred and five years, and he died. Kenan lived seventy years and fathered Mahalalel. And Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel eight hundred and forty years and had sons and daughters. And all the days of Kenan were nine hundred and ten years, and he died. Mahalalel lived sixty-five years and fathered Jared. And Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared eight hundred and thirty years and had sons and daughters. And all the days of Mahalalel were eight hundred and ninety-five years, and he died. Jared lived one hundred and sixty-two years and fathered Enoch. And Jared lived after he fathered Enoch eight hundred years and had sons and daughters. And all the days of Jared were nine hundred and sixty-two years, and he died. Enoch lived sixty-five years and fathered Methuselah. And Enoch walked with God. And Enoch lived after he fathered Methuselah three hundred years and had sons and daughters. And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years:

Genesis                                                                                                              7.

And Enoch walked with God, and was not found, for God took him. And Methuselah lived three hundred and eighty-seven years and fathered Lamech. And Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech seven hundred and eighty-two years, and fathered sons and daughters. And all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died. And Lamech lived one hundred and eighty-two years and fathered a son, and called his name Noah, saying: This one shall comfort us from our works and from the toil of our hands in the land which the Lord has cursed. And Lamech lived after he fathered Noah five hundred and ninety-five years, and fathered sons and daughters. And all the days of Lamech were seven hundred and seventy-seven years, and he died. And Noah, when he was five hundred years old, fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Chapter 6.
When men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives any they chose. And God said: My spirit shall not remain in man forever, for he is flesh. His days shall be one hundred and twenty years. There were giants on the earth in those days. After the sons of God came in to the daughters of men, and they bore children to them: these were the mighty men of old, men of renown. And God saw that the wickedness of men was great on the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually; and it repented God that he had made man on the earth. And being touched inwardly with sorrow of heart, he said: I will destroy man whom I have created from the face of the earth, from man to animals, from creeping things to the birds of heaven; for I repent that I have made them. But Noah found grace in the eyes of the Lord. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a just man
and perfect in his generations; he walked with God and fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And the earth was corrupt before God, and was filled with iniquity. And when God had seen that the earth was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted its way upon the earth, he said to Noah: The end of all flesh is come before me. The earth is filled with iniquity through them, and I will destroy them with the earth. Make yourself an ark of smooth wood. Make rooms in the ark, and caulk it inside and out with pitch, and thus you shall make it. The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits. You shall make a window in the ark, finishing it to a cubit above; and the door of the ark you shall set in the side; with lower, second, and third decks you shall make it. Behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven; everything that is in the earth shall perish. But I will establish my covenant with you; and you shall come into the ark, you, and your sons, and your wife, and your sons' wives with you. And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every kind into the ark to keep them alive with you; they shall be male and female. Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive. Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up; and it shall serve as food for you and for them. And Noah did all that God commanded him. Chapter 7.
And the Lord said to him: Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation. Of all clean animals you shall take seven pairs, the male and his female; and of animals that are not clean

Genesis

two and two, male and female; and of the birds of the sky, seven and seven, male and female, to preserve seed upon the face of all the earth. For yet seven days, and I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and every living substance that I have made will I destroy from off the face of the earth. And Noah did everything that the Lord commanded him. And Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters was upon the earth. And Noah went in, and his sons, and his wife, and his sons' wives with him, into the ark, because of the waters of the flood. Of clean beasts, and of beasts that are not clean, and of birds, and of every thing that creeps upon the earth, there went in two and two unto Noah into the ark, the male and the female, as God had commanded Noah. And it came to pass after seven days, that the waters of the flood were upon the earth. In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month, the same day were all the fountains of the great deep broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened. And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights. In the selfsame day entered Noah, and Shem, and Ham, and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and Noah's wife, and the three wives of his sons with them, into the ark; they, and every beast after his kind, and all the cattle after their kind, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth after his kind, and every bird after his kind, every bird of every sort. And they went in unto Noah into the ark, two and two of all flesh, in which is the breath of life. And they that went in, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him: and the Lord shut him in. And the flood was forty days upon the earth; and the waters increased, and bore up the ark, and it was lifted up above the earth. And the waters prevailed, and were increased greatly upon the earth; and they covered the face of the whole earth.

And the ark floated upon the waters: and the waters prevailed exceedingly upon the earth; and all the high hills that were under the whole heaven were covered. Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail; and the mountains were covered. And all flesh died that moved upon the earth, both of birds, and of cattle, and of beasts, and of every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, and every man. And all in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died. And every living substance was destroyed which was upon the face of the ground, both man, and cattle, and the creeping things, and the birds of the heaven; and they were destroyed from the earth. And only Noah remained alive, and they that were with him in the ark. And the waters prevailed upon the earth a hundred and fifty days. Chapter VIII.

And God remembered Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that was with him in the ark: and God made a wind to pass over the earth, and the waters subsided. The fountains also of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained. And the waters receded from the earth continually: and after the end of the hundred and fifty days the waters diminished. And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat. And the waters decreased continually until the tenth month: in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, were the tops of the mountains seen. And it came to pass at the end of forty days, that Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made: and he sent forth a raven, which went forth to and fro, until the waters were dried up from off the earth. Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground. But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark. For the waters were on the face of the whole earth. Then he put out his hand, and took her, and pulled her in unto him into the ark. And he stayed yet another seven days; and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark. And the dove came in to him in the evening, carrying

Genesis

a branch of olive with green leaves in its mouth. Noah understood from this that the waters had ceased upon the earth. He waited yet another seven days and sent forth the dove, which did not return to him again. So in the six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, the waters were dried up upon the earth. And Noah opened the covering of the ark and looked out, and saw that the surface of the ground was dry. In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dried. Then the Lord spoke to Noah, saying: Go out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons, and your sons' wives with you. Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh — birds, and animals, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth — that they may abound on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth. So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him. And every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves upon the earth, went out by families from the ark. Then Noah built an altar to the Lord, and taking of all the clean animals and all the clean birds, offered burnt offerings on the altar. And the Lord smelled the sweet odor and said in his heart: I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the imagination and thought of man's heart are prone to evil from his youth. I will therefore strike all living flesh no more as I have done. All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day shall not cease.

Chapter IX
And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: Increase and multiply and fill the earth. And let the fear and dread of you be upon all the animals of the earth, and upon all the birds of the air, and all that moves upon the earth. All the fishes of the sea are delivered into your hand, and every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. As the green plants I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with blood in it. For your blood of your lives I will require: at the hand of every beast will I require it, and at the hand of man. At the hand of every man's brother I will require the life of man. Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. But you, be fruitful and multiply, and spread over the earth and increase in it. This is what God said to Noah and to his sons with him: Behold, I will establish my covenant with you and with your descendants after you, and with every living creature that is with you — birds, cattle, and every beast of the earth — all that came out of the ark, and every beast of the earth. I will establish my covenant with you, and never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood, nor shall there ever again be a flood to destroy the earth. And God said: This is the sign of the covenant which I make between me and you, and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations. I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. When I bring clouds over the earth, the bow shall be seen in the clouds, and I will remember my covenant which is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh, and the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. The bow shall be in the clouds, and I will look upon it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is upon the earth. And the Lord said to Noah: This is the sign of the covenant which I have established between me and all flesh upon the earth. The sons of Noah who went out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And Ham himself is

Genesis

And they set out from the east and found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they dwelt there. And one said to his neighbor: Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire. And they had bricks instead of stones, and bitumen for mortar. And they said: Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose top may reach to heaven, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth. And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower which the children of Adam were building. And he said: Behold, the people is one, and they all have one language. And they have begun to do this, and they will not stop from their purposes until they complete the work. Come therefore, let us go down, and there confuse their language, so that they may not hear one another's voice. And thus the Lord dispersed them from that place into all lands, and they ceased to build the city. And therefore the name of that place was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confused. And from there the Lord scattered them abroad over the face of all the earth. These are the generations of Shem. Shem was a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the flood. And Shem lived after he begot Arphaxad five hundred years, and begot sons and daughters. And Arphaxad lived thirty-five years and begot Salah. And Arphaxad lived after he begot Salah four hundred and three years, and begot sons and daughters. And Salah lived thirty years and begot Eber. And Salah lived after he begot Eber four hundred and three years, and begot sons and daughters. And Eber lived thirty-four years and begot Peleg. And Eber lived after he begot Peleg four hundred and thirty years, and begot sons and daughters. And Peleg lived thirty years and begot Reu. And Peleg lived after he begot Reu two hundred and nine years,

and begot sons and daughters. And Reu lived thirty-two years and begot Serug. And Reu lived after he begot Serug two hundred and seven years, and begot sons and daughters. And Serug lived thirty years and begot Nahor. And Serug lived after he begot Nahor two hundred years, and begot sons and daughters. And Nahor lived twenty-nine years and begot Terah. And Nahor lived after he begot Terah a hundred and nineteen years, and begot sons and daughters. And Terah lived seventy years and begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Now these are the generations of Terah. Terah begot Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran begot Lot. And Haran died before his father Terah in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans. And Nahor and Abram took wives: the name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah and the father of Iscah. But Sarai was barren and had no child. And Terah took Abram his son, and Lot the son of Haran his son's son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram's wife, and they went forth with them from Ur of the Chaldeans, to go into the land of Canaan. And they came to Haran and dwelt there. And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Haran.

Chapter XII. Now the Lord said to Abram: Get out of your country and from your kindred and from your father's house, to a land that I will show you. And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great, and you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed. So Abram departed, as the Lord had spoken to him, and Lot went with him. And Abram was seventy-five years old when

Genesis

[Abram] departed from Haran. And he took Sarai his wife, and Lot the son of his brother, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came. And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Shechem, unto the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land. And the Lord appeared unto Abram and said: Unto your seed will I give this land. And there he built an altar unto the Lord, who appeared unto him, and called upon the name of the Lord. And he removed from there unto a mountain on the east of Bethel, and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he built an altar unto the Lord, and called upon the name of the Lord. And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south. And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was severe in the land. And it came to pass, when he was come near to enter into Egypt, that he said unto Sarai his wife: I know that you are a fair woman to look upon: and it shall come to pass, when the Egyptians shall see you, that they shall say: This is his wife; and they will kill me, but they will save you alive. Say, I pray you, that you are my sister: that it may be well with me for your sake; and my soul shall live because of you. And it came to pass, that, when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians beheld the woman that she was very fair. The princes also of Pharaoh saw her, and commended her before Pharaoh: and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house. And he treated Abram well for her sake: and he had sheep, and oxen, and asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and camels. And the Lord plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai Abram's wife. And Pharaoh called Abram, and said: What is this that you have done unto me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Why did you say: She is my sister? So that I took her to be my wife.

Now therefore behold your wife, take her, and go your way. And Pharaoh commanded his men concerning him: and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that he had. Chapter 13.

And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south. And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold. And he went on his journeys from the south even to Bethel, unto the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Hai; unto the place of the altar, which he had made there at first: and there Abram called on the name of the Lord. And Lot also, who went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents. And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together. And there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's cattle and the herdsmen of Lot's cattle: and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land. And Abram said unto Lot: Let there be no strife, I pray you, between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen; for we are brothers. Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself, I pray you, from me: if you will take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if you depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left. And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered everywhere, before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt, as you come unto Zoar. Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan; and Lot journeyed east: and they separated themselves the one from the other. Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom. But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the Lord exceedingly. And the Lord said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him: Lift up now your eyes, and look

· Genesis ·

And look from the place where you are now, northward and southward, eastward and westward. All the land which you see, I will give to you and to your descendants forever. And I will make your descendants as the dust of the earth, so that if anyone can count the dust of the earth, then your descendants can also be counted. Arise, walk through the length and breadth of the land, for I will give it to you. Then Abram moved his tent and came and dwelt by the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron, and he built an altar there to the Lord.

Chapter 14. In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Pontus, and Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations, these made war with Bera king of Sodom, and with Birsha king of Gomorrah, and with Shinab king of Admah, and with Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, which is Zoar. All these joined together in the Valley of Siddim, which is the Salt Sea. Twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled. In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer came, and the kings that were with him, and they struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth Karnaim, and the Zuzim with them, and the Emim in Shaveh Kiriathaim, and the Horites in their mount Seir, even unto El-paran, which is by the wilderness. And they returned and came to En-mishpat, which is Kadesh, and struck all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites that dwelt in Hazazon-tamar. Then the king of Sodom, and the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, and the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela which is Zoar, went out and drew up their battle lines in the Valley of Siddim against Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of nations, and Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Pontus.

Four kings against five. Now the Valley of Siddim was full of tar pits. And the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there, and the rest fled to the mountains. And they took all the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their food, and went away. They also took Lot, Abram's brother's son, who dwelt in Sodom, and his goods, and departed. Then one who had escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who dwelt by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner; and these were allies with Abram. And when Abram heard that his kinsman Lot had been taken captive, he led out his trained men, born in his house, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued as far as Dan. And he divided his forces against them by night, and struck them and pursued them as far as Hobah, which is north of Damascus. And he brought back all the goods, and also brought back his kinsman Lot with his goods, and the women also, and the other people. And the king of Sodom went out to meet him, after his return from the defeat of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, at the Valley of Shaveh, which is the King's Valley. And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High. And he blessed him and said: Blessed be Abram of God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth. And blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand. And he gave him a tenth of everything. And the king of Sodom said to Abram, Give me the persons, and take the goods for yourself. But Abram said to the king of Sodom, I have lifted my hand to the Lord, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, that I would not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours, lest you should say, I have made Abram rich, except only what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me.

and Phoenicians

. Genesis .

[names of companions: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre]. These shall receive their share. After these things, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: Do not be afraid, Abram; I am your protector, and your reward shall be very great. And Abram said: Lord God, what will you give me? I shall go without children, and the son of the steward of my house is this Damascus Eliezer. And Abram added: You have given me no offspring, and behold, one born in my house shall be my heir. Immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying: This man shall not be your heir, but one who shall come from your own body shall be your heir. And he brought him outside and said to him: Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can. And he said to him: So shall your descendants be. Abram believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. And he said to him: I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land to possess. But he said: Lord God, how shall I know that I will possess it? And the Lord answered: Bring me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old female goat, and a three-year-old ram, a turtledove, and a young pigeon. He took all these and divided them down the middle, placing each half opposite the other. But the birds he did not divide. And birds of prey came down upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away. Now when the sun was about to set, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great and dark dread came over him. And it was said to him: Know for certain that your descendants will be strangers in a land not their own, and they will be enslaved and afflicted for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation they serve, and afterward they shall come out with great wealth. As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace and be buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.

When the sun had set and darkness had fallen, there appeared a smoking furnace and a flaming torch that passed between the divided pieces. On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram, saying: To your descendants I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates — the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites.

Chapter 16. Now Sarai, the wife of Abram, had borne him no children. She had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar, and she said to her husband: Behold, the Lord has kept me from bearing children; go in to my maidservant, so that perhaps through her I may obtain children. And when he agreed, she took Hagar the Egyptian, her maidservant, and gave her to her husband Abram as a wife, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan. He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, she looked on her mistress with contempt. Then Sarai said to Abram: You are doing me wrong. I gave my maidservant into your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised me. May the Lord judge between me and you. Abram said to Sarai: Behold, your maidservant is in your power; do with her as you please. Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her. The angel of the Lord found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road to Shur. And he said: Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going? She answered: I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai. The angel of the Lord said to her: Return to your mistress and submit to her authority. And again he said: I will greatly multiply your descendants so that they cannot be numbered for multitude. And furthermore he said: Behold, you have conceived and shall bear a son; you shall call his name Ishmael, because the Lord has heard your affliction. He shall be a wild man;

Genesis

His hand against all men, and every man's hand against him. And he shall dwell over against all his brethren. And Hagar called the name of the Lord who had spoken to her: Thou art the God who hast seen me. For she said: Surely here have I seen the hinder parts of him that seeth me. Therefore she called that well: The well of him that liveth and seeth me. It is between Kadesh and Bered. And Hagar bore Abram a son, and he called his name Ishmael. And Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore him Ishmael. [Chapter 17]

After Abram was ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him and said to him: I am God Almighty. Walk before me, and be perfect. And I will make my covenant between me and thee, and will multiply thee exceedingly. Abram fell on his face. And God spoke to him saying: I am, and my covenant is with thee, and thou shalt be a father of many nations. Neither shall thy name be called Abram any more, but thou shalt be called Abraham, because I have made thee a father of many nations. And I will make thee to grow exceedingly, and I will make nations of thee, and kings shall come out of thee. And I will establish my covenant between me and thee, and between thy seed after thee in their generations, by a perpetual covenant, to be a God unto thee and to thy seed after thee. And I will give to thee and to thy seed after thee the land of thy sojourn, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God. God said moreover to Abraham: And thou therefore shalt keep my covenant, and thy seed after thee in their generations. This is my covenant which you shall observe between me and you and thy seed after thee: All the male among you shall be circumcised. And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be for a sign of the covenant between me and you. An infant of eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every male in your generations,

both he that is born in the house and he that is bought: and whosoever is of your stock shall be circumcised. And my covenant shall be in your flesh for a perpetual covenant. The male whose flesh of his foreskin shall not be circumcised, that soul shall be destroyed out of his people, because he hath broken my covenant. God said also to Abraham: Sarai thy wife thou shalt not call Sarai, but Sarah. And I will bless her, and of her I will give thee a son, whom I will bless, and he shall be a father of nations, and kings of peoples shall spring from him. Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart: Shall a son, thinkest thou, be born to him that is a hundred years old? and shall Sarah that is ninety years old bring forth? And he said to God: O that Ishmael might live before thee. And God said to Abraham: Sara thy wife shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name Isaac, and I will establish my covenant with him for a perpetual covenant, and with his seed after him. And as for Ishmael I have also heard thee. Behold, I will bless him and increase and multiply him exceedingly. He shall beget twelve chiefs, and I will make him a great nation. But my covenant I will establish with Isaac, whom Sara shall bring forth to thee at this time in the next year. And when he had left off speaking with him, God went up from Abraham. And Abraham took Ishmael his son, and all that were born in his house, and all whom he had bought, and every male among the men of his household, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskin forthwith the very same day as God had commanded him. Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin. And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old at the time of his circumcision. The selfsame day was Abraham circumcised and Ishmael his son. And all the men of his house, as well those born in the house as those bought,

were circumcised together. [Chapter 18]
And the Lord appeared to him in the vale

Genesis.

Mamre, sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. And when he had lifted up his eyes, there appeared to him three men standing near him. When he saw them, he ran from the door of the tent to meet them and bowed down to the ground and said: Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant, but I will bring a little water and wash your feet, and rest under the tree. And I will set bread, and strengthen your heart, then you shall pass on. For this reason have you come aside to your servant. And they said: Do as you have spoken. Abraham hastened into the tent to Sara and said to her: Make haste, take three measures of fine flour, knead it, and make cakes under the ashes. But he himself ran to the herd and took from there a calf, very tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who made haste to dress it. He also took butter and milk, and the calf which he had boiled, and set them before them. And he stood by them under the tree. When they had eaten, they said to him: Where is Sara your wife? He answered: She is in the tent. And he said: I will return to you at this time, life permitting, and Sara your wife shall have a son. Sara heard this at the door of the tent behind him. Now they were both old and Sara was past the age of bearing children. And she laughed secretly, saying: After I am grown old, and my lord is old, shall I give myself to pleasure? And the Lord said to Abraham: Why did Sara laugh, saying: Shall I, who am old, bear a child indeed? Is anything hard for God? At the appointed time I will return to you, and Sara shall have a son. Sara denied it, saying: I did not laugh. For she was afraid. And he said: No, but you did laugh. And when the men rose up from there, they turned their faces toward Sodom: and Abraham walked with them to bring them on their way. And the Lord said: Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,

seeing he shall become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him? For I know that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord, to do justice and judgment: that the Lord may bring to Abraham all the things he has promised him. And the Lord said: The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is multiplied, and their sin is exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry that is come to me, or whether it be not so, that I may know. And they turned from there and went toward Sodom: but Abraham still stood before the Lord. And drawing near, he said: Will you destroy the just with the wicked? If there be fifty just men in the city, will you destroy them and not spare the place for the sake of the fifty just, if they be therein? Far be it from you to do this thing, and to slay the just with the wicked, and for the just to be in like case as the wicked. This is not fitting for you: you who judge all the earth. And the Lord said to him: If I find fifty just men in the midst of Sodom, I will spare the whole place for their sake. And Abraham answered and said: Seeing I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes. What if there be five less than fifty just? Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five? And he said: I will not destroy it, if I find forty-five there. And again he said to him: But if forty should be found there, what will you do? He said: I will not strike it for the sake of forty. He said: I beseech you, Lord, be not angry if I speak. What if thirty should be found there? He answered: I will not do it if I find thirty there. Since I have once begun, said he, I will speak to my Lord. What if twenty should be found there? He said:

· Genesis ·

His wife, looking back behind him, was turned into a pillar of salt. But Abraham rising up in the morning, where he had stood before with the Lord, looked towards Sodom and Gomorrah and the whole land of that country, and he saw the ashes rise up from the earth as the smoke of a furnace. For when God destroyed the cities of that country, remembering Abraham, he delivered Lot out of the destruction of the cities wherein he had dwelt. And Lot went up out of Zoar and dwelt in the mountain, and his two daughters with him. For he was afraid to stay in Zoar, and he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters with him. And the elder said to the younger: Our father is old, and there is no man left on the earth to come in unto us after the manner of the whole earth. Come, let us make our father drink wine and lie with him, that we may preserve seed from our father. They gave their father wine to drink that night, and the elder went in and lay with her father, but he perceived it not, neither when his daughter lay down, nor when she rose up. The next day the elder said to the younger: Behold I lay last night with my father; let us make him drink wine also tonight, and thou shalt lie with him, that we may save seed from our father. They gave their father wine to drink that night also, and the younger daughter went in and lay with him, and he perceived not when she lay down, nor when she rose up. So the two daughters of Lot were with child by their father. And the elder bore a son, and she called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites unto this day. And the younger also bore a son, and she called his name Ammon, that is, the son of my people. He is the father of the Ammonites unto this day. Chapter 20.

Abraham set forward from there into the south country and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar. And Abraham said of Sarah his wife: She is my sister. And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took her. But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: Behold thou shalt die because of the woman thou hast taken, for she has a husband. Now Abimelech had not touched her, and he said: Lord, wilt thou slay a nation that is ignorant and just? Did he not say to me: She is my sister? And she herself said: He is my brother. In the simplicity of my heart and the cleanness of my hands have I done this. And God said to him: And I know that thou didst it with a sincere heart, and therefore I withheld thee from sinning against me, and I did not suffer thee to touch her. Now therefore restore the man his wife, for he is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee, and thou shalt live. But if thou wilt not restore her, know that thou shalt surely die, thou and all that are thine. And Abimelech rising up immediately in the night, called all his servants, and spoke all these words in their hearing, and all the men were exceedingly afraid. And Abimelech called also Abraham, and said to him: What hast thou done to us? What have we sinned against thee, that thou hast brought upon me and upon my kingdom a great sin? Thou hast done to us what thou oughtest not to do. And again he expostulated with him and said: What sawest thou, that thou hast done this? Abraham answered: I thought with myself, saying: Perhaps there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me for my wife's sake. Yet in very deed she is my sister, the daughter of my father, and not the daughter of my mother, and I took her to wife. And after God brought me out from my father's house, I said to her: This kindness shalt thou do with me: in every place to which we shall come, thou shalt say that I am thy brother. And Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and menservants and womenservants, and gave them to Abraham, and restored to him Sarah his wife. And said: The land is before you; dwell wheresoever it shall please thee. And to Sarah he said: Behold I have given thy brother a thousand pieces of silver. This shall serve thee

. Genesis .

before all who were with you, remember this as your vindication." And Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants, so they bore children. For the Lord had closed up every womb in the household of Abimelech, because of Sarah, Abraham's wife. CHAPTER XXI.

The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised, and fulfilled what he had spoken. And she conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the very time God had foretold. Abraham called the name of his son, whom Sarah had borne him, Isaac. And he circumcised him on the eighth day, as God had commanded him, when he was very old. Now Abraham was old when Isaac was born. And Sarah said, "God has made laughter for me; whoever hears of this will laugh with me." And again she said, "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age." And the child grew and was weaned, and Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned. And when Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with her son Isaac, she said to Abraham, "Cast out this maidservant and her son, for the son of this maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac." This matter was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son. But God said to him, "Do not let it be displeasing in your sight because of the boy and because of your maidservant. Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, for in Isaac your seed shall be called. Yet I will also make a nation of the son of the maidservant, because he is your seed." So Abraham rose early in the morning, and took bread and a skin of water, and put them on Hagar's shoulder, and gave her the boy, and sent her away. And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. And when the water in the skin was used up, she cast the boy under one of the shrubs that were there, and went and sat down across from him, about as far as a bowshot away. And she said, "Let me not see the death of the boy." And

sitting opposite, she lifted up her voice and wept. And God heard the voice of the boy. And the angel of the Lord called to Hagar out of heaven and said, "What ails you, Hagar? Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is. Arise, lift up the boy and hold him by the hand, for I will make him a great nation." Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water, and gave the boy a drink, and God was with him as he grew up. And he became an archer and lived in the wilderness of Paran. And his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
