And at that time Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, spoke to Abraham, saying, "God is with you in all that you do. Now therefore swear to me by God that you will not deal falsely with me, or with my son, or with my posterity; but according to the kindness that I have shown you, you shall deal with me and with the land where you have dwelt." And Abraham said, "I will swear." Then Abraham rebuked Abimelech concerning a well of water which Abimelech's servants had seized. And Abimelech said, "I do not know who has done this; you did not tell me, and I did not hear of it until today." So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two of them made a covenant. And Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs from the flock. And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What is the meaning of these seven ewe lambs which you have set apart by themselves?" He said, "You shall take these seven ewe lambs from my hand, that they may be my witness that I dug this well." Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both of them swore an oath, and they made a covenant at the well of the oath. So Abimelech and Phicol, the commander of his army, arose and returned to the land of the Philistines. Then Abraham planted a grove in Beersheba, and called there on the name of the everlasting God, and dwelt as a sojourner in the land

Genesis

These things happened in the land of the Philistines for many days. Chapter 22.
After these things were done, God tested Abraham and said to him: "Abraham, Abraham." He answered: "Here I am." He said to him: "Take your only-begotten son Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of vision, and there you shall offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will show you." So Abraham rose up in the night, saddled his donkey, taking with him two young men and his son Isaac. When he had cut wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place which God had told him. On the third day, lifting up his eyes, he saw the place afar off. And he said to his young men: "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over yonder, and after we have worshipped we will return to you." He took the wood for the burnt offering and laid it upon his son Isaac; and he himself carried fire and a sword. As they went on together, Isaac said to his father: "My father." And he answered: "What is it, son?" He said: "Behold the fire and the wood; where is the victim for the burnt offering?" Abraham said: "God will provide himself a victim for the burnt offering, my son." So they went on together and came to the place which God had shown him. There he built an altar, and laid the wood upon it, and bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood. He stretched out his hand and took the sword to sacrifice his son. But an angel of the Lord called to him from heaven saying: "Abraham, Abraham." He answered: "Here I am." He said to him: "Do not lay your hand upon the boy, and do not do anything to him; for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only-begotten son for my sake." Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw behind him a ram caught among the thorns by its horns. He took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. And he called the name of that place: "The Lord will see."

Therefore it is said to this day: "On the mountain the Lord will see." The angel of the Lord called to Abraham a second time from heaven saying: "By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and have not withheld your only-begotten son for my sake, I will bless you and multiply your descendants like the stars of heaven and like the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will possess the gates of their enemies, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice." Abraham returned to his young men, and they went together to Beersheba, and he dwelt there. After these things it was told Abraham that Milcah had also borne children to his brother Nahor: Huz the firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemuel the father of Aram, and Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel, from whom Rebecca was born. These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother. And his concubine, named Reumah, bore also Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah.

Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years, and she died in the city of Arba, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Chapter 23. Abraham came to mourn for her and to weep. When he had risen from the funeral rites, he spoke to the children of Heth, saying: "I am a stranger and a sojourner among you; give me a burying place with you, that I may bury my dead." The children of Heth answered him, saying: "Hear us, my lord: you are a mighty prince among us; bury your dead in the choicest of our sepulchres; none of us will refuse you his tomb, that you may bury your dead." Abraham rose up and bowed to the people of the land, to the children of Heth. And he said to them: "If it pleases you that I should bury my dead, hear me, and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar, that he may give me the cave of Machpelah which he owns, at the end of his field; for the full price let him give it to me."

Genesis.

"Is she your daughter?" She answered: "She is the daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor, whom Milcah bore to him." So I put the earrings on her face and the bracelets on her hands, and I bowed and worshipped the Lord. And I blessed the Lord, the God of my master Abraham, who led me by the right way to take the daughter of my master's brother for his son. And now, if you will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, so that I may turn to the right hand or to the left." Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said: "This thing has come from the Lord; we cannot speak to you bad or good. Behold, Rebekah is before you; take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master's son, as the Lord has spoken." When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed himself to the earth before the Lord. And the servant brought out jewelry of silver and gold and garments and gave them to Rebekah; he also gave precious things to her brother and to her mother. Then they ate and drank, he and the men who were with him, and stayed the night. When they arose in the morning, he said: "Send me away to my master." Her brother and her mother said: "Let the young woman remain with us for at least ten days; after that she may go." But he said to them: "Do not delay me, for the Lord has prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master." And they said: "We will call the young woman and ask her." And they called Rebekah and said to her: "Will you go with this man?" And she said: "I will go." So they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse, and Abraham's servant and his men. And they blessed Rebekah and said to her: "You are our sister; may you become thousands of ten thousands, and may your offspring possess the gate of those who hate him." Then Rebekah and her young women arose, and they rode on the camels and followed the man. The servant took Rebekah and went his way.

Now Isaac had come from the way of the well called "The Living One Who Sees Me," for he lived in the land of the Negev. And Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening. And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, there were camels coming. And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel and said to the servant, "Who is that man, walking in the field to meet us?" The servant said, "It is my master." So she took her veil and covered herself. And the servant told Isaac all the things that he had done. Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death. Chapter 25.

Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah. She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Enoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah. Abraham gave all he had to Isaac. But to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still living he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the east country. These are the days of the years of Abraham's life, 175 years. Abraham breathed his last and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people. Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, east of Mamre, the field that Abraham purchased from the Hittites. There Abraham was buried, with Sarah his wife. After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac lived near the well called "The Living One Who Sees Me." These are the generations of Ishmael,

· Genesis ·

The sons of Abraham whom Hagar the Egyptian handmaid of Sarah bore: and these are the names of her sons in their order and generations. The firstborn of Ishmael was Nabajoth: then Kedar and Adbeel and Mibsam and Mishma and Dumah and Massa and Hadar and Tema and Jetur and Naphish and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael, and these are their names by their villages and by their encampments, twelve princes according to their tribes. And the years of the life of Ishmael were one hundred and thirty-seven years: and he gave up the ghost and died and was gathered to his people. He dwelt from Havilah to Shur, which is before Egypt as you go toward Assyria. He died in the presence of all his brothers. These are the generations of Isaac the son of Abraham. Abraham begat Isaac. And Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah to wife, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Mesopotamia, the sister of Laban. And Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren. And the Lord was entreated by him, and Rebekah his wife conceived: but the children struggled together within her; and she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to inquire of the Lord. And the Lord said to her, Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be separated from your body: and one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger. When her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb. The first one to come out was red, all over like a hairy garment; and they called his name Esau. And after that came his brother out, and his hand took hold of Esau's heel; and his name was called Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them. When the boys grew up, Esau became a skilled hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his venison: but

Rebekah loved Jacob. Now Jacob cooked a stew. And when Esau came from the field and he was faint, he said, Feed me, I pray you, with that same red stew; for I am faint. Therefore his name was called Edom. And Jacob said, Sell me this day your birthright. And Esau said, Behold, I am about to die; and what profit shall this birthright be to me? And Jacob said, Swear to me this day; and he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob: and Jacob gave Esau bread and a dish of lentils; and he did eat and drink and rose up and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright. Chapter XXVI.

And there was a famine in the land, beyond the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines, in Gerar. And the Lord appeared to him and said, Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land of which I shall tell you; sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and to your descendants I will give all these lands, fulfilling the oath which I swore to Abraham your father: and I will multiply your descendants as the stars of heaven. And I will give to your descendants all these lands; and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. And Isaac dwelt in Gerar. And the men of the place asked him about his wife; and he said, She is my sister. For he was afraid to say, She is my wife; thinking, lest the men of the place should kill him for Rebekah; because she was beautiful. And when he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out a window and saw, and behold, Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife. And Abimelech called Isaac and said, Behold, she is your wife. Why did you say, She is my sister? And Isaac said to him, Because I thought I would die

. Genesis .

Because of her. And Abimelech said: Why have you done this to us? Someone from the people might have lain with your wife, and you would have brought great guilt upon us. And he commanded all the people, saying: Whoever touches this man's wife shall surely be put to death. And Isaac sowed in that land, and found in the same year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him. And the man grew rich and continued growing richer until he became very wealthy, having possessions of flocks and herds and a great household. The Philistines therefore envied him, and stopped up all the wells which his father's servants had dug in the time of Abraham his father, filling them with earth, so that Abimelech said to Isaac: Depart from us, for you have become much more powerful than we. So Isaac departed and came to the valley of Gerar and dwelt there. And he dug again the wells which had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, and which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham's death, and he called them by the same names by which his father had called them. And they dug in the valley and found living water. But there too the shepherds of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's shepherds, saying: The water is ours. So he called the name of the well Calumny, because of what had happened. Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that one too, and he called it Enmity. Moving on from there, he dug another well, over which they did not quarrel. So he called its name Broad Places, saying: Now the Lord has made room for us and caused us to grow in the land. He went up from there to Beersheba, and the Lord appeared to him that same night, saying: I am the God of Abraham your father. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of my servant Abraham. So he built an altar there and called upon the name of the Lord, and he pitched his tent there, and his servants dug a well. And when Abimelech came to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his friend and Phicol the commander of his army, Isaac said to them: Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have driven me away from you? They answered: We have seen plainly that the Lord is with you, and so we said: Let there be an oath between us, and let us make a covenant with you, that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done you nothing but good, and have sent you away in peace. You are now blessed of the Lord. So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank. And rising early in the morning, they swore an oath to one another, and Isaac sent them away in peace. And on that same day Isaac's servants came and told him about a well they had dug, saying: We have found water. So he called it Abundance, and the name of the city was called Beersheba to this day. When Esau was forty years old, he took as wives Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and these made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah. Chapter 27.

When Isaac was old and his eyes had grown dim so that he could not see, he called Esau his elder son and said to him: My son. And he answered: Here I am. And Isaac said: Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death. Take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out into the field. Hunt game for me, and make me the kind of savory food that I love, and bring it to me to eat, so that my soul may bless you before I die. Now Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to Esau his son. And when Esau went to the field to hunt game and bring it, Rebekah said to her son Jacob: I heard your father say to Esau your brother, Bring me game and make me food

· Genesis ·

"Have you only one blessing, father? I beg you, bless me also." And when he wept with a great cry, Isaac was moved and said to him: "Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above. You shall live by the sword and serve your brother: but the time will come when you shall shake off and break his yoke from your neck." So Esau always hated Jacob for the blessing his father had given him. And he said in his heart: "The days of mourning for my father are coming; and then I will kill my brother Jacob." When Rebecca heard this, she sent for her son Jacob and said to him: "Behold, your brother Esau threatens to kill you. Now therefore, my son, listen to my voice: arise and flee to my brother Laban in Haran. You shall stay with him a few days, until your brother's fury subsides and his anger ceases, and he forgets what you have done to him; afterward I will send for you and bring you back from there. Why should I be deprived of both of you in one day?" Rebecca said to Isaac: "I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of this land, I do not wish to live." Chapter number XXVIII.

Then Isaac called Jacob and blessed him, and commanded him, saying: "Do not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan, but arise and go to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel your mother's father, and take a wife there from the daughters of Laban your mother's brother. And may God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, so that you may become a multitude of peoples; and may he give you the blessing of Abraham, to you and to your descendants, that you may inherit the land of your sojourning, which God promised to your grandfather." So when Isaac had sent Jacob away, he journeyed to Mesopotamia of Syria, to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian, the brother of Rebecca, mother of Jacob and Esau. Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Mesopotamia of Syria to take a wife from there, and that when he blessed him he had commanded him saying: "You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan," and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and had gone to Syria; and also that Esau saw his father did not look favorably on the daughters of Canaan—he went to Ishmael and took as wife, in addition to the wives he already had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham, sister of Nebaioth. Meanwhile Jacob set out from Beersheba and was traveling toward Haran. When he came to a certain place and wished to rest there after sunset, he took some of the stones of the place and put them under his head and lay down to sleep in that place. And he dreamed: he saw a ladder set up on the earth, with its top reaching to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it; and the Lord stood above it and said to him: "I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your descendants, and your descendants shall be like the dust of the earth; you shall spread abroad to the east and to the west and to the north and to the south; and in you and in your descendants shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land; for I will not leave you until I have done all that I have promised you." When Jacob awoke from his sleep, he said: "Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it." And trembling, he said: "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." So Jacob rose early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on top of it. He called the name of that place Bethel, though the city was formerly called Luz. Then Jacob made a vow, saying: "If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me

and Simeon. And she conceived again a third time and bore another son, saying: Now my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons. And therefore she called his name Levi. The fourth time she conceived and bore a son, and said: Now I will praise the Lord. And for this reason she called him Judah. And she left off bearing.
Now Rachel, seeing that she was barren and bore Jacob no children, envied her sister, and said to her husband: Give me children, otherwise I shall die. Jacob was angry and answered her: Am I in God's place, who has deprived you of the fruit of your womb? She said: I have my handmaid Bilhah; go in to her, that she may bear upon my knees, and I may have children by her also. And she gave him Bilhah as a wife. Jacob went in to her, and she conceived and bore a son. And Rachel said: God has judged me, and has also heard my voice, and has given me a son. Therefore she called his name Dan. And Bilhah conceived again and bore another son, for whom Rachel said: God has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed. And she called him Naphtali. Leah perceiving that she had left off bearing, gave her handmaid Zilpah to her husband. When Zilpah had conceived and borne a son, she said: Happily! And therefore she called his name Gad. Zilpah bore another son, and Leah said: This is for my happiness. For women will call me blessed. Therefore she called him Asher. And Reuben went out in the time of the wheat harvest into the field, and found mandrakes, which he brought to his mother Leah. And Rachel said: Give me part of your son's mandrakes. She answered: Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband from me, unless you also take my son's mandrakes? Rachel said: He shall sleep with you tonight for your son's mandrakes. When Jacob returned in the evening from the field, Leah went out to meet him and said:
You shall come in to me, because I have hired you for my son's mandrakes. And he slept with her that night, and God heard her prayers. And she conceived and bore a fifth son, saying: God has given me my reward, because I gave my handmaid to my husband. And she called his name Issachar. Leah conceived again and bore a sixth son, and said: God has endowed me with a good dowry; now also my husband will dwell with me, because I have borne him six sons. And she called his name Zebulun. After that she bore a daughter, and called her Dinah. And God remembered Rachel, and heard her, and opened her womb. And she conceived and bore a son, saying: God has taken away my reproach. And she called his name Joseph, saying: The Lord shall add another son to me. After Joseph was born, Jacob said to his father-in-law: Let me return to my country and to my land. Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, that I may go. You know the service which I have done for you. Laban said to him: Let me find favor in your sight; I have learned by experience that God has blessed me for your sake. Appoint your wages, and I will give them. But he answered: You know how I have served you, and how great your possessions have become in my hands. You had little before I came to you, and now you have become rich; and the Lord has blessed you at my coming. But now, when shall I provide for my own household? And Laban said: What shall I give you? And Jacob said: Nothing; but if you will do what I ask, I will feed and keep your flocks again. Go through all your flocks, and separate all the speckled and spotted animals, and all the brown ones among the lambs, and the spotted and speckled among the goats; and such shall be my wages. And my honesty will answer for me when the time of the agreement comes

· Genesis ·

come before you: and everything that is not speckled and spotted and mixed, both among the sheep and the goats, shall be counted as stolen by me. Laban said: I am pleased with what you ask. And he separated that same day the she-goats and sheep and he-goats and rams, the speckled and spotted ones. And he delivered the entire flock of one color, that is, of white and black fleece, into the hands of his sons: and put a distance of three days' journey between himself and his son-in-law, who fed the rest of the flocks. Then Jacob took rods of green poplar, and of almond and plane trees, and partly peeled the bark off them. So in the places where the bark was stripped off, whiteness appeared: but the parts that were whole remained green, and thus the rods were of two colors. And he put these rods in the troughs where the water was poured out: that when the flocks came to drink, they might have the rods before their eyes and conceive in the sight of them. And so it came to pass that in the very heat of coition, the sheep beheld the rods and brought forth spotted and speckled and of divers colors. And Jacob separated the flock, and put the rods in the troughs before the eyes of the rams. And all the white and black belonged to Laban: and the rest were Jacob's, the flocks being separated from one another. So when the first early sheep were conceiving, Jacob put the rods in the troughs of water before the eyes of the rams and ewes, that they might conceive while looking at them: but when the later ones were conceiving, he did not put them. And those that were late became Laban's, and those of the first time Jacob's. And the man was enriched exceedingly, and had many flocks, maidservants and menservants, camels and asses. Chapter XXXI.

And when Jacob heard the words of Laban's sons saying these things, he took everything that was his father-in-law's and all his wealth and departed secretly, having turned away

the face of Laban, that he was not toward him as yesterday and the day before: the Lord especially having said to him: Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred: and he sent and called Rachel and Leah into the field where he was feeding the flocks, and said to them: I see the face of your father, that it is not toward me as yesterday and the day before. But the God of my father has been with me: and you yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength. And your father has deceived me and changed my wages ten times: and yet God has not allowed him to hurt me. When he said: The speckled shall be your wages, all the flocks brought forth speckled: but when he said: You shall take all the white ones for your wages, all the flocks brought forth white. And God has taken your father's wealth and given it to me. After the time of conception came, I lifted up my eyes and saw in a dream the males ascending the females, speckled and spotted and of divers colors. And the angel of God said to me in the dream: Jacob. And I answered: Here I am. And he said: Lift up your eyes and see that all the males ascending the females are speckled, spotted and of divers colors: for I have seen all that Laban has done to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a stone, and where you made a vow to me. Now therefore arise and depart from this land, returning to the land of your birth. And Rachel and Leah answered: Have we anything left among the goods and inheritance of our father's house? Has he not counted us as strangers and sold us, and eaten up our money? But God has taken our father's riches and given them to us and to our children. Therefore do all that God has commanded you. Then Jacob rose up and having set his children and wives upon camels, he departed, taking all his substance and his flocks.

. Genesis .

And whatever he had acquired in Mesopotamia, as he went to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan. For Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel had stolen the idols of her father. And Jacob had deceived Laban, his father-in-law, that he might not tell him that he was fleeing. And when he had departed, he and all that was his, and having crossed the river he made his way toward Mount Gilead; it was told Laban on the third day that Jacob had fled. And he took his brethren with him and pursued him for seven days, and overtook him in Mount Gilead. And God appeared to him in a dream by night, saying: Take heed that you speak not anything harshly against Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent in the mountain; and when Laban with his brethren had followed him there, he pitched his tent in the same mount of Gilead. And he said to Jacob: What have you done, that you have stolen away without my knowledge, and carried off my daughters as captives taken with the sword? Why did you flee away secretly, and not tell me, that I might have brought you on your way with joy and with songs, with timbrel and with harp? You did not even allow me to kiss my sons and daughters. You have done foolishly. And now indeed my hand could harm you: but the God of your father spoke to me yesterday, saying, Take care you speak not to Jacob anything that is harsh. You longed intensely to go to your father's house; but why have you stolen my gods? Jacob answered: I left without telling you because I was afraid you would take your daughters from me by force. As for your gods, with whomever you find them, let him be put to death before our brethren; search, and take whatever of yours is with me. And he did not know that Rachel had taken the idols. So Laban went into Jacob's tent, and into Leah's tent, and into the tent of both the maidservants, and found nothing. Then when he entered Rachel's tent, she hastily hid the idols under the camel's furniture and sat upon them.

And when he had searched and found nothing, she said: Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, for it is with me after the manner of women. So his search was in vain. But Jacob, being angry, said: What is my trespass? What is my sin, that you have so hotly pursued after me? Whereas you have searched through all my goods, what have you found of all your household goods? Set it here before my brethren and your brethren, that they may judge between us both. These twenty years I have been with you; your ewes and your she-goats have not cast their young, and the rams of your flock I have not eaten. That which was torn of beasts I brought not to you; I bore the loss of it myself. You required it of my hand, whether stolen by day or stolen by night. Thus I was; in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from my eyes. Thus have I been twenty years in your house; I served you fourteen years for your two daughters, and six years for your flock, and you have changed my wages ten times. Unless the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had been with me, surely you would have sent me away now empty. God has seen my affliction and the labor of my hands, and rebuked you last night. And Laban answered and said to Jacob: These daughters are my daughters, and these children are my children, and these flocks are my flocks, and all that you see is mine: and what can I do this day to these my daughters, or to their children which they have borne? Come therefore, let us make a covenant, I and you; and let it be for a witness between me and you. And Jacob took a stone, and set it up as a pillar. And Jacob said to his brethren: Gather stones. And they took stones and made a heap, and they ate there upon the heap. And Laban called it Jegarsahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed; each according to the proper tongue of his language. And Laban said: This heap is a witness between me and you this day. Therefore was the name of it called Galeed; that is, the heap of witness. And Laban added: May the Lord watch between us when

Genesis.

if I have departed from you: if you afflict my daughters, or if you bring in other wives over them. None of our words has witness except God, who looks upon all things. And he said again to Jacob: This mound and this stone which I have erected shall be witness between me and you. This mound, I say, and this stone shall be a testimony: if I shall pass it going toward you to do evil, and if you shall pass it with evil intent toward me. The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor judge between us, the God of their father. So Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac, and having offered sacrifice on the mountain, he called his brethren to eat bread. And after they had eaten, they lodged there. But Laban rose up in the night, and kissed his sons and daughters, and blessed them, and returned to his place.
Jacob went on his journey, Chapter XXXII, and the angels of God met him. And when he saw them, he said: These are the camps of God. And he called the name of that place Mahanaim, that is, Camps. And he sent messengers before him to his brother Esau, in the land of Seir, in the country of Edom. And he commanded them, saying: Thus shall you speak to my lord Esau: Thus says your brother Jacob: I have sojourned with Laban, and have been with him until now. I have oxen, and asses, and sheep, and menservants, and womenservants: and I send now to tell my lord, that I may find grace in your sight. And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying: We came to your brother Esau, and behold he comes with speed to meet you with four hundred men. Then Jacob was greatly afraid; and being struck with fear, he divided the people that was with him, and the flocks, and the sheep, and the oxen, and the camels, into two companies. Saying: If Esau come to one company and destroy it, the other company that is left shall escape. And Jacob said: O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac: O Lord, who said to me: Return to your land and to the place of your birth, and I will do good to you: I am less than all your mercies, and your truth which you have fulfilled to your servant. With my staff I passed over this Jordan: and now I return with two companies. Deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am greatly afraid of him; lest he come and kill the mother with the children. You said that you would do good to me, and multiply my seed like the sand of the sea, which cannot be numbered for multitude. And when he had slept there that night, he set apart, of the things he had, gifts for his brother Esau: two hundred she-goats, twenty he-goats, two hundred ewes, and twenty rams, thirty milch camels with their colts, forty kine, and twenty bulls, twenty she-asses, and ten of their foals. And he sent them by the hands of his servants, every drove by itself, and he said to his servants: Go before me, and let there be a space between drove and drove. And he commanded the first, saying: If you shall meet my brother Esau, and he shall ask you: Whose are you? or whither do you go? or whose are these before you? you shall answer: They are your servant Jacob's gifts, sent to my lord Esau; and he also follows behind us. In like manner he commanded the second and the third, and all that followed the droves, saying: Speak the same words to Esau when you find him. And you shall add: Your servant Jacob himself also follows behind us. For he said: I will appease him with the gifts that go before, and afterwards I will see him; perhaps he will be gracious to me. So the gifts went before him, but he himself lodged that night in the camp. And rising early, he took his two wives, and his two handmaids, with his eleven sons, and passed over the ford of Jabbok. And when all things were brought over that belonged to him, he remained alone: and behold a man wrestled with him until morning. And when he saw that

· Genesis ·

that he could not overcome him, he touched the hollow of his thigh, and it shrank. And he said to him, "Let me go, for dawn is breaking." He answered, "I will not let you go unless you bless me." He said, "What is your name?" He answered, "Jacob." And he said, "You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel: for if you have been strong against God, how much more shall you prevail against men?" Jacob asked him, "Tell me your name." He answered, "Why do you ask my name?" And he blessed him there. And Jacob called the name of that place Peniel, saying, "I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved." And the sun rose upon him after he passed Peniel, and he limped on his hip. Therefore the children of Israel do not eat the sinew that shrank, which is in the hollow of the thigh, to this day, because he touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh in the sinew that shrank.

Chapter 33.
And Jacob lifted up his eyes and saw Esau coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two handmaids, and set each handmaid and her children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph last. And he himself went on ahead and bowed to the ground seven times until he came near to his brother. Then Esau ran to meet him and embraced him, and fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept. And lifting up his eyes, Esau saw the women and the children and said, "Who are these with you?" He answered, "They are the children God has given to your servant." And the handmaids and their children came near and bowed. Leah also and her children came near and bowed; and last, Joseph and Rachel came near and bowed. And Esau said, "What did you mean by all the droves I met?" He answered, "That I might find grace in the sight of my lord." But Esau said, "I have enough, my brother; keep what you have for yourself." Jacob said, "No, I pray you: if I have found favor in your sight, accept my gift from my hand, for truly to see your face is like seeing the face of God, and you have received me graciously. Accept my blessing that I have brought you, for God has been generous to me." And when Esau was persuaded, he accepted it. And he said, "Let us journey together, and I will go alongside you." Jacob said, "My lord knows that the children are tender, and I have flocks and herds with young: if they are driven hard even one day, all the flock will die. Let my lord go on before his servant, and I will follow slowly, at the pace that the livestock and the children can bear, until I come to my lord in Seir." Esau said, "At least let some of my men stay with you." He answered, "There is no need; it is enough that I find grace in your sight, my lord." So Esau turned back that day on his way to Seir. And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built himself a house there and made shelters for his livestock; therefore the place is called Succoth, that is, Tabernacles. And Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria, and camped before the city. And he bought the piece of land where he had pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs, and erected an altar there, calling upon the most mighty God of Israel.

Chapter 34.
And Dinah the daughter of Leah went out to see the women of that region. And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of that land, saw her, he seized her and lay with her, violating the young woman. And his soul was bound

Genesis.

And his soul clung to her and he comforted her with kind words. And going to Hamor his father, he said: Get me this girl for a wife. And when Jacob had heard this, his sons being absent and employed in feeding the cattle, he held his peace until they came back. And when Hamor the father of Shechem was going out to speak to Jacob, behold his sons came from the field. And when they heard it, they were very much grieved, because he had done a foul thing in Israel, and violated the daughter of Jacob, and had done what ought not to be done. And Hamor spoke to them, saying: The soul of my son Shechem has a longing for your daughter. Give her to him for a wife, and let us make marriages one with another. Give us your daughters, and take our daughters: and dwell with us. The land is at your command, trade in it and possess it. Moreover Shechem said to her father and to her brothers: Let me find favor in your sight, and whatsoever you shall appoint I will give. Raise the dowry, and ask gifts, and I will freely give what you shall demand: only give me this maiden for a wife. The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father deceitfully, being enraged at the deflowering of their sister. We cannot do what you ask, nor give our sister to one that is uncircumcised, for that is unlawful and abominable with us. But in this we will consent to you: if you will be like us, and all the males among you be circumcised, then will we give and take your daughters and ours, and we will dwell with you, and will be one people. But if you will not be circumcised, we will take our daughter and depart. Their offer pleased Hamor and Shechem his son: and the young man delayed not to fulfil what was asked, for he loved the girl exceedingly, and he was the most honorable of all his household. And going in to the gate of the city, they spoke to the people of the city.

These men are peaceable, and are willing to dwell with us. Let them trade in the land and travel through it, which is wide enough for them. We will take their daughters for wives, and we will give them ours. Only on this condition will men consent to dwell with us, to be one people: that all our males be circumcised, as they are. And their cattle and substance and all they possess shall be ours. Only let us consent, and they will dwell with us. And all agreed that every male should be circumcised. And on the third day, when the pain of the wound was greatest, two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, the brothers of Dinah, taking their swords, entered boldly into the city and slew all the males. And they killed Hamor and Shechem, and took Dinah out of the house of Shechem, and went away. And the other sons of Jacob coming upon the slain plundered the city in revenge of the rape: their sheep and herds and asses, wasting all they had in the houses and in the fields. And their children and wives they took captive. After these things were boldly done, Jacob said to Simeon and Levi: You have troubled me, and made me hateful to the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the inhabitants of this land. We are few, and they gathering themselves together will strike me, and I shall be destroyed, I and my household. They answered: Should they treat our sister as a harlot? Chapter XXXV: And God said to Jacob: Arise, and go up to Bethel, and dwell there, and make an altar there to God, who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau. And Jacob having called together all his household said: Put away the strange gods that are among you, and be cleansed, and change your garments. Arise, and let us go up to Bethel, that we may make there an altar to God, who heard me in the day of my affliction, and was my companion in the way. And they gave him all the strange gods they had, and their earrings.

. Genesis .

which were in their ears. But he buried them under the terebinth tree which is near the city of Shechem. And when they had departed, a terror from God came upon all the cities round about, so that they durst not pursue after the sons of Jacob. So Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, also called Bethel, he and all the people with him. And he built there an altar, and called the place the house of God: for there God appeared to him when he fled from his brother. And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel under an oak: and the name of it was called The oak of weeping. And God appeared again to Jacob, after he returned out of Mesopotamia of Syria, and came to Bethel: and blessed him. And God said to him: Your name shall not be called Jacob anymore, but Israel shall be your name. And he called his name Israel. And God said to him: I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of you, and kings shall come out of your loins. And the land which I gave Abraham and Isaac, to you I will give it, and to your seed after you will I give the land. And God went up from him in the place where he talked with him. And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he talked with him, a pillar of stone: and he poured a drink offering on it, and he poured oil on it: and Jacob called the name of the place where God spoke with him Bethel. And they journeyed from Bethel; and there was but a little way to come to Ephrath: and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labor. And it came to pass when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said to her: Fear not; for this son also shall you have. And it came to pass, as her soul was departing — for she died — that she called his name Benoni: that is, son of my sorrow. But his father called him Benjamin: that is, son of the right hand. And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. And Jacob set a pillar upon her grave: that is the pillar of Rachel's grave to this day. And Israel journeyed, and spread his tent beyond the tower of Eder.

And it came to pass, when Israel dwelt in that land, that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Israel heard it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve. The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Simeon, and Levi, and Judah, and Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid: Dan and Naphtali. And the sons of Zilpah, Leah's handmaid: Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria. And Jacob came to Isaac his father at Mamre, unto the city of Arbah, which is Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac sojourned. And the days of Isaac were a hundred and eighty years. And Isaac gave up the ghost, and died, and was gathered unto his people, being old and full of days: and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him. Chapter 36.

Now these are the generations of Esau, who is Edom. Esau took his wives of the daughters of Canaan: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Aholibamah the daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon the Hivite, and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebajoth. And Adah bore to Esau Eliphaz. And Basemath bore Reuel. And Aholibamah bore Jeush, and Jaalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau which were born to him in the land of Canaan. And Esau took his wives, and his sons, and his daughters, and all the persons of his house, and his cattle, and all his beasts, and all his substance which he had got in the land of Canaan, and went into a country away from his brother Jacob. For their riches were more than they could bear together, and the land of their sojourning could not bear them because of their cattle. Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom. And these are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in mount Seir: these are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, and Reuel the son of Basemath the wife of Esau. And the sons of Eliphaz were: Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Gatam:

Genesis

while bundles were in the field, and behold, my bundle arose and stood upright, and your bundles stood round about and bowed down to my bundle. His brothers said to him: Are you to be our king, or shall we be subject to your rule? Therefore this was the source of his dreams and words, ministering envy and hatred. He saw another dream, and told his brothers: I saw in a dream the sun and moon and eleven stars bowing down to me. When he had told this to his father and brothers, his father rebuked him and said: What is this dream you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers come to bow down to you on the earth? His brothers therefore envied him, but his father considered the matter quietly. When his brothers were feeding their father's flock in Shechem, Israel said to him: Your brothers are feeding the flock in Shechem; come, I will send you to them. He answered: I am ready. He said: Go and see whether all is well with your brothers and the flocks, and bring me word. He was sent from the valley of Hebron and came to Shechem. A man found him wandering in the field and asked him what he was looking for. He said: I am looking for my brothers. Tell me where they are feeding their flocks. The man said to him: They have moved on from this place; I heard them say, Let us go to Dothan. So Joseph went after his brothers and found them in Dothan. They saw him from a distance, and before he came near they plotted to kill him. They said to one another: Here comes this dreamer. Come, let us kill him and throw him into one of the old cisterns; then we can say that a wild beast has devoured him, and we shall see what becomes of his dreams. But Reuben heard this and tried to rescue him from their hands, saying: Let us not take his life or shed his blood; throw him into this old cistern in the wilderness, but do not lay hands on him. He said this intending to rescue him from their hands and restore him to his father. So when Joseph reached his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the long robe with sleeves that he wore, and they took him and threw him into the cistern. The cistern was empty; there was no water in it. Then they sat down to eat, and looking up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry these goods down to Egypt. Judah said to his brothers: What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh. His brothers listened to him. When the Midianite merchants passed by, they drew Joseph up out of the cistern and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They took Joseph to Egypt. When Reuben returned to the cistern and did not find Joseph there, he tore his clothes and returned to his brothers and said: The boy is gone; and I, where can I go? Then they took Joseph's robe, killed a goat and dipped the robe in its blood, and sent the long robe back to his father, saying: This we have found; see now whether it is your son's robe or not. He recognized it and said: It is my son's robe. A fierce animal has devoured him; Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces. Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days. All his sons and daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted, saying: I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning. And his father wept for him. The Midianites meanwhile sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.

and she told him the same story, saying: The Hebrew servant whom you brought to us came in to me to mock me; but when I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled outside. When his master heard the words of his wife, saying, This is what your servant did to me, he was furious. He took Joseph and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were confined, and he was there in the prison. But the Lord was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison. The keeper of the prison committed to Joseph's care all the prisoners who were in the prison, and whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph's care, because the Lord was with him. And whatever he did, the Lord made it succeed.

After these things had happened, it came to pass that the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker offended their lord the king of Egypt. Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker, and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was confined. The captain of the guard assigned Joseph to them, and he attended to them. After they had been in custody for some time, both of them, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were confined in the prison, had a dream on the same night, each his own dream with its own meaning. When Joseph came to them in the morning and saw them, they were troubled. So he asked Pharaoh's officers who were in custody with him, saying: Why are your faces downcast today? They said to him: We have each had a dream, and there is no one to interpret it. Joseph said to them: Do not interpretations belong to God? Tell me your dreams. So the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream: In my dream there was a vine before me, and on the vine there were three branches; as soon as it budded, its blossoms shot forth and the clusters ripened into grapes. Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand. Joseph said to him: This is its interpretation

of the dream. "Three branches are three days yet remaining, after which Pharaoh will remember your service and restore you to your former rank, and will give him the cup according to your office, as you were accustomed to do before. Joseph answered and said, "This is the interpretation: the three baskets are three days. On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants, and he remembered the chief cupbearer and the chief baker among his servants, restoring the one to his position so that he handed the cup to Pharaoh, and hanging the other, as Joseph had interpreted. Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.

is one. What God is about to do he has shown to Pharaoh. Seven beautiful cows and seven full, plump ears of grain are seven years of plenty; they share the same meaning in the dream. And the seven thin and gaunt cows that came up after them, and the seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, are seven years of famine that are to come, which shall be fulfilled in this order. This pleased Pharaoh and all his servants, and he said to them: Can we find such a man, one in whom the spirit of God dwells? Then he said to Joseph: Since God has shown you all this, is there anyone as wise and understanding as you? And Joseph gathered all the money in exchange for grain and brought it into the royal treasury. When the buyers had run out of money, all Egypt came to Joseph saying: Give us bread. Why should we die before you? Our money is gone. And he answered them: Bring your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for them, if you have no money. And when they brought their livestock, he gave them food in exchange for horses and sheep and cattle and asses, and sustained them that year in exchange for all their livestock. And they came to him in the second year and said to him: We will not hide from our lord that our money is spent and our livestock are gone too, as you well know, and we have nothing left but our bodies and our land. Why should we die before your eyes? Buy us and our land in exchange for food, and we and our land will be servants of Pharaoh; give us seed, lest the land become desolate without a farmer. So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt, each one selling his possessions because the famine was so severe. And he subjected it to Pharaoh, and all its people from one end of Egypt's borders to the other, except the land of the priests, which had been given to them by the king, and to whom fixed rations were provided from the public granaries; and therefore they were not compelled to sell their possessions. Then Joseph said to them: Now you know that you and your land belong to Pharaoh; take seed and sow the fields, so that you may have crops. A fifth part you shall give to the king; the remaining four parts I allow you for seed and for food for your families and children. They answered: Our life is in your hand; let only our lord look upon us, and we will gladly serve the king. And from that time until this present day throughout all the land of Egypt a fifth part is paid to the kings, and it has become as a law, except for the land of the priests, which was free from this obligation. So Israel dwelt in Egypt, that is in the land of Goshen, and possessed it; and he grew and multiplied greatly, and lived there seventeen years. And all the days of his life were one hundred and forty-seven years. When he saw that the day of his death was approaching, he called his son Joseph and said to him: If I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh, and show me kindness and faithfulness; do not bury me in Egypt, but let me lie with my fathers; carry me out of this land and bury me in their burial place. Joseph answered: I will do what you have asked. And he said: Swear it to me. And when he had sworn, Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed.

But he, stretching forth his right hand, put it upon the head of Ephraim, the younger brother, and his left hand upon the head of Manasseh who was the elder, crossing his hands. And he blessed Joseph's son and said: God, in whose sight my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, God who has fed me from my youth until this day, the angel who has delivered me from all evils, bless these boys; and let my name be called upon them, and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth. But Joseph seeing that his father had put his right hand upon the head of Ephraim was displeased; and taking his father's hand, he tried to remove it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head. saying: In you shall Israel be blessed, and it shall be said: God do to you as to Ephraim and as to Manasseh. And he set Ephraim before Manasseh. And he said to his son Joseph: Behold, I die, and God will be with you, and will bring you back to the land of your fathers. These things lie within. And having finished the commandments with which he instructed his sons, he gathered his feet into the bed and expired, and was gathered to his people. Chapter 50.

When Joseph saw this, he fell upon his father's face and wept over him and kissed him, and he commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father, and the physicians embalmed Israel. Forty days were fulfilled for him, for so are fulfilled the days of embalming. And Egypt mourned for him seventy days. And when the days of mourning were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying: If now I have found favor in your sight, speak, I pray you, in the ears of Pharaoh, saying: My father made me swear, saying: Behold, I am dying; in my tomb which I have dug for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me. Now therefore let me go up and bury my father, and I will return. And Pharaoh said: Go up and bury your father, as he made you swear. And Joseph went up to bury his father, and with him went all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, and all the house of Joseph, and his brothers, and his father's house; only their little ones, and their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen. And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen, and it was a very great company. And they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, and there they mourned with a great and very solemn lamentation; and he made a mourning for his father seven days. And when the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said: This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians; wherefore the name of it was called Abel Mizraim, which is beyond the Jordan. And his sons did to him as he had commanded them; for his sons carried him into the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field for a burial possession from Ephron the Hittite, before Mamre. And Joseph returned into Egypt, he and his brothers and all

In his company, with the father buried. After his death, his brothers continued to speak with one another, fearing that perhaps he remembered the wrong they had done him, and would repay them all the evil they had committed: that he had commanded it. Your father commanded us before he died to say these words to him. We beg you to forget the wickedness, the sin and malice that your brothers committed against you. We also ask that you forgive the iniquity of the servants of your father's God. When Joseph heard this, he wept. His brothers came to him and fell down before him, saying: We are your servants. He answered them: Do not be afraid. Can we resist the will of God? You intended evil against me, but God turned it to good, so that He might exalt me as you now see, and save many people. Do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones. And he comforted them and spoke kindly and gently to them. And he lived in Egypt with all his father's household. He lived one hundred and ten years, and saw Ephraim's children to the third generation. The children of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were also born on Joseph's knees. When he had spoken to his brothers, he said: After my death, God will visit you and lead you out of this land to the land he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And when he had charged them and said: God will visit you, carry my bones with you from this place. He died, having lived one hundred and ten years of his life, and being embalmed was laid in a coffin in Egypt. Here begins the book called Hellesinoths, which we call Exodus.

These are the names of the children of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob. Each came with his household. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin; Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. All the souls that came from the loins of Jacob were seventy in number. But Joseph was already in Egypt. After he died, and all his brothers, and all that generation, the children of Israel were fruitful and increased abundantly, and multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them. Then a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph. And he said to his people: Look, the people of the children of Israel are many and mightier than we are. Come, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply further, and if war should come, they might join our enemies and fight against us, and then leave the land. So they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. And they built for Pharaoh store cities: Pithom and Ramesses. But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread, so that the Egyptians came to dread the children of Israel. And the Egyptians made the children of Israel serve with harsh labor, and made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in mortar and brick, and in all manner of labor in the field, and in all their work they compelled them with rigor. Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, of whom one was named Shiphrah and the other Puah, saying: When you serve as midwives to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him; but if it is a daughter, she shall live. But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded, but let the boys live. So the king called for the midwives and said: Why have you done this, and let the boys live? They answered: Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women; for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them. Therefore God dealt well with the midwives, and the people multiplied and grew very strong.

Exodus

And because the midwives feared God, he built them houses. Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying: Every male child that is born, cast into the river; every female child, keep alive.

After this, a man of the house of Levi went and took a wife of his own tribe; and she conceived and bore a son. Seeing that he was a beautiful child, she hid him for three months. And when she could no longer conceal him, she took a basket made of rushes and coated it with bitumen and pitch; and placing the little child within it, she laid it in the reeds along the bank of the river. And his sister stood at a distance to see what would happen. Then the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe in the river, and her maidens walked along the riverside. When she saw the basket among the reeds, she sent one of her maids to fetch it; and when it was opened, she saw the child within, crying. She took pity on it and said: This is one of the Hebrew children. Then the child's sister said to Pharaoh's daughter: Shall I go and call a Hebrew woman to nurse the child for you? She replied: Go. The girl went and called the child's mother. Pharaoh's daughter said to her: Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay you. So the woman took the child and nursed him; and when he was grown, she delivered him to Pharaoh's daughter, who adopted him as her own son, calling him Moses, saying: Because I drew him out of the water. In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his own people and saw their hardships; and he saw an Egyptian striking one of his Hebrew brothers. Looking this way and that, and seeing no one about, he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. The next day he went out and saw two Hebrews quarreling; and he said to the one who was in the wrong: Why do you strike your neighbor? He answered: Who made you a prince and judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday? Moses was afraid, and said: Surely the matter has become known. When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, who came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father's flock. But shepherds came and drove them away. Moses stood up and defended them, and watered their flock. When they returned to their father Jethro, he said: Why have you come back so soon today? They answered: An Egyptian delivered us from the shepherds, and moreover he drew water for us and watered the flock. He said: Where is he? Why did you leave the man? Call him, so that he may eat bread. Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses as a wife. She bore him a son, whom he called Gershom, saying: I have been a stranger in a foreign land. She bore another, whom he called Eliezer, saying: The God of my father is my help, and he has delivered me from the hand of Pharaoh. After a long time the king of Egypt died. And the children of Israel groaned under their bondage and cried out; and their cry rose up to God from their labor. And God heard their groanings, and remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And God looked upon the children of Israel, and took notice of them.

Now Moses was tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the desert and came to the mountain of God, to Horeb. And the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from within a bush; and he saw that the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed. Then God said:

Moses said: "I will go and see this great vision, why the bush is not burned." And when the Lord saw that he was going to look, he called to him from the middle of the bush and said: "Moses, Moses." And he answered: "Here I am." And the Lord said: "Do not come closer. Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground." And he said: "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses hid his face, for he did not dare to look at God. And the Lord said to him: "I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of the harshness of those who are over them. And knowing their sorrow, I have come down to free them from the hands of the Egyptians, and to bring them out of that land into a good and spacious land, into a land flowing with milk and honey, to the places of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. The cry of the children of Israel has come to me, and I have seen their affliction with which they are oppressed by the Egyptians. But come, I will send you to Pharaoh, so that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt." And Moses said to God: "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh, and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?" And he said: "I will be with you, and this shall be a sign to you that I have sent you. When you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God upon this mountain." And Moses said to God: "If I go to the children of Israel and say to them: 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?" God said to Moses: "I AM WHO I AM." And he said: "Say this to the children of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'" And God said again to Moses: "Say this to the children of Israel: 'The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations.

Go and gather together the elders of Israel, and say to them: 'The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying: I have visited you and have seen all that has happened to you in Egypt. And I have said that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, to a land flowing with milk and honey.' And they shall listen to your voice. And you shall go, you and the elders of Israel, to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: 'The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has called us. We will go a journey of three days into the desert, to sacrifice to our God.' But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand. So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders which I will do in the midst of them. After that he will let you go. And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that when you go you will not go empty-handed. But every woman shall ask of her neighbor and of her who lives in her house, articles of silver and gold and clothing. You shall put them on your sons and daughters, and so you will plunder Egypt." Chapter 4.

Then Moses answered and said: "But they will not believe me, nor listen to my voice. They will say: 'The Lord has not appeared to you.'" And the Lord said to him: "What is that in your hand?" He replied: "A staff." And the Lord said: "Cast it on the ground." He cast it on the ground and it became a serpent, so that Moses fled from it. And the Lord said: "Stretch out your hand and take it by the tail." He stretched out his hand and took hold of it, and it became a staff again. "So that they may believe that the Lord, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you." And the Lord said to him again: "Put your hand into your bosom." And when he had put it into his bosom, he brought it out and it was leprous like snow. And he said: "Put your hand back into your bosom." He put it back and brought it out again, and it was restored like the rest of his flesh.

After this Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Let my people go, that they may celebrate a feast to me in the wilderness." But he said, "Who is the Lord, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go." Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens." Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers, and they also, the magicians of Egypt, did the same with their enchantments. Every man threw down his rod, and they became serpents. But Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods. And Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said. Then the Lord said to Moses: "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go. Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the water. Stand on the bank of the river to meet him, and take in your hand the rod that was turned to a serpent, and say to him: 'The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you, saying, Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness. But so far you have not listened.'"

And the fish that were in the river died, and the river rotted, and the Egyptians could not drink the water of the river, and there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt. And the magicians of Egypt did the same with their enchantments. And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had commanded. And he turned himself away and went into his house, and he did not care about this matter either. And all the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the river. And seven days were completed after the Lord had struck the river. Chapter 8.
And the Lord spoke to Moses: Go to Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says the Lord: Let my people go that they may sacrifice to me. But if you refuse to let them go, behold I will strike all your borders with frogs. And the river shall bring forth frogs abundantly, which shall go up and come into your house, and into your bedchamber, and upon your bed, and into the houses of your servants, and upon your people, and into your ovens, and into your food: and the frogs shall come up both on you and on your people and on all your servants.

And the Lord said to Moses: Say to Aaron, Stretch out your hand over the rivers, the streams, and the ponds, and bring up frogs upon the land of Egypt. And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. But the magicians also did the same with their enchantments, and they brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt. Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said: Pray to the Lord to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord. And Moses said to Pharaoh: Appoint a time for me, when I shall pray for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs may be driven away from you and from your house and from your servants and from your people, and remain only in the river. And he said: Tomorrow. And Moses replied: According to your word, so that you may know that there is none like the Lord our God: the frogs shall depart from you and from your house and from your servants and from your people; they shall remain only in the river. And Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the Lord concerning the frogs which he had promised Pharaoh. And the Lord did according to the word of Moses: and the frogs died out of the houses, the villages, and the fields. And they gathered them together in great heaps, and the land stank. But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and did not listen to them, as the Lord had commanded. And the Lord said to Moses: Say to Aaron, Stretch out your rod and strike the dust of the earth, and there shall be lice throughout all the land of Egypt. And they did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his rod and struck the dust of the earth, and there came lice on man and on beast. All the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt. And the magicians did likewise

Exodus.

The magicians tried with their enchantments to bring forth lice, but they could not. And there were lice on both men and animals. The magicians said to Pharaoh: This is the finger of God. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had foretold. The Lord said to Moses: Rise up early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh, for he will go out to the water. And you shall say to him: Thus says the Lord. Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. But if you will not let them go, behold, I will send swarms of flies upon you and your servants and your people and your houses, and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of swarms of flies of all kinds, and the land where they dwell. And I will set apart in that day the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, so that you may know that I am the Lord in the midst of the earth. And I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow shall this sign be. And the Lord did so. There came great swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh and into his servants' houses, and into all the land of Egypt; the land was ruined by reason of the swarms of flies. Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said: Go, sacrifice to your God here in the land. But Moses said: It would not be right to do so, for the offerings we make to the Lord our God would be an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice what the Egyptians regard as sacred before their eyes, will they not stone us? We must go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God as he commands us. And Pharaoh said: I will let you go to sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness, only do not go very far away. Pray for me. And Moses said: As soon as I leave you I will pray to the Lord, and the flies shall depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people tomorrow. But let Pharaoh no more deceive us by refusing to let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord. And Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord. And the Lord did as Moses had said, and he removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people. Not one remained. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened once again, and he would not let the people go. Chapter 9.
Then the Lord said to Moses: Go in to Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews. Let my people go, that they may serve me. For if you refuse to let them go and still hold them, behold, the hand of the Lord will fall on your livestock in the field, on the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herds, and the flocks, with a very severe plague. But the Lord will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that nothing shall die of all that belongs to the children of Israel. And the Lord set a time, saying: Tomorrow the Lord will do this thing in the land. And the Lord did this thing the next day, and all the livestock of Egypt died. But of the livestock of the children of Israel not one died. Pharaoh sent to look, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go. And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Take handfuls of soot from the kiln, and let Moses throw it in the air before Pharaoh, and it shall become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and cause boils breaking out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt. So they took soot from the kiln and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses threw it up toward heaven, and it caused boils breaking out in sores on man and beast. And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils were on them and on all the Egyptians. And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not

. Exodus .

The Lord heard them as he had spoken to Moses. And the Lord said to Moses: Rise up early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: Let my people go to sacrifice to me. For this time I will send all my plagues upon your heart and upon your servants and upon your people: that you may know there is no one like me in all the earth.
