But if you cannot solve it, you shall give me thirty linen garments and the same number of changes of clothing. They answered him: Propose your riddle that we may hear it. And he said to them: Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. And they could not for three days solve the riddle. And when the seventh day came, they said to Samson's wife: Coax your husband and persuade him to tell us

Judges.

what the riddle means to you. If you will not do this, we will burn you and your father's house. Was it to rob us that you invited us to the wedding? And she wept before Samson and said: You hate me and do not love me; that is why you will not explain to my people the riddle you proposed. He answered her: I would not tell my own father and mother; must I then tell you? She wept before him the seven days that the feast lasted; and on the seventh day, because she was troublesome to him, he explained it to her. She then told the riddle to her fellow citizens. And they said to him on the seventh day before sunset: What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion? He said to them: If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle. And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men there; he took their garments and gave them to those who had answered the riddle. Then in great anger he went back to his father's house; and his wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.

After some time, when the wheat harvest was approaching, Samson went to visit his wife, bringing a young goat. But when he wanted to go into the inner room to her, her father stopped him, saying: I was sure that you hated her, so I gave her to your companion. But her younger sister is more beautiful than she; let her be your wife instead. Samson said to him: This time I shall be blameless in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm. So he went and caught three hundred foxes, tied them tail to tail, and fastened a torch between each pair of tails. He then set the torches on fire and let the foxes run through the standing grain of the Philistines, so that they ran this way and that through the fields. He burned up not only the standing grain, but also the grain already cut, as well as the vineyards and olive orchards. The Philistines asked: Who did this? They were told: Samson, son-in-law of the Timnite, because his father-in-law took his wife and gave her to his companion. So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father. Samson said to them: Since you did this, I will not stop until I have taken revenge on you. He struck them with a great slaughter, so that they were struck thigh upon hip. Then he went down and dwelt in the cave of the rock of Etam. The Philistines went up and encamped in Judah, spreading out near Lehi, which means jawbone. The men of Judah said: Why have you come up against us? They answered: We have come to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us. Three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave of the rock of Etam and said to Samson: Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? What then is this that you have done to us? He said to them: As they did to me, so I have done to them. They said to him: We have come down to bind you, to hand you over to the Philistines. Samson said to them: Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves. They told him: No, we will only bind you and hand you over to them. So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock. When he came to Lehi, and the Philistines came shouting to meet him, the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him; and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that catches fire, and his bonds melted from his hands. Then he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand, and took it, and with it he killed a thousand men, saying: With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men. When he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone.

Judges

...the jawbone from his hand, and he called the name of that place Ramath-lehi, which is interpreted "the lifting up of the jawbone." And being very thirsty, he cried out to the Lord and said: You have given into the hand of your servant this great deliverance and victory; and now I shall die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised. So the Lord opened a hollow tooth in the jawbone of the donkey, and water came out of it. And when he had drunk it, he refreshed his spirit and recovered his strength. Therefore the name of that place was called "En-hakkore," which is the spring of him that called upon the jawbone, to this day. And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines for twenty years. Chapter XVI.
And Samson went to Gaza and saw there a harlot woman, and he went in to her. And when the Philistines had heard this and it was reported among them that Samson had entered the city, they surrounded him, placing guards at the gate of the city; and they waited all night in silence, so that they might kill him when he came out in the morning. But Samson slept until midnight, and rising up at midnight, he took hold of both the doors of the city gate with their posts, and lifting them up with the bars, he carried them on his shoulders to the top of the mountain which looks toward Hebron. After this he loved a woman who dwelt in the valley of Sorek, and her name was Delilah. And the princes of the Philistines came to her and said: Deceive him and learn from him what his great strength lies in and by what means we can overcome him, so that we may bind and afflict him. If you do this, each of us will give you a thousand and one hundred pieces of silver. Delilah therefore said to Samson: Tell me, I beg you, where your great strength lies, and what you might be bound with so that you could not break free. Samson answered her: If I am bound with seven green cords not yet dried, I will become weak like other men. And the princes of the Philistines brought her seven green cords

...with which she bound him at his sides, with men lying in wait in the inner room. And she cried out to him: The Philistines are upon you, Samson! And he broke the cords as a man would snap a thread of tow touched by the smell of fire; and his strength was not known. And Delilah said to him: Behold, you have mocked me and spoken false things. But now tell me at least with what you may be bound. He answered her: If I am bound with new ropes that were never used, I shall become weak and be like other men. And Delilah again bound him with these, and cried out: The Philistines are upon you, Samson! — with men lying in wait ready in the inner room. And he broke them off his arms like threads. And Delilah said to Samson again: How long will you deceive me and speak false things? Tell me with what you may be bound. He answered: If you weave the seven locks of my head together with a loom pin and fasten them, I shall become weak. And when Delilah had done this, she said to him: The Philistines are upon you, Samson! And rising from sleep, he pulled out the pin with the weaving. And Delilah said to him: How can you say you love me, when your heart is not with me? Three times you have deceived me and would not tell me where your great strength lies. And pressing him daily and giving him no time to rest, she wearied him greatly until his soul was brought almost to death. Then he opened his heart fully to her and told her all: No razor has ever come upon my head, for I am a Nazirite, that is, consecrated to God from my mother's womb. If my head were shaved, my strength would leave me and I would become weak and be like other men. Then she, seeing that he had confessed to her all his heart, sent to the princes of the Philistines and commanded them: Come up once more...

Judges

Now he opened his heart to her. Those who had gone up returned with the money they had promised. But she made him sleep upon her knees and laid his head in her lap. She called for a barber and shaved his seven locks of hair, and began to drive him away and push him from her. For at once his strength left him. And the Philistines said to him: Samson, the enemy is upon you. He woke from sleep and said in his heart: I will go out as before and shake myself free — not knowing that the Lord had departed from him. The Philistines seized him and immediately put out his eyes, and brought him bound in chains to Gaza, and shut him in prison to grind. But his hair began to grow back. And the princes of the Philistines gathered together to offer great sacrifices to their god Dagon and to feast, saying: Our god has delivered our enemy Samson into our hands. And when the people saw him, they praised their god, saying: Our god has delivered our enemy, who destroyed our land and killed so many of us. So feasting and rejoicing, they ordered Samson to be brought out that he might perform before them. He was brought from prison and performed before them, and they made him stand between two pillars. He said to the boy who guided his steps: Let me touch the pillars on which the house rests, so that I may lean against them and rest a little. Now the house was full of men and women, and all the princes of the Philistines were there; and on the roof and galleries about three thousand persons of both sexes were watching Samson perform. He called upon the Lord and said: Lord God, remember me and restore my strength this once, O God, that I may at one stroke take revenge on the Philistines for my two eyes. And grasping the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and leaning upon them, one with his right hand and one with his left, he said: Let me die with the Philistines. He bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the princes and all the people who were in it. So he killed more at his death than he had killed during his life. His brothers and all his kinsmen came down and took his body and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years. Chapter XVII.

There was a certain man of the hill country of Ephraim named Micah, who said to his mother: The eleven hundred pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse in my hearing — I have that silver with me; I took it. And his mother said: Blessed be my son by the Lord. He returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said: I had wholly dedicated the silver to the Lord from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image; now therefore I will return it to you. So he returned the money to his mother. His mother took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to the silversmith, who made of them a carved image and a metal image; and it was in the house of Micah. And Micah had a shrine; he made an ephod and household idols, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest. In those days there was no king in Israel; every man did what was right in his own eyes. Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite; and he sojourned there. The man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to reside wherever he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah. And Micah said to him: Where do you come from? He replied: I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to find a place to live wherever I may. And Micah said to him: Stay with me and be my father and priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year

Judges.

and double garments and whatever is necessary for sustenance. The man was content and stayed with him, and was to him almost as one of his sons. And Micah filled his hand and had the young man as a priest in his house, saying: Now I know that God will do good to me, since I have a priest of the Levitical tribe. Chapter 18.

In those days there was no king in Israel, and the tribe of Dan was seeking a possession to dwell in, for until that day they had not received their lot among the other tribes. The sons of Dan sent five of the most valiant men of their family, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and examine it carefully. They said to them: Go and survey the land. When they came to the hill country of Ephraim and entered the house of Micah, they rested there. Recognizing the voice of the young Levite and lodging with him, they said to him: Who brought you here? What are you doing here? What is your purpose in coming? He answered them: Micah has given me such and such things and has hired me for wages to be his priest. They asked him to consult God, that they might know whether their journey would be prosperous and their undertaking would succeed. He answered them: Go in peace. The Lord looks with favor upon your way and the journey you are taking. The five men went on and came to Laish, and they saw the people who were there living without fear, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and secure, with no one troubling them or possessing great power, and far from Sidon, and having no dealings with anyone. When they came back to their kindred at Zorah and Eshtaol, their kindred said to them: What do you report? They answered: Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and it is very good. Will you do nothing? Do not hesitate to go and enter and possess the land. When you arrive, you will come to a people that lives without care in a spacious land, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that the earth produces.

So six hundred men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol and camped in Kiriath-jearim in Judah. That place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; it is west of Kiriath-jearim. From there they passed on to the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah. Then the five men who had gone to spy out the land said to their companions: Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, teraphim, a carved image, and a metal idol? Now therefore consider what you will do. So they turned aside and came to the house of the young Levite, at the house of Micah, and greeted him kindly. The six hundred men armed with weapons of war stood by the gate. The five men who had gone to spy out the land went in and took the carved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the metal idol, while the priest stood by the gate with the six hundred armed men. When the men went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the teraphim, and the metal idol, the priest said to them: What are you doing? They said to him: Be quiet, put your hand over your mouth, come with us and be our father and priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and family in Israel? The priest's heart was glad; he took the ephod, the teraphim, and the carved image and went among the people. So they turned and departed, putting the little ones, the livestock, and the goods in front of them. When they had gone some distance from the house of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house gathered and overtook the people of Dan and called out to them. The people of Dan turned and said to Micah: What is the matter with you that you come with such a company? He said: You have taken my gods that I made and the priest, and have gone away, and what do I have left? And you say to me: What is the matter with you? The people of Dan said to him: Do not let your voice be heard among us, or else angry men will attack you and you and your household will lose your lives. Then the people of Dan went their way, and when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his house.

Judges I.

the men were downcast in spirit, and he with all the household went first. And so the journey was resumed. But seeing that stronger men were pressing him back, he returned to his own house. The men of the city took the priest and the above-mentioned things, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and secure, and struck them with the edge of the sword, and burned the city with fire, with no one to rescue them, because they lived far from Sidon and had no dealings with any man. The city was situated in the region of Rehob, and they who returned to settle it called it Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor who was born to Israel. They set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land. And they kept Micah's graven image all the time that the house of God was in Shiloh. In those days there was no king in Israel.

There was a certain Levite living on the far side of the hill country of Ephraim, who took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah. But she was unfaithful to him and returned to her father's house in Bethlehem, where she stayed for four months. Then her husband set out to speak kindly to her and bring her back, having with him a servant and two donkeys. She brought him into her father's house, and when her father saw him, he was glad to meet him. His father-in-law, the girl's father, detained him, and he stayed with him three days, eating and drinking and lodging there. On the fourth day they rose early in the morning, and he prepared to leave. But the girl's father said to his son-in-law, "Sustain yourself with a morsel of bread, and then you may go." So they sat down and the two of them ate and drank together. Then the girl's father said to the man, "Please stay tonight and let your heart be merry."

They rose to depart, but the father-in-law urged him and he stayed again. In the morning he rose early to go, but the father-in-law said, "Refresh yourself, and wait until the afternoon." So they ate together. And when the man and his concubine and his servant rose to go, his father-in-law said, "Look, the day has now drawn toward evening; please stay the night. See, the day is coming to an end. Stay here and let your heart be merry, and tomorrow you can get up early for your journey and go home." But the man would not spend the night, so he rose and departed and came toward Jebus, which is Jerusalem, with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine. When they were near Jebus, the day was nearly gone, and the servant said to his master, "Come, let us turn aside to this city of the Jebusites and spend the night in it." But his master said to him, "We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners who do not belong to the people of Israel, but we will pass on to Gibeah." And as they passed on and went their way, the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin. They turned aside there to spend the night in Gibeah. And they went in and sat down in the open square of the city, but no one took them in to spend the night. And behold, an old man was coming from his work in the field at evening. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he was sojourning in Gibeah. The men of the place were Benjaminites. He lifted up his eyes and saw the traveler in the open square of the city. And the old man said, "Where are you going and where do you come from?" He said to him, "We are passing from Bethlehem in Judah to the far side of the hill country of Ephraim, from where I come. And now

Judges

we are going to the house of God, and no one is willing to take us under their roof; we have straw and fodder for the donkeys, and bread and wine for myself, and for your maidservant, and for the young man who is with me; we lack nothing except lodging. The old man answered: Peace be with you; I will supply all your needs; only do not stay in the street. And he brought them into his house, and gave fodder to the donkeys; and they washed their feet, and he received them to eat with him. While they were eating and refreshing their bodies after the toil of the journey with food and drink, the men of that city, sons of Belial, that is, without yoke, surrounded the house of the old man and began beating on the doors, crying out to the master of the house and saying: Bring out the man who came into your house, so that we may abuse him. The old man went out to them and said: Do not, brothers, do not commit this evil; because this man has come into my lodging, and do not be so foolish. I have a virgin daughter, and this man has a concubine; I will bring them out to you and you may humble them and satisfy your lust upon them; only, I beg you, do not commit this unnatural crime against the man. They were unwilling to agree to these words. The man, therefore, took his concubine and brought her out to them, and they abused her all night long and released her in the morning. And the woman, as the darkness was lifting, came to the door of the house where her master was staying, and fell down there. In the morning the man rose and opened the door to go on his way, and behold his concubine lay before the door with her hands spread on the threshold. He thought she was resting and spoke to her: Rise up, let us go. But when she gave no answer, he understood that she was dead; he put her on the donkey and returned home. When he had arrived at his house he took a sword and cut up her body with her bones into twelve parts, and sent them

into all the territories of Israel. And when all who saw it cried out together: Never has such a thing been done in Israel from the day when our fathers came up out of Egypt until this present day. Consider it, take counsel, and speak your mind. Chapter 20. Then all the children of Israel went out and gathered together as one man, from Dan to Beersheba and the land of Gilead, to the Lord in Mizpah; all the leaders of all the tribes of Israel assembled in the congregation of the people of God, four hundred thousand foot soldiers ready for war. Nor was it hidden from the children of Benjamin that the children of Israel had gone up to Mizpah. The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, being asked how so great a crime had come about, replied: I came to Gibeah of Benjamin with my wife, and there I lodged; and behold, the men of that city surrounded the house by night, intending to kill me, and they subjected my wife to incredible violence in their lust, and she died. I took her and cut her in pieces and sent her parts into all the territories of your possession, because so great a wickedness and so serious an offense has never been done in Israel. All you children of Israel, consider what you ought to do. And all the people arose as one man, saying: We will not return to our tents, nor shall any man enter his own house; but this is what we will do against Gibeah in common. Ten men shall be chosen out of a hundred from all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred from a thousand, and a thousand from ten thousand, to procure supplies for the army, and that we may fight against Gibeah of Benjamin and repay it for the wickedness it has committed. And all of Israel gathered together against the city as one man, united in one mind and of one counsel; and they sent messengers to all the tribe of Benjamin saying: Why has so great a wickedness been found among you? Deliver up the men of Gibeah who have committed this crime, that they may die, and the evil may be put away from Israel. But they

Judges.

The men of Israel were not willing to listen to their brothers, the sons of Israel. But gathering from all the cities that were in their region, they came to Gibeah to bring help to it, and to fight against all the people of Israel. And they found among the men of Benjamin twenty-five thousand men who drew the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who numbered seven hundred very strong men who could use both right and left hand, and who could sling stones at a hair and not miss. And the men of Israel, apart from the children of Benjamin, were found to be four hundred thousand men drawing swords, all of these warriors. They came to the house of God, that is, to Shiloh, and consulted the Lord, saying: Who shall be our leader in the battle against the children of Benjamin? And the Lord answered them: Judah shall be your leader. And straightway the children of Israel rose up in the morning and encamped near Gibeah; and going out from there they went to fight against Benjamin and to attack the city. And the children of Benjamin came out of Gibeah and slew of the children of Israel that day twenty-two thousand men. Again the children of Israel, confident in their strength and numbers, drew up their battle line in the same place as before: yet first they went up and wept before the Lord until evening, and consulted him, saying: Shall I go on to fight against the children of Benjamin my brothers, or not? And he answered them: Go up against them and give battle. Then the children of Israel on the second day went out to fight against the children of Benjamin, but the children of Benjamin came out from the gates of Gibeah against them, and made such a great slaughter of them that they struck down eighteen thousand men, all of them swordsmen. Then all the children of Israel came to the house of God, and sitting there wept before the Lord. And they fasted that day until evening,

and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before him, and asked of him, with the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord there, and Phinehas the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, standing before it. And they inquired of the Lord, saying: Shall we go out again to battle against the children of Benjamin our brothers, or shall we cease? And the Lord said: Go up, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hands. And the children of Israel set ambushes all around Gibeah, and the third time went out to battle against Benjamin as before. And the children of Benjamin boldly came out of the city, and pursuing those who fled they were drawn far away, so that they wounded some of them as on the first and second day, and they withdrew by two paths, one toward Bethel and the other toward Gibeah, and struck down about thirty men. For they thought that the Israelites were fleeing as before. But the Israelites had led them away by a feigned retreat, meaning to draw them away from the city and lead them toward the ambushes. Then all the men of Israel rose from their places and formed their battle line at Baal-tamar. And the men in ambush near the city began gradually to advance and come out from the western side of the city. And another ten thousand choice men of all Israel pressed those in the city. The battle grew heavy against Benjamin, and they did not understand that disaster threatened them on every side. And the Lord defeated them before the children of Israel, and the Israelites struck down twenty-five thousand one hundred men of Benjamin that day, all of them warriors who drew the sword. And the children of Benjamin saw that they were defeated and began to flee. And the children of Israel, seeing this, gave them room to flee, so that they might reach the ambushes which had been set near the city. And when they suddenly

Judges.

When they rose from their ambush and Benjamin turned their backs to them, they entered the city and struck it with the edge of the sword. Now the men of Israel had given this signal to those in ambush: that after they had taken the city, they should set it on fire, so that the rising smoke would show that the city was captured. When the men of Israel saw this while still in the heat of battle, they thought the men of Benjamin were fleeing and pressed harder in pursuit. Thirty men of their army had fallen, and they saw what appeared to be a column of smoke rising from the city. Benjamin also looked back and saw their city captured and the flames rising high; those who had pretended to flee now turned and fought more vigorously. When the men of Benjamin saw that they were surrounded, they turned and headed toward the desert road, where their enemies pursued them. And those who had set fire to the city also came against them, so that they were pressed from both sides by enemies with no escape. They fell and were struck down on the east side of the city of Gibeah. Eighteen thousand men fell in that place, all of them mighty warriors. When the survivors of Benjamin saw this, they fled into the wilderness toward the rock called Rimmon. They scattered and fled in various directions, and another thousand were killed. The pursuers continued after them and killed yet another two thousand. So all who fell from Benjamin in various places numbered twenty-six thousand fighting men in all. Six hundred men who survived and managed to escape fled into the wilderness and stayed at the rock of Rimmon for four months.

But the men of Israel returned and struck all the people in the cities with the sword, from humans to livestock, and all the cities of Benjamin were consumed by fire. Chapter XXI. The men of Israel had also sworn at Mizpah, saying: None of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Benjamin. All the people came to the house of God at Shiloh and sat there until evening, raising their voices and weeping bitterly, saying: O Lord God of Israel, why has this evil come upon us, that today one tribe is cut off from Israel? The next day they rose early and built an altar there, offering burnt offerings and peace offerings, and they said: Who from all the tribes of Israel did not come up to the assembly of the Lord? For they had solemnly sworn that anyone who did not come to Mizpah would be put to death. The people of Israel grieved for their brother Benjamin and said: One tribe is cut off from Israel today. Where will they get wives? For we have all sworn not to give them our daughters as wives. So they asked: Who from all the tribes of Israel did not come up to the Lord at Mizpah? And it was found that no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp to the assembly. For at that time when the people were at Shiloh, none of them were there. So the assembly sent twelve thousand of the bravest men with orders to go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the sword, including the women and children, with these instructions: You shall destroy every male and every woman who has slept with a man, but save the virgins. And they found four hundred young virgins from Jabesh-gilead who had not known a man, and they brought them to the camp

Ruth.

in Shiloh in the land of Canaan. And they sent messengers to the sons of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon, and called them, and received them in peace. And the sons of Benjamin came at that time, and wives were given to them from the daughters of Jabesh-gilead; but they did not find enough for all of them. And all the people grieved deeply and performed penance over the destruction of one tribe of Israel, and the elders said: What shall we do for those who remain, who have not received wives? All in Benjamin have fallen by the sword, and it is a great care for us to provide by ingenuity, lest one tribe be wiped out from Israel. For we cannot give our daughters to them, being bound by the oath and curse which we pronounced: Cursed be he who gives his daughter as wife to Benjamin. And they took counsel and said: Behold, there is a yearly feast of the Lord in Shiloh, which is to the north of the city of Bethel, to the east of the road that goes from Bethel to Shechem, and to the south of the town of Lebonah. And they commanded the sons of Benjamin and said: Go and hide yourselves in the vineyards. And when you see the daughters of Shiloh come out to lead the dances in the customary manner, come out quickly from the vineyards and each of you seize a wife from among them and go into the land of Benjamin. And when their fathers and brothers come to complain and contend against you, we will say to them: Take pity on them. For they did not take them by right of war and conquest; but since you would not give them when they asked, you are on your side at fault. And the sons of Benjamin did as they had been instructed, and according to their number carried off wives from those who were dancing and went to their own territory, building cities and dwelling in them. The children of Israel also returned by their tribes and families

to their tents. In those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes. Here ends the Book of Judges. Here begins the Book of Ruth. Chapter I.
In the days of one of the judges, when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab, he and his wife and his two sons. The man's name was Elimelech, and his wife's name was Naomi, and his two sons were named Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came to the country of Moab and remained there. And Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons. They took Moabite wives; the name of one was Orpah and the name of the other Ruth. They lived there about ten years, and both Mahlon and Chilion died, and the woman was left bereaved of her two sons and her husband. Then she arose to return to her homeland with her two daughters-in-law from the country of Moab, for she had heard that the Lord had visited his people and given them food. So she set out from the place where she had been living, and her two daughters-in-law went with her; and they were on the road to return to the land of Judah, when she said to them: Go, return each to your mother's house. May the Lord deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me. May the Lord grant that you find rest, each of you in the house of the husband you will follow. Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept and said to her: We will return with you to your people. But she replied: Return, my daughters. Why will you go with me? Have I yet more sons in my womb, that they might become your husbands? Return, my daughters, go. For I am too old to have a husband. Even if I thought there was hope for me, if I were to be married this night and should bear sons, would you wait for them until they were grown and would you remain unmarried for them?

Ruth.

May it be fulfilled before you grow old, before you marry again. Do not ask me, my daughters, for your hardship weighs more heavily upon me; the hand of the Lord has gone out against me. Then she lifted up her voice and wept again. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and returned, but Ruth clung to her. Naomi said to her: See, your sister-in-law has returned to her people and to her gods; go with her. She answered: Do not press me to leave you and turn back. Wherever you go, I will go; wherever you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Whatever land receives you when you die, there I will die; and there I will be buried. May God do this to me and more besides, if anything but death separates me from you. When Naomi saw that Ruth was firmly resolved to go with her, she ceased to urge her and stopped trying to persuade her to return to her own people. So they both set out and came to Bethlehem. When they entered the city, the news spread quickly among all the people, and the women said: Is this Naomi? She replied to them: Do not call me Naomi, that is, beautiful; call me Mara, that is, bitter, for the Almighty has filled me with great bitterness. I went out full, and the Lord has brought me back empty. Why then do you call me Naomi, whom the Lord has humbled and the Almighty has afflicted? So Naomi returned with her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabite, coming back from the land of her sojourn; and they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.

Now Naomi had a kinsman of her husband's, a man of great wealth and power, by the name of Boaz. Ruth the Moabite said to her mother-in-law: If you permit, I will go into the field and gather the ears of grain that escape the harvesters' hands, wherever I find someone kind enough to receive me. She replied: Go, my daughter. She went and gleaned in the field behind the reapers. Now it happened that the field belonged to a man named Boaz, who was of the family of Elimelech. And behold, Boaz himself came from Bethlehem and said to the reapers: The Lord be with you. They replied: The Lord bless you. Then Boaz said to the young man who was set over the reapers: Whose young woman is this? He answered: She is a Moabite who came back with Naomi from the land of Moab; and she asked to glean and gather behind the reapers. She has been on her feet from morning until now, and has not rested even a moment at home. Then Boaz said to Ruth: Listen, my daughter. Do not go to glean in another field, and do not leave this place; stay with my young women. Watch which fields they are reaping and follow after them. I have ordered my young men not to bother you; and when you are thirsty, go to the jars and drink what my young men have drawn. She fell on her face, bowed to the ground, and said to him: How have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, a foreign woman? Boaz answered her: I have been told all that you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, and how you left your father and your mother and the land of your birth, and came to a people you did not know before. May the Lord repay you for your deeds; may you receive a full reward from the Lord, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have come to take refuge. She said: May I find favor in your eyes, my lord, for you have comforted me and spoken kindly to your servant, though I am not even worthy to be compared to one of your maidservants. And Boaz said to her: When it is time to eat, come here and have bread, and dip your piece in the vinegar. She went back then

. Ruth .

He went to the side of the reapers and heaped up grain for her; she ate and was satisfied, and had some left over. Then she rose to glean again. Boaz commanded his servants, saying: Even if she wants to reap alongside you, do not hinder her; and from the bundles deliberately drop some and leave them, so that she may gather without shame, and let no one rebuke her. So she gleaned in the field until evening, and what she had gleaned, when she beat it out, was about an ephah of barley — that is, three measures — which she carried back to the city and showed to her mother-in-law. She also brought out and gave her what she had left over from her meal when she was satisfied. Her mother-in-law said to her: Where did you glean today? And where did you work? Blessed be the one who took notice of you. She told her with whom she had worked, and said that the man's name was Boaz. And Naomi said: Blessed be he by the Lord, who has not abandoned his kindness to the living and to the dead. And she added: The man is our kinsman. Ruth also said: He told me this — to stay close to his servants until all the harvest is finished. And her mother-in-law said: It is better, my daughter, that you go out with his young women, lest in another man's field someone trouble you. So she kept close to the young women of Boaz, and gleaned until the barley and wheat harvests were finished and all was stored in the barns. Chapter III.

After she returned to her mother-in-law, Naomi said to her: My daughter, I must seek rest for you, that it may be well with you. Boaz, whose young women you have been with, is our kinsman; tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor. Wash therefore and anoint yourself, and put on your best clothes and go down to the threshing floor.

Do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking. But when he lies down, note the place where he lies; then go and uncover his feet and lie down, and he will tell you what you are to do. She replied: Whatever you say I will do. So she went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had told her. When Boaz had eaten and drunk, and his heart was merry, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain; and she came softly and uncovered his feet and lay down. At midnight the man was startled and turned over, and behold, a woman lay at his feet. He said: Who are you? And she answered: I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your cloak over your servant, for you are a kinsman-redeemer. He said: Blessed are you by the Lord, my daughter; you have made this last kindness greater than the first, in that you have not gone after young men, whether poor or rich. Do not fear; I will do for you whatever you ask. All the people of my city know that you are a woman of worth. And it is true that I am a kinsman-redeemer, yet there is a kinsman-redeemer closer than I. Rest here tonight, and in the morning, if he will redeem you, well and good; but if he is not willing, then as the Lord lives, I will redeem you. Lie down until morning. So she lay at his feet until morning, but rose before one could recognize another. And Boaz said: Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor. And he said: Hold out the cloak you are wearing. And when she held it out, he measured six measures of barley and put it on her.

· Prologue ·

Here begins the Prologue to the Books of Kings ·

There are, then, two kinds of letters among the Hebrews, as the language of the Syrians and Chaldeans attests — a language which is in large part related to Hebrew. For they too have twenty-two letters, of the same sound, but with distinct characters. The Samaritans also copy out the Pentateuch of Moses in the same letters, differing only in the forms and points. It is certain that Ezra the scribe and doctor of the law, after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the Temple under Zerubbabel, devised the letters which we now use, since up to that time the Samaritans and the Hebrews had shared the same characters. In the book of Numbers this same reckoning, under the census of the Levites and priests, is mystically shown; and the name of the Lord in tetragram form is found in certain Greek volumes even to this day, written in the old letters. Moreover, Psalms 37, 102, 111, 119, and 145 are composed in separate metrical sections, yet all follow the same alphabetical scheme. And the Lamentations and the Prayer of Jeremiah, as well as the work of Solomon beginning with "Who shall find a valiant woman," are reckoned according to the same alphabets or divisions. Furthermore, among the Hebrews there are five double letters: raph, mem, nun, phe, sade. They are written one way at the beginning and middle of a word, and another way at the end. Hence some count the following as double books: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Jeremiah with his Lamentations. Just as there are twenty-two letters by which we write in Hebrew everything we speak — from the first breath of the human voice to its end — so too

twenty-two volumes are reckoned, in which, as in letters and boundaries, the tender and still-nursing infant of the just man is educated in the doctrine of God. The first book among them is called Bresith, which we call Genesis. The second is Ellesmoth, which is called Exodus. The third is Va-icra, that is, Leviticus. The fourth is Vagedaber, which we call Numbers. The fifth is Ellcaddebarim, which is denoted as Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which they properly call Thorath, that is, the Law. The second order is made up of the Prophets, and they begin with Joshua son of Nun, whom they call among themselves Iosue Betun. Then follow the Sophim, that is the Book of Judges; and with it they join Ruth, since in the days of the judges the history it narrates took place. Third comes Samuel, which we call the first and second Books of Kings. Fourth is Malachim, that is, Kings, distinguished into two volumes of the Kings. It is better, following Malachim meaning Kings, than Malakoth meaning Kingdoms — for it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but the one kingdom of Israel, divided among the twelve tribes. Fifth is Isaiah. Sixth is Jeremiah. Seventh is Ezekiel. The eighth book is the Twelve Prophets, whom they call Thareapha. The third order belongs to the Hagiographa. The first book of it begins with Job. Next comes David, which is arranged in five divisions and one volume of Psalms. Third is Solomon, containing three books: Proverbs, which they call Malloth or Parables; Ecclesiastes, which is Coeleth; and the Song of Songs, which is noted under the title Srasym. Fourth is Daniel. Seventh is Chronicles, which we may more significantly call the Chronicle of all divine history; this book among us is inscribed as the first and second Books of Paralipomenon. Eighth is Ezra, which likewise among the Greeks and Latins is divided into two —

· Prologue ·

The books are divided thus. Moses is the witness. And so the books of the old law are twenty-two in number: that is, five of Moses, eight of the prophets, nine of the hagiographers. Although some count Ruth and Lamentations among the hagiographers and reckon them separately in their enumeration, and so hold that the ancient law has twenty-four books, which the Apocalypse of John mentions when it speaks of the twenty-four elders worshipping the Lamb, casting their crowns before the four living creatures standing before them, before and behind — that is, in the past and future — and with unceasing voice crying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come. This prologue to the Scriptures, serving as a kind of helmeted preface, may fitly apply to all the books which we have translated from Hebrew into Latin, so that we may know that whatever is outside these is to be placed among the apocrypha. Therefore the book of Wisdom, commonly attributed to Solomon, and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith, and Tobit, and the Shepherd, are not in the canon. The first book of Maccabees I have found in Hebrew; the second is Greek, as can be proved by its very style. Since this is so, I beg you, reader, not to regard the labor I have spent as a criticism of the ancients. In the temple of God each person offers what he can. Some offer gold, silver, and precious stones; others offer linen, purple, scarlet, and blue. It goes well with us if we offer skins and goat hair. And yet the Apostle judges the more contemptible things to be the more necessary. Hence, that whole splendor of the tabernacle and all the individual coverings belonging to the future church are covered with skins and cilices, which protect against the sun's heat and the injury of rain — the things that are inferior serve as a shield. Read therefore first Samuel,

and my Kings. My own, I say, my own. Whatever through frequent revision and correction I have carefully learned and retained, is faithful. And when you understand what you did not know before, you may consider me an interpreter if you are grateful, or a paraphraser if ungrateful; although I am fully aware that I have changed nothing in anyone's reckoning of the Hebrew truth. Certainly, if you are incredulous, read the Greek and Latin codices, and compare them with the little works which we have recently corrected, and wherever you see them disagreeing with each other, ask any Hebrew to whom you should give greater credence; and if our text is confirmed, I think you will not consider that he prophesied in the same place as I. But I also beg you, handmaids of Christ, who anoint with precious myrrh of faith the head of the reclining Lord, who seek the Savior no longer in the tomb — for Christ has already ascended to the Father — to raise the shields of your prayers against the barking dogs who rage against me with rabid mouths, who go about the city and, boasting themselves learned, detract from others. For I, knowing my own lowliness, shall always recall the words of the sentence: I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue. I set a guard to my mouth, when the sinner stood before me. I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silence even from good things.

Here ends the Prologue. Here begins the first Book of Kings. Chapter I.

There was a man of Ramathaim-Sophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite. And he had two wives; the name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.

He was a free man. And this man went up from his city on the appointed days to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts in Shiloh. And there were two sons of Eli there, Hophni and Phinehas, priests of the Lord. And so on that day Elkanah offered sacrifice and gave portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave one portion with sadness, because he loved Hannah. Yet the Lord had closed her womb. And her rival afflicted her greatly and vexed her bitterly, so much so that she reproached her because the Lord had closed her womb. He did this every year, when they went up to the temple of the Lord, and in this way she provoked her. But Hannah wept and did not eat. Then Elkanah her husband said to her: Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons? So Hannah rose up after she had eaten and drunk in Shiloh. And Eli the priest was sitting upon a seat before the posts of the temple of the Lord. Hannah, with a bitter soul, prayed to the Lord, weeping bitterly, and made a vow, saying: O Lord of hosts, if you will look down and see the affliction of your handmaid, and will be mindful of me and not forget your handmaid, and will give your servant a male child, I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head. Now as she was praying before the Lord, Eli watched her mouth. For Hannah spoke in her heart, and only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard at all. So Eli thought her to be drunk, and said to her: How long will you be drunk? Put away your wine. Hannah answered and said: No, my lord. I am a most unhappy woman, and I have drunk neither wine nor anything that could make me drunk, but I have poured out my soul before the Lord. Do not regard your handmaid as one of the daughters of Belial, for out of the abundance of my grief and sorrow have I spoken until now. Then Eli said to her: Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant you the petition that you have asked of him. And she said: Let your handmaid find grace in your eyes. And the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer downcast in different ways. And they rose up early in the morning and worshipped before the Lord, and then returned and came to their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the Lord remembered her. And in the course of time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, because she had asked him of the Lord. And Elkanah and all his household went up to offer the solemn sacrifice to the Lord and his vow. But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband: I will not go until the child is weaned, and then I will bring him, that he may appear before the Lord and remain there forever. And Elkanah her husband said to her: Do what seems good to you; remain until you have weaned him; only may the Lord fulfill his word. So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him. And she brought him with her when she had weaned him, with three bullocks, and three measures of flour, and a flask of wine, and she brought him to the house of the Lord in Shiloh. And the child was still very young. And they slaughtered the bullock and brought the child to Eli. And Hannah said: Oh, my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood before you here praying to the Lord. For this child I prayed, and the Lord has granted me my petition that I asked of him. Therefore I also

I have lent him to the Lord; as long as he lives he shall be lent to the Lord. And they worshiped the Lord there. And Hannah worshiped and said. Chapter II.
My heart rejoices in the Lord; my horn is exalted in my God. My mouth is opened wide against my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation. There is none holy as the Lord: for there is none beside you, and there is no rock like our God. Speak no more so proudly; let not arrogance come from your mouth, for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed. The bows of the mighty men are broken, and those who stumbled are girded with strength. Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, and those who were hungry have ceased. While the barren woman has borne seven, she who had many children has become feeble. The Lord kills and makes alive: he brings down to the grave and raises up. The Lord makes poor and makes rich: he brings low and lifts up. He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dunghill, to set them among princes and to make them inherit a throne of glory; for the pillars of the earth are the Lord's, and he has set the world upon them. He will keep the feet of his saints, and the wicked shall be silent in darkness; for by strength shall no man prevail. The adversaries of the Lord shall be broken in pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth; and he shall give strength to his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed. And Elkanah went to Ramah to his house. The boy was ministering before the Lord, before Eli the priest. Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they did not know the Lord, nor the duty of the priests toward the people. When any man offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant would come with a three-pronged fork in his hand while the meat was boiling, and he would thrust it into the pan

or into the kettle, or into the cauldron, or into the pot; and all that the fork brought up the priest would take for himself. Thus they did to all Israel who came to Shiloh. Also, before they burned the fat, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, Give me meat to roast for the priest, for he will not take boiled meat from you, but raw. And if the man said to him, Let the fat first be burned as is the custom, and then take as much as your heart desires, he would say, No, but you must give it to me now; and if not, I will take it by force. So the sin of the young men was very great before the Lord, for the men despised the offering of the Lord. Samuel ministered before the Lord, a boy girded with a linen ephod. And his mother used to make him a little robe and bring it to him each year when she came up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice. And Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, The Lord give you offspring from this woman in place of the loan she made to the Lord. Then they would return home. And the Lord visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew up before the Lord. Now Eli was very old, and he heard all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting. And he said to them, Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all the people. No, my sons; it is not a good report that I hear the people of the Lord spreading abroad. If someone sins against a man, God may mediate for him; but if someone sins against the Lord, who can intercede for him? But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for

The Lord wished to kill them. But the boy Samuel continued to grow and please both God and men. And a man of God came to Eli and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Did I not plainly reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in the house of Pharaoh? And I chose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, and to wear the ephod before me; and I gave to the house of your father all the offerings of the children of Israel. Why have you kicked at my sacrifice and at my offering which I commanded in my dwelling place, and have honored your sons more than me, to eat the firstfruits of all the offerings of Israel my people? Therefore the Lord God of Israel says: I said indeed that your house and the house of your father should walk before me forever; but now the Lord says, be it far from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed. Behold, the days come that I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father's house, so that there shall not be an old man in your house. And you shall see an adversary in my dwelling place in all the prosperity of Israel, and there shall not be an old man in your house forever. Nevertheless I will not cut off every man of yours from my altar, that your eyes may fail and your soul may grieve; and all the increase of your house shall die in the flower of their age. And this shall be the sign to you that shall come upon your two sons Hophni and Phinehas: in one day they shall die both of them. And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind; and I will build him a sure house, and he shall walk before my anointed forever. And it shall come to pass that everyone who is left in your house will come to bow down before him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread, and shall say: Put me, I pray you, into one of the priestly offices, that I may eat a piece of bread.

Chapter 4.

And the boy Samuel ministered before the Lord before Eli. The word of the Lord was rare in those days; there was no open vision. And it came to pass at that time, when Eli was lying down in his place, and his eyes had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, and before the lamp of God went out, Samuel was lying down in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was. The Lord called Samuel, and he answered: Here I am. And he ran to Eli and said: Here I am, for you called me. But Eli said: I did not call; lie down again. And he went and lay down. The Lord called again: Samuel! And Samuel arose and went to Eli and said: Here I am, for you called me. But he answered: I did not call, my son; lie down again. Now Samuel did not yet know the Lord, and the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him. The Lord called Samuel again a third time, and he arose and went to Eli and said: Here I am, for you called me. Then Eli understood that the Lord was calling the boy, and Eli said to Samuel: Go, lie down, and if he calls you again, you shall say: Speak, Lord, for your servant hears. So Samuel went and lay down in his place. And the Lord came and stood and called as at other times: Samuel! Samuel! And Samuel said: Speak, Lord, for your servant hears. Then the Lord said to Samuel: Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which both ears of everyone who hears it will tingle. On that day I will carry out against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end. For I have told him that I will judge his house forever for the iniquity which he knew, because his sons...

he established his household forever, because of the iniquity of which he knew, namely that his sons were acting wickedly and he did not rebuke them. Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of his house shall not be atoned for by sacrifices or offerings forever. And Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the Lord. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli of the vision. Then Eli called Samuel and said: Samuel, my son. And he answered and said: Here I am. And he asked him: What is the word that the Lord spoke to you? Do not hide it from me. May God do so to you and more, if you hide from me anything of all the words that were spoken to you. So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he answered: It is the Lord. Let him do what is good in his sight. And Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of his words fell to the ground. And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a faithful prophet of the Lord. And the Lord appeared again in Shiloh, for the Lord revealed himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the Lord; and the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Chapter III, IV.

And it came to pass in those days that the Philistines gathered to fight. And Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and camped at Ebenezer. And the Philistines came to Aphek and drew up their forces against Israel. When the battle was joined, Israel was defeated by the Philistines, and they slew in the field about four thousand men. When the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said: Why has the Lord struck us down today before the Philistines? Let us bring from Shiloh

the ark of the covenant of the Lord, that it may come among us and save us from the hand of our enemies. So they sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts who sits enthroned upon the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God. When the ark of the covenant of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel shouted with a great shout, so that the earth resounded. And when the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said: What does this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews mean? And they understood that the ark of the Lord had come into the camp. And the Philistines were afraid, saying: God has come into the camp. And they cried out: Woe to us! For such a thing has not happened before. Woe to us! Who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck Egypt with every kind of plague in the desert. Take courage and be men, O Philistines, lest you be slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you. Be men and fight. So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and they fled every man to his tent. And there was a very great slaughter, and there fell of Israel thirty thousand foot soldiers. And the ark of God was captured. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were slain. And a man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh that same day with his clothes torn and with dust on his head. When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God. When the man came into the city and told the news, all the city cried out. And when Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said: What is this noise of tumult? And the man hurried and came and told Eli. Now Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes were set so that he could not see.

[page header: Primus]

And he said to Eli: I am the one who came from the battle, and I fled from the field today. Eli said to him: What happened, my son? And the one who brought the news said: Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Moreover, your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured. When he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backwards from his seat beside the gate, and his neck was broken and he died, for he was an old man and heavy, and he had judged Israel forty years. Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and near the time of delivery. When she heard the news about the capture of the ark of God and the death of her father-in-law and her husband, she bowed down and gave birth, for her labor pains came upon her. In the very moment of her death, the women standing around her said: Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son. But she did not respond or pay attention. And she named the child Ichabod, saying: The glory has departed from Israel, because the ark of God was captured. And regarding her father-in-law and her husband she said: The glory has departed from Israel, because the ark of God was taken. Chapter 4.

The Philistines took the ark of God and carried it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon and placed it beside Dagon. When the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the Lord. They took Dagon and put him back in his place. But when they rose early the next morning, Dagon had again fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the Lord, and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold; only the trunk of Dagon was left to him. This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day. The hand of the Lord was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he devastated them and afflicted Ashdod and its territory with tumors. And in the fields of the region mice swarmed, and there was a great deadly panic in the city. When the men of Ashdod saw how things were, they said: The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god. So they sent and gathered all the lords of the Philistines and said: What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel? The men of Gath answered: Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to us. So they brought the ark of the God of Israel around. But after they had brought it around, the hand of the Lord was against the city, causing a very great panic, and he struck the men of the city, both young and old, and tumors broke out on them. So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But when the ark of God came to Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, saying: They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us to kill us and our people. They sent therefore and gathered all the lords of the Philistines and said: Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill us and our people. For there was a deadly panic throughout the whole city; the hand of God was very heavy there, and those who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven. Chapter 6.

The ark of the Lord was in the region of

Kings.

The Philistines had the ark for seven months. After this they called together their priests and diviners, saying: What shall we do about the ark of God? Tell us how we should send it back to its place. They said: If you send back the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it back empty, but return to him an offering for sin, and then you will be healed, and you will know why his hand has not been removed from you. They said: What is the offering we should make to him for our sin? They answered: Five golden tumors and five golden mice, for the same plague has been on all of you and on your rulers. Make images of your tumors and images of the mice that have ravaged the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lift his hand from you and from your gods and from your land. Why do you harden your hearts as Egypt and Pharaoh hardened theirs? Was it not after he struck them that they let the people go, and they departed? Now therefore, take and make a new cart, and take two milk cows on which no yoke has come, and hitch the cows to the cart and take their calves home away from them. Take the ark of the Lord and place it on the cart, and put in a box beside it the golden objects you are returning to him as a guilt offering; then send it off and let it go. Watch: if it goes up on the road to Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has done us this great harm; but if not, then we will know that it is not his hand that struck us — it happened by chance. So they did this: they took two milking cows and hitched them to the cart, and shut up their calves at home. They placed the ark of the Lord on the cart and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors.

The cows went straight on the road toward Beth-shemesh, going along the highway, lowing as they went, turning neither to the right nor to the left. The rulers of the Philistines followed them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh. Now the people of Beth-shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. When they looked up and saw the ark, they rejoiced to see it. The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. There was a large stone there. They split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the Lord. The Levites took down the ark of the Lord and the box that was beside it, in which were the golden objects, and placed them on the great stone. The men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and made sacrifices on that day to the Lord. When the five rulers of the Philistines saw this, they returned that day to Ekron. These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the Lord: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron; also the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five rulers, from fortified city to country village, as far as the great stone of Abel on which they set the ark of the Lord, which is to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh. And he struck down some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the Lord. He struck seventy men of them and fifty thousand of the people. The people mourned because the Lord had struck the people with a great blow. The men of Beth-shemesh said: Who is able to stand before the Lord, this holy God? To whom shall he go up from us? They sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying: The Philistines have returned the ark of the Lord. Come down and take it up to you. Chapter VII. And the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the Lord and brought it into

the house of Abinadab in Gibeah. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to keep the ark of the Lord. And from the day that the ark remained in Kirjath-jearim, the time was long; for it was twenty years. And all the house of Israel lamented after the Lord. Then Samuel spoke to all the house of Israel, saying: If you return to the Lord with all your heart, remove the foreign gods from among you, the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and prepare your hearts to the Lord and serve him alone; and he will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines. So the children of Israel put away the Baals and Ashtaroth, and served the Lord alone. Then Samuel said: Gather all Israel to Mizpeh, that I may pray to the Lord for you. And they gathered together at Mizpeh, and drew water, and poured it out before the Lord, and fasted on that day and said: We have sinned against the Lord. And Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpeh. And the Philistines heard that the children of Israel were gathered together at Mizpeh, and the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. When the children of Israel heard it, they were afraid of the Philistines. And the children of Israel said to Samuel: Do not cease to cry to the Lord our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines. And Samuel took a suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the Lord. And Samuel cried to the Lord for Israel, and the Lord heard him. And as Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to battle against Israel. But the Lord thundered with a great noise on that day upon the Philistines, and they were confused, and they were defeated before Israel. And the men of Israel went out of Mizpeh and pursued the Philistines and struck them, as far as below Beth-car. Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpeh and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer,

saying: Hitherto the Lord has helped us. So the Philistines were subdued, and they came no more into the border of Israel. And the hand of the Lord was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. And the cities which the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored, from Ekron even to Gath; and Israel delivered their borders from the hand of the Philistines. And there was peace between Israel and the Amorites. And Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. He went from year to year in circuit to Bethel and Gilgal and Mizpeh, and judged Israel in all those places. And he returned to Ramah, for there was his house; and there he judged Israel. And there he built an altar to the Lord. Chapter 8.

And it came to pass, when Samuel had grown old, that he made his sons judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn was Joel, and the name of his second was Abiah; they were judges in Beersheba. But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside after gain and took bribes and perverted justice. Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah. And they said to him: Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint us a king to judge us, like all the nations. But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said: Give us a king to judge us. And Samuel prayed to the Lord. And the Lord said to Samuel: Hear the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them. According to all the works which they have done since the day I brought them out of Egypt even to this day — forsaking me and serving other gods — so they are doing to you also. Now therefore, listen to their voice. Nevertheless, warn them and show them the ways of the king who shall reign over them.

Kings (1 Samuel)

Samuel spoke all the words of the Lord to the people who had asked him for a king, and said: This will be the right of the king who will reign over you. He will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and make them his horsemen and his runners before his chariots. He will appoint them as commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and to plow his fields and reap his harvest, and to make his weapons and equipment for his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of your grain and your vineyards and give it to his officers and servants. He will take your male servants and your female servants and your finest young men and your donkeys and put them to his work. He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you shall be his servants. And you will cry out in that day because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the Lord will not answer you in that day. But the people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel, and they said: No! There shall be a king over us, so that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles. Samuel heard all the words of the people and spoke them in the ears of the Lord. And the Lord said to Samuel: Listen to their voice and set a king over them. And Samuel said to the men of Israel: Let every man return to his city.

There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite, a man of great strength. And he had a son whose name was Saul, a fine and handsome young man, and there was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people. Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost. So Kish said to his son Saul: Take one of the servants with you and arise, go and look for the donkeys. And when he had passed through the hill country of Ephraim,

and through the land of Shalishah and did not find them, they passed through the land of Shaalim and they were not there, and through the land of Benjamin, and they did not find them. When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to the servant who was with him: Come, let us turn back, lest my father stop worrying about the donkeys and be anxious about us. But the servant said to him: Look, there is a man of God in this city, and he is a man who is held in honor; everything he says comes true. Let us go there now; perhaps he will tell us about our journey on which we have set out. And Saul said to his servant: But if we go, what can we bring the man? For the bread in our sacks is gone, and there is no present to bring to the man of God. What do we have? The servant answered Saul again and said: Here, I have in my hand a quarter of a shekel of silver; I will give it to the man of God to tell us our way. Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said thus: Come, let us go to the seer, for he who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer. And Saul said to his servant: Well said; come, let us go. So they went to the city where the man of God was. As they went up the hill to the city, they met young women coming out to draw water, and said to them: Is the seer here? They answered them and said: He is; look, he is just ahead of you. Hurry now, for he has come just today to the city, because the people have a sacrifice today on the high place. As soon as you enter the city, you will find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat until he comes, since he must bless the sacrifice; afterward those who are invited will eat. So go up now, for you will find him immediately. They went up to the city. As they were going into the city, Samuel came out toward them on his way up to the high place. Now the Lord had revealed to Samuel the day before Saul came, saying:

· Kings ·

And they came to the aforementioned hill, and behold, a company of prophets met him. And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he prophesied among them. And all who had known him before, when they saw that he prophesied with the prophets, said to one another: What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets? And one of them answered and said: And who is their father? Therefore it became a proverb: Is Saul also among the prophets? And when he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place. And Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant: Where did you go? And they said: To look for the donkeys, and when we could not find them, we went to Samuel. And Saul's uncle said: Tell me what Samuel said to you. And Saul said to his uncle: He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found. But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he did not tell him. And Samuel called the people together before the Lord at Mizpah, and said to the children of Israel: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians, and from the hand of all the kingdoms that oppressed you. But you have today rejected your God, who himself saved you out of all your adversities and your tribulations, and you have said: Set a king over us. Now therefore present yourselves before the Lord by your tribes and by your families. And Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the lot fell upon the tribe of Benjamin. And he brought the tribe of Benjamin near by their families, and the lot fell upon the family of Matri, and then upon Saul the son of Kish. And when they sought him, he could not be found. And they inquired of the Lord further: Is there a man yet to come? And the Lord said: Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage. And they ran and fetched him from there, and when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward. And Samuel said to all the people: Do you see whom the Lord has chosen? There is none like him among all the people. And all the people shouted and said: Long live the king! Then Samuel told the people the rights and duties of the kingship, and wrote them in a book and laid it before the Lord. And Samuel sent all the people away, each to his own home.
