Give thanks to him, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. And all the people, worshipping the Lord, said to her: The Lord has blessed you by his power, because through you he has brought our enemies to nothing. And Ozias, prince of Israel, said to her: Blessed are you, daughter, by the Lord the Most High God, above all the women upon the earth. Blessed be the Lord who made heaven and earth, who guided you to cut off the head of the leader of our enemies; for today he has so magnified your name that your praise shall not depart from the mouths of men who shall be mindful of the power of the Lord forever — for whom you did not spare your own life, on account of the distress and tribulation of your people, but prevented their ruin in the sight of our God. And all the people said: So be it, so be it. Then Achior was summoned and came. And she said to him: The God of Israel, to whom you bore testimony — that he would take vengeance on his enemies — he has cut off the head of all the unbelievers this night by my hand. And that you may know that it is so: here is the head of Holofernes, who in the pride of his contempt despised the God of Israel, and threatened you with death, saying: When the people of Israel are captured, I will have your sides run through with a sword. Seeing the head of Holofernes, Achior fell upon his face on the ground in terror, and his spirit fainted. But afterward, when he had recovered his breath, he went to her feet and worshipped her and said: Blessed are you by your God in every tent of Jacob, for in every nation that shall hear your name the God of Israel shall be glorified. Chapter 14.
And Judith said to all the people: Hear me, brothers. Hang this head upon our walls; and as soon as the sun rises, let every man take up his arms and go out with great noise, not going down but as though making an attack. Then the scouts will need to flee to their commander to report for battle. And when their leaders rush to the tent of Holofernes and find him headless, wallowing in his own blood, fear will fall upon them. When you know they are fleeing, go after them in safety, for the Lord will crush them under your feet. Then Achior, seeing the power that the God of Israel had shown, left the rite of the gentiles, believed in God, and was circumcised, and was joined to the people of Israel, and all his descendants to this day. As soon as day broke, they hung the head of Holofernes upon the walls, and every man took his weapons, and they went out with great noise and shouting. Seeing this, the scouts ran to the tent. And those who were in the tent came and made a clamor before the entrance to the chamber, trying to rouse him by noise — not by calling, but by sounds — so that Holofernes would wake on his own. For no one dared to enter the chamber of the captain of the Assyrians by knocking or entering. But when his commanders and tribunes and all the chief officers of the Assyrian army arrived, they said to the chamberlains: Go in and wake him, for the mice have come out of their holes in the walls.

Judith.

they dared to call us to battle. Then entering the empty tent of Holofernes, he stood before the curtain and clapped his hands together, thinking that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith. But when he heard no sound from the one lying there, he came forward and drew back the curtain, and found the corpse of Holofernes lying upon the ground, headless, swimming in his own blood. He cried out with a loud voice and wept, and tore his garments. He then entered Judith's tent and did not find her. He rushed outside and cried: "One Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar. For Holofernes lies upon the ground, and his head is not with him." When the leaders of the Assyrian army heard this, they all tore their garments, and unbearable fear and trembling fell upon them, and their minds were greatly troubled. And there arose a great cry throughout the camp. Chapter XV.

When the whole army heard that Holofernes had been beheaded, all courage and counsel fled from them, and seized with trembling and fear they took to flight, so that no one spoke to his neighbor, but each bowed his head and fled, hoping to escape the Hebrews, whom they heard coming upon them armed, rushing along roads, fields, and hillsides. The sons of Israel, seeing them flee, followed after them, coming down with blaring trumpets and shouting. And since the Assyrians were fleeing in disorder, the sons of Israel, pursuing in one body, cut down all they could find. Ozias sent messengers to all the cities and regions of Israel. And so every region and every city sent out their armed young men in pursuit of them.

And they pursued them at sword's point until they had reached the far borders of their territory. But those who remained in Bethulia entered the camp of the Assyrians and carried off the plunder that the fleeing Assyrians had left behind, and they were laden down greatly. And those who returned victorious to Bethulia brought with them everything the enemy had owned, so that there was no counting the cattle, the oxen, and all the moveable goods — so that from the least to the greatest, all became rich from the spoils. And Joachim the high priest came from Jerusalem to Bethulia with all his priests to see Judith. When she came out to him, they all blessed her with one voice, saying: "You are the glory of Jerusalem, you are the joy of Israel, you are the honor of our people. For you have acted bravely, and your heart was strengthened because you loved chastity and after your husband you have not known another man: therefore the hand of the Lord has strengthened you, and therefore you shall be blessed forever." And all the people said: "So be it, so be it." For thirty days they gathered the spoils of the Assyrians, and all the personal possessions of Holofernes that were found to be his were given to Judith in gold, silver, garments, gems and all his furnishings, and all these were delivered to her by the people. And all the people rejoiced with women, virgins, and young men, with organs and harps. Chapter XVI.

Then Judith sang this song to the Lord, saying: Begin to the Lord with timbrels, sing to the Lord with cymbals, raise up a new psalm to him, exalt and call upon his name. The Lord crushes wars; the Lord is his name. He placed his camp in the midst of his people to deliver us from the hand of all our enemies.

Esther.

to find by what words one could express the injury suffered by a person, or the one who committed the injury. But you, O Paula and Eustochium, since you have endeavored to enter the Hebrew libraries and have verified the debates of the interpreters, examine the Hebrew book of Esther word by word alongside our translation: so that you may recognize that I have added nothing beyond what was there, but have faithfully and simply transmitted the Hebrew history into the Latin tongue, just as it is in Hebrew. We do not seek the praises of men, nor do we shrink from their reproaches: for seeking to please God, we do not at all fear the threats of men, since God scatters the bones of those who seek to please men, and those who are of such a kind, as the apostle says, cannot be servants of Christ. Furthermore, in the book of Esther we have made the alphabet from aleph through the letter teth diverge in various places, wishing thereby to suggest to the studious reader the order of the seventy interpreters. But we have preferred to follow the Hebrew order in the Septuagint edition.

Here ends the preface. Here begins the book of Esther. Chapter 1.

In the days of Ahasuerus, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces: when he sat on the throne of his kingdom, the city of Susa was the seat of his reign. In the third year of his reign, he gave a great banquet for all his princes and his servants, the most powerful of the Persians and Medes, the nobles and governors of the provinces, to display before them the riches of the glory of his kingdom and the great splendor of his power for many days, namely one hundred and eighty days. And when the days of the banquet were over, he invited all the people who were found in Susa, from the greatest to the least:

and he commanded that a banquet be prepared for seven days in the courtyard of the garden and grove, which was adorned with royal furnishings and decorations. And hangings of linen in colors of sky-blue and violet were stretched out on every side, supported by cords of fine linen and purple, fastened to ivory rings and marble columns. Couches of gold and silver were placed upon a pavement of emerald and Parian stone of marvelous variety, decorated with wondrous painting. Those who were invited drank from golden cups, and food was brought in various and different vessels. Wine was provided in abundance, as befitted the royal magnificence, and was placed before the chief guests: nor was there anyone to compel those who were unwilling to drink, but the king had appointed stewards over each of the princes, that everyone might take as much as he wished. Queen Vashti also gave a banquet for the women in the palace where King Ahasuerus was accustomed to dwell. So on the seventh day, when the king was merry and had grown warm after much wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven eunuchs who served in his presence, to bring Queen Vashti before the king with the royal crown upon her head, to show her beauty to all the peoples and princes. For she was very beautiful. But she refused and despised the king's command which he had sent through the eunuchs. Whereupon the king was angry and burned with great fury, and consulted the wise men who according to royal custom were always at his side and who directed all things by their counsel, knowing the laws and ordinances of their elders: and the chief among them were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, seven princes

+ Esther.

of the Persians and the Medes who saw the face of the king and who sat first in the kingdom: as to what sentence queen Vashti should receive for not obeying the command of king Ahasuerus which he had sent to her by his chamberlains. Then Memucan answered before the king and the princes: Vashti the queen has not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of king Ahasuerus. For this deed of the queen shall become known to all women, so that they shall despise their husbands in their eyes, when it shall be reported: the king Ahasuerus commanded Vashti the queen to be brought in before him, but she came not. Likewise shall the ladies of Persia and Media say this day to all the king's princes, which have heard of the deed of the queen. Thus shall there arise too much contempt and wrath. If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate to another that is better than she. And when the king's decree which he shall make shall be published throughout all his empire, all the wives shall give to their husbands honor. This pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan: for he sent letters into all the king's provinces, into every province according to the writing thereof, and to every people after their language, that every man should bear rule in his own house. Chapter 2.

After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her. Then said the king's servants that ministered unto him: Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king: and let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto the city of Susa, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hegai the king's chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given them. And let the maiden which pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti. This pleased the king; and he did so. Now in the city of Susa there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite; who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away. And he brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle's daughter: for she had neither father nor mother, and the maid was fair and beautiful; whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter. So it came to pass, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto the city of Susa into the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king's house. Now when every maid's turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus, after that she had completed twelve months, according to the manner of the women...

Esther

They would anoint them with oil of myrrh and other fine spices and ointments. And those who went in to the king received whatever they asked for to adorn themselves, and as it pleased them: they were brought from the women's quarters to the king's chamber. She who entered in the evening would leave in the morning, and from there would be led to the second house, which was under the care of Shaashgaz the king's eunuch, who was in charge of the concubines. She could not return to the king again unless he wished it and called her by name. Now when the turn came, in due order, for Esther, the daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai — who had adopted her as his own daughter — to go in to the king, she did not seek women's ornaments, but whatever Hegai the eunuch, keeper of the virgins, advised, that he gave her for her adornment. She was exceedingly beautiful and lovely to look upon, gracious and pleasing in the eyes of all. So she was brought to the chamber of King Ahasuerus in the tenth month, which is called Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. And the king loved her more than all the women, and she obtained grace and favor in his sight more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown upon her head and made her queen in place of Vashti. And he commanded a great feast to be prepared for all his princes and servants, for the union and marriage of Esther. And he gave rest to all the provinces and bestowed gifts with royal generosity. And while virgins were being sought and gathered together, Mordecai remained at the gate of the king. Esther had not yet revealed her homeland and her people, according to his command. For whatever he commanded, Esther observed, and did all things just as

she had been accustomed to do in the time when he had raised her as a child. Now at that time, while Mordecai was staying at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two eunuchs of the king who were doorkeepers and resided at the first threshold of the palace, were angered and plotted to rise up against the king and kill him. This did not escape Mordecai. He immediately told Queen Esther, and she reported it to the king in the name of Mordecai, who had informed her. The matter was investigated and found to be true, and both of them were hanged on a gallows. And the king commanded it to be recorded in the book of chronicles in his presence, so that a reward might be found for him. And it was entrusted to the histories and annals before the king. Chapter III.

After these things, King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hammedatha, who was of the race of Agag, and set his throne above all the princes he had. And all the king's servants who were at the palace gate bowed the knee and did reverence to Haman, for so the king had commanded concerning him. But Mordecai alone did not bow the knee, nor did he do reverence to him. Then the king's servants who were at the palace gate said to him: Why do you not observe the king's command? And when they spoke this to him day after day, and he would not listen, they told Haman, wishing to know whether he would hold to his purpose, for he had told them that he was a Jew. When Haman heard this and verified by experience that Mordecai did not bow his knee nor do him reverence, he was filled with anger. And he thought it beneath him to lay hands on Mordecai alone, for he had learned what people he belonged to, and rather sought to destroy all the Jews who were in the kingdom of Ahasuerus. In the first month, whose name is Nisan, in the twelfth year of the reign of Ahasuerus, a lot was cast into the urn

· Esther ·

which in Hebrew is called Pur, cast before Haman, to determine on what day and in what month the Jewish people should be destroyed; and the twelfth month, which is called Adar, fell. And Haman said to King Ahasuerus: There is a people scattered and dispersed among all the provinces of your kingdom, separated from one another, using new laws and ceremonies, and furthermore despising the king's decrees; and you know well that it is not expedient for your kingdom that they should grow insolent through indulgence. If it please you, decree that they shall perish, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into your treasury. So the king took the ring from his hand and gave it to Haman, son of Hammedatha of the race of Agag, the enemy of the Jews, and said to him: The silver which you offer shall be yours; do with the people as you please. Then the king's scribes were summoned in the first month, Nisan, on the thirteenth day of that month, and it was written as Haman had commanded to all the satraps of the king, and to the governors of all the diverse provinces, and to each people according to their language, in the name of King Ahasuerus, and the letters sealed with his ring were sent by the king's couriers to all the provinces, to kill and destroy all Jews, young and old, women and children, on one day, which is the thirteenth of the twelfth month, which is called Adar, and to plunder their goods. The sum of the letters was that all provinces should know and prepare themselves for that day. The couriers who were sent hastened to fulfill the king's command. And immediately the decree was posted in Susa; and the king and Haman celebrated with a banquet, while all the Jews who were in the city wept. Chapter 4.

When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he tore his garments and put on sackcloth, sprinkling ashes on his head, and went through the middle of the city crying out with a loud voice, showing the bitterness of his soul, and he went lamenting all the way to the doors of the palace. For no one clothed in sackcloth was permitted to enter the king's court. In all the provinces, towns, and places where the king's cruel decree had arrived, there was great lamentation among the Jews, fasting, wailing, and weeping, with many lying on sackcloth and ashes. Then Esther's maids and eunuchs came and told her. Hearing this she was greatly troubled, and sent garments to clothe Mordecai, so that he might put off the sackcloth; but he would not accept them. Then she called Hathach, the eunuch whom the king had appointed to serve her, and commanded him to go to Mordecai and learn from him why he was doing this. Hathach went out to Mordecai and found him standing in the open square of the city before the palace gate. Mordecai told him everything that had happened, and how Haman had promised to pay silver into the king's treasury for the destruction of the Jews. He also gave him a copy of the decree that had been posted in Susa, to show to Esther, and to urge her to go to the king and plead with him for her people. Hathach returned and told Esther all that Mordecai had said. She answered him and commanded him to say to Mordecai: All the king's servants and all the people of the king's provinces know that if any man or woman enters the king's inner court without being called, the law is that they shall be put to death immediately, unless the king holds out to them the golden scepter as a sign of clemency, so that they may live. How then can I go to the king, since I have not been called to him for thirty days? When Mordecai heard this, he again sent word to Esther, saying: Do not think that you alone among all the Jews will escape with your life, because you are in

Esther

You are the foremost among all the Jews before the king. If you remain silent now, the Jews will be freed by some other means, but you and your father's house will perish. And who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this? Then Esther sent back this reply to Mordecai: Go and gather together all the Jews who are in the city, and pray for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day; I and my maidens will likewise fast. Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law, and if I perish, I perish. So Mordecai went away and did everything that Esther had commanded him. Chapter 5.

On the third day, Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the palace, opposite the king's hall. The king was sitting on his royal throne in the throne room, opposite the entrance to the palace. When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his sight, and he held out to her the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther approached and touched the top of the scepter. The king said to her: What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even if it is half of my kingdom, it shall be given to you. And she answered: If it please the king, let the king and Haman come today to a banquet that I have prepared. The king immediately said: Bring Haman quickly, that Esther's wish may be fulfilled. So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared. And the king said to her after the wine had been drunk abundantly: What is your petition? It shall be granted you. Even if you ask for half of my kingdom, you shall have it. Esther replied: My petition and my request is this: If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it please the king to grant my petition and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and tomorrow I will do as the king has said.

Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when he saw Mordecai at the king's gate, who neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with anger against Mordecai. Nevertheless, Haman restrained himself, and went home. Then he sent and called for his friends and his wife Zeresh, and told them of the glory of his riches and the multitude of his children, and how the king had advanced him above the princes and servants of the king. He also said: Moreover, Queen Esther invited no one but me to come with the king to the banquet she prepared, and tomorrow also I am invited by her together with the king. Yet all this means nothing to me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate. Then his wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him: Let a gallows fifty cubits high be made, and in the morning tell the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then you may go cheerfully with the king to the banquet. This advice pleased Haman, and he had the gallows made. Chapter 6.

That night the king could not sleep, and he commanded that the book of records, the chronicles, be brought and read to him. And as they were reading before the king, they came to the passage where it was recorded how Mordecai had reported the plot of Bigthana and Teresh, the two eunuchs of the king who had sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. The king asked: What honor and distinction has been given to Mordecai for this? His servants said: Nothing has been done for him. The king then said: Who is in the court? Now Haman had just entered the outer court of the king's palace.

· Esther ·

that he should suggest to the king and have Mordecai hanged on the gallows that had been prepared for him. The servants answered: Haman is standing in the courtyard. The king said: Let him come in. And when he had come in, the king said to him: What should be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor? Now Haman thought in his heart, and supposed that the king wished to honor no one but himself. And he answered: The man whom the king wishes to honor should be dressed in the king's robes, and set upon the horse that the king rides, and have the royal crown placed upon his head, and let one of the king's most noble princes lead the horse through the streets of the city, proclaiming and calling out: Thus shall he be honored whom the king wishes to honor. The king then said to him: Make haste, and take the robe and the horse, and do as you have said to Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king's gate. Leave out nothing of all that you have spoken. So Haman took the robe and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai in the street of the city, and had him ride through it, proclaiming before him: Thus shall he be honored whom the king wishes to honor. And Mordecai returned to the king's gate, but Haman hurried to his house, mourning and with his head covered, and told Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His wise men and his wife Zeresh said to him: If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him, but will surely fall before him. While they were still speaking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared. Chapter VII.

So the king and Haman went to drink with Queen Esther. And the king said to Esther again on the second day, as the wine was flowing: What is your petition, Esther, that it may be granted you? And what is your request? Even to half of my kingdom it shall be granted. Then Queen Esther answered and said: If I have found favor in your sight, O king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be given me as my petition, and my people as my request. For we have been sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be killed, and to perish. And if we had been sold merely as slaves, I would have held my tongue, for the affliction is not to be compared with the harm to the king. Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther: Who is he, and where is he, who dares to do this? And Esther said: The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman! Then Haman was terrified before the king and queen. The king arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking and went into the palace garden; and Haman stood up to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that harm was determined against him by the king. And when the king returned from the palace garden to the banquet room, Haman had thrown himself on the couch where Esther was. And the king said: Will he even assault the queen in my own house? The words had barely left the king's mouth when they covered Haman's face. Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs who served the king, said: Behold, the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, who spoke good on the king's behalf, stands at Haman's house, fifty cubits high. And the king said: Hang him on it. So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king's wrath was appeased. Chapter VIII.

On that day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews; and Mordecai came before the king, for Esther had revealed what he was to her. And she took...

· Esther ·

She received the ring which she had ordered to be taken back from Haman and gave it to Mordecai. Esther also set Mordecai over her house. Not content with this, she went to the feet of the king, wept and spoke to him, and begged him that he would put away the evil of Haman the Agagite and all his wicked devices which he had devised against the Jews. Then the king held out the golden scepter toward Esther with his hand, as a sign of his clemency. And she rising up stood before him and said: If it please the king and if I have found favor in his eyes, and my petition be not disagreeable to him, I beseech him that the former letters of Haman the enemy and traitor of the Jews, which he sent to destroy them in all the king's provinces, may be corrected. For how can I endure the murder and slaughter of my people? And king Ahasuerus answered Esther the queen, and Mordecai the Jew: I have given Haman's house to Esther, and him they have hanged on a gibbet because he durst lay hands on the Jews. Write therefore to the Jews as it pleaseth you in the king's name, and seal the letters with my ring. For this was the custom, that no one could contradict the letters which were sent in the king's name and sealed with his ring. Then the king's scribes and secretaries were called. It was now the third month, which is called Sivan, and on the twenty-third day of that month, letters were written as Mordecai wished to the Jews and to the princes and governors and judges of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia; to each province in its own script and language, and to the Jews in their script and language, as they were able to read and hear. These letters, which were sent in the king's name, were sealed with his ring, and sent by couriers throughout all the provinces,

so that they might run ahead with new messengers before the previous letters. The king commanded that the Jews should gather together in every city, and assemble themselves to stand for their lives, and to destroy, kill, and cause to perish all the power of the people and province that would assault them, with their children and women, and to take the spoil of them for a prey. The day appointed for this throughout all the provinces was the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is called Adar. The sum of the letters was that in all lands and peoples subject to the rule of king Ahasuerus, it should be made known that the Jews were ready to take vengeance upon their enemies. And the couriers went out being hastened by the king's commandment, and the decree was given in Susa the palace. And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal apparel of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and with a garment of fine linen and purple. And the city of Susa rejoiced and was glad. The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honor. And in every province and in every city, whithersoever the king's commandment and his decree came, the Jews had joy and gladness, a feast and a good day. And many of the people of the land became Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell upon them. Chapter 9. Now in the twelfth month, which is called Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, on the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, it was turned to the contrary that the Jews had rule over them that hated them. The Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces to lay hand on such as sought their hurt. And no man could withstand them, because

. Esther .

the fear of his greatness would penetrate all peoples. For even the judges, commanders, and administrators of the provinces, and all persons of rank who presided over individual places and duties, were exalting the Jews out of fear of Mordecai, whom they recognized as a chief official of the palace and a man of great influence. His fame grew daily and spread through the mouths of all. And so the Jews struck down their enemies with a great slaughter and killed them, repaying those who had prepared evil against them: so that they killed even five hundred men in Susa, including the ten sons of Haman the Agagite, enemy of the Jews. These are their names: Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha. But when they had killed them, they did not touch their property. Immediately the number of those killed in Susa was reported to the king. He said to the queen: "In the city of Susa the Jews have killed five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman. How much more do you think they have accomplished in all the provinces? What more do you ask? What else do you wish to be done?" She answered: "If it please the king, let permission be given to the Jews to do tomorrow in Susa as they have done today, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the gallows." The king commanded that this be done. Immediately a decree was published in Susa, and the ten sons of Haman were hanged. When the Jews had assembled on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar in Susa, they killed three hundred men there; but they did not seize any of their goods. Throughout all the provinces that were subject to the king's rule, the Jews stood up for their lives against their enemies and persecutors, so that as many as seventy-five thousand of the slain were counted, and no one seized any of their property. The thirteenth day of the month of Adar was the day of the killing for all, and on the fourteenth day they ceased. They appointed that day to be solemn, so that thereafter they would spend it each year in feasting, joy, and banqueting. But those who had been engaged in Susa on the thirteenth and fourteenth days rested on the fifteenth, and therefore established that same day as a day of feasting and gladness. The Jews who dwelt in unwalled towns and villages appointed the fourteenth day of the month of Adar for feasting and joy, so that they might rejoice on it and send portions of food to one another. And Mordecai wrote down all these things and sent letters to all the Jews dwelling in all the provinces of the king, both near and far, that they should observe the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar as feasts every year, and should celebrate them with solemn honor when they came again each year, because on those days the Jews had taken vengeance on their enemies, and their mourning and sorrow had been turned into joy and gladness; and that these should be days of feasting and gladness, in which they should send portions of food to one another and give gifts to the poor. And the Jews took upon themselves, as a solemn obligation, all that they had begun to do and that Mordecai had directed them in his letters. For Haman, son of Hammedatha, of the race of Agag, the enemy and adversary of the Jews, had plotted evil against them to kill them and destroy them, and had cast the lot (which in our language is called purim), and afterward Esther went in to the king, begging that his schemes might be made void by the king's letters, and that the evil which he had

· Esther ·

against the Jews had turned back upon his own head. And they also hanged him and his sons upon the gallows; and from that time these days are called Purim, that is, lots; because the lot (Hebrew: pur) was cast into the urn. And all things that were done are contained in this book, that is, in the volume of this epistle; and whatever they underwent, and what was changed afterwards, the Jews took upon themselves and their descendants, and upon all those who wished to join their religion: that it should be lawful for no one to pass over these two days without solemnity, as the scripture testifies; and so on, repeating through the years that succeed one another. These are the days which no forgetfulness shall ever blot out; and in every province throughout the whole world, these days shall be celebrated in all generations; nor is there any city in which the days of Purim, that is of lots, shall not be observed by the Jews, and by their posterity, which is bound to these ceremonies. And Esther the queen, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, also wrote a second letter, that with all diligence this solemn day should be established for the future. And they sent to all the Jews that dwelt in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of King Ahasuerus, that they should have peace and receive the truth, observing the days of lots, and celebrating them with joy, as Mordecai and Esther had appointed. And they received it as a duty for themselves and their descendants: the fasts and cries and the days of lots; and all things that were contained in the history of this book called Esther. Chapter 10.

King Ahasuerus made all the land and all the islands of the sea tributary; whose strength and empire and dignity and greatness by which he exalted Mordecai are written in the books of the Medes and Persians; and how Mordecai, of Jewish descent, was second to King Ahasuerus and great among the Jews, and acceptable to the multitude of his brethren, seeking the good of his people, and speaking those things which pertained to the peace of his descendants. What is contained in Hebrew with full authority is here compressed; but what follows is found in the common edition which is contained in the Greek language and letters; and I found this chapter after the end of the book, which according to our custom I have marked as supplementary. Mordecai said: These things are done by God. I remembered the dream I had seen signifying these same things: and none of them was without fulfillment. A small spring which grew into a river and turned into a great light and overflowed into many waters — that is Esther, whom the king took for his wife and wished to be queen. The two dragons are myself and Haman. The nations that gathered together — these are they who attempted to blot out the name of the Jews. But my people Israel is the one that cried out to the Lord; and the Lord saved his people and delivered us from all evils; and he worked great signs and wonders among the nations: and he commanded there should be two lots — one for the people of God, and another for all the nations. And both lots came to their appointed hour from that time before God for all nations; and the Lord remembered his people and had mercy on his inheritance. And these days shall be observed in the month of Adar, on the fourteenth and fifteenth day of the same month, with all diligence and joy, when the people themselves are gathered together into the cities, throughout the succeeding generations of the people of Israel. Chapter 11.

In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said he was a priest and of the Levitical race, and Ptolemy his son, brought this letter of Purim, which they said Lysimachus, the son of Ptolemy,

Esther

in Jerusalem. This was the preface in the Vulgate edition, which is found neither in Hebrew nor printed anywhere else. In the second year of the reign of the great Artaxerxes, on the first day of the month of Nisan, Mordecai had a dream — the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin — a Jewish man who dwelt in the city of Susa, a great man and among the first of the royal court. He was of the number of the captives whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away from Jerusalem with Jeconiah king of Judah. And this was his dream: There appeared voices and tumults, and there were thunderings and earthquakes and a disturbance over the land; and behold two great dragons came forward, ready to fight one another; and at their cry all nations were roused to fight against the nation of the just. And that day was one of darkness and trial, of tribulation and anguish, and great dread over the land. And the nation of the just was troubled, fearing their own evils and prepared for death. And they cried out to God; and from their great crying, a little spring grew into a great river and overflowed with many waters. Light and sun rose up, and the humble were exalted, and they devoured the mighty. When Mordecai had seen this and risen from his bed, he pondered what God wished to do, and was determined to understand what the dream might mean. Chapter XII.

Now he was staying at that time in the king's court, with Bagatha and Thara, the eunuchs of the king who were keepers of the palace. And when he had learned their intentions and understood their plans more carefully, he discovered that they were plotting to lay hands on King Artaxerxes, and he reported it to the king. The king questioned both of them, and when they confessed, he ordered them to be led to their death. And the king wrote down what had taken place in the chronicles. But also Mordecai put the matter on record in writing. And the king commanded him to remain in the royal court, and gave him gifts for his information. But Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, was most glorious before the king, and he wished to harm Mordecai and his own people on account of the two eunuchs of the king who had been killed. Thus far the prologue. The things that follow were placed in that location in the book, and they plundered their goods or possessions. These things are found only in the Vulgate edition. The letter moreover was as follows. Chapter XIII.

The great king Artaxerxes, to the princes and governors of the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia that are subject to his rule, greetings. When I had come to rule over many nations and brought the whole world under my dominion, I wished in no way to abuse the greatness of my power, but rather to govern my subjects with clemency and gentleness, so that, living their lives without any terror, they might enjoy the peace desired by all mortals. But when I inquired of my counselors how this might be accomplished, one who surpassed the rest in wisdom and loyalty, second only to the king, named Haman, informed me that there was scattered throughout the whole world a people that used strange laws, and acting contrary to the customs of all nations, despised the commands of kings and violated the concord of all peoples by their dissension. When we learned this, seeing that one nation was rebellious against all humanity, living by perverse laws, opposing our commands and disturbing the peace and harmony of the provinces subject to us, we commanded that whomever Haman — who is set over all the provinces —

· ESTHER ·

And he is known to the king, and him whom we honor in the place of a father — let them be destroyed along with their wives and children by their enemies, and let none of them be spared. On the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar, in the full year, so that the wicked men may descend to the underworld in a single day and restore to our rule the one who had thrown it into turmoil. And further, regarding the copy of the letter: what follows after that place where it is written I found recorded — that Mordecai, going forth, did all things that Esther had commanded him — yet it is not found in the Hebrew text and is found with none of the interpreters. But Mordecai prayed to the Lord, mindful of all His works, and said: O Lord, Lord, almighty King, all things are in Your power, and there is none who can resist Your will, if You have decided to save Israel. You made heaven and earth and all that is contained within the circuit of heaven; You are the Lord of all, and there is none who can resist Your majesty. You know all things, and You know that it was not out of pride or contempt or any desire for glory that I did this — that I would not bow to the arrogant Haman — for I would willingly have kissed even the soles of his feet for the salvation of Israel; but I feared lest I should transfer the honor of my God to a man, and lest I should bow down to any but You, my God. And now, O Lord, O King, O God of Abraham, have mercy on Your people, for our enemies desire to destroy us and to blot out Your inheritance. Do not despise the portion You redeemed from Egypt. Hear my prayer and be gracious to Your lot and inheritance, and turn our mourning into joy, that we who live may praise Your name, O Lord; and do not close the mouths of those who sing to You. And all Israel likewise, with one mind and supplication, cried out to the Lord, because certain death hung over them. Chapter 14.

Esther also, the queen, fled to the Lord, fearing the danger that threatened her. And having laid aside her royal garments, she put on garments fitting for mourning and lamentation; and instead of costly ointments, she covered her head with ashes and dung, and humbled her body with fasting, and all the places where she had formerly rejoiced she filled with the dishevelment of her grief. And she prayed to the Lord God of Israel, saying: O my Lord, You alone are our king; help me, a woman alone, for I have no helper but You, and my danger is in my own hands. I have heard from my father that You, O Lord, took Israel from among all the nations, and our fathers from all their ancestors before them, to possess an everlasting inheritance, and You did for them what You had promised. We have sinned before You, and therefore You delivered us into the hands of our enemies. We worshipped their gods. You are just, O Lord. And now it is not enough for them that they oppress us with the harshest servitude, but attributing strength to the power of their idols, they wish to change Your promises and to destroy Your inheritance, and to stop the mouths of those who praise You, and to extinguish the glory of Your temple and altar, so that they may open the mouths of the nations and praise the strength of idols, and proclaim a mortal king forever. Do not surrender Your scepter, O Lord, to those who are nothing, lest they mock our ruin; but turn their counsel against themselves, and destroy him who has begun to rise against us. Remember, O Lord, and show Yourself to us in the time of our tribulation, and give me courage, O Lord, King, God of all power. Grant me speech well-composed in my mouth before the lion, and turn his heart to hatred of our enemy, so that he himself may perish, and all those who agree with him. But we,

Lord,

. Esther .

free in your hand: and help me, for I have no other helper but you, O Lord, who have knowledge of all things. And you know that I hate the glory of the wicked, and abhor the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner. You know my necessity, that I abhor the sign of pride and of my glory which is upon my head in the days of my display, and that I detest it like a menstrual rag, and do not wear it in the days of my silence; and that I did not eat at Haman's table, nor did the king's banquet please me, and I have not drunk the wine of libations; and that your handmaid has never rejoiced since I was brought here until this present day, except in you, O Lord God of Abraham. O mighty God above all, hear the voice of those who have no other hope, and deliver us from the hand of the wicked, and rescue me from my fear. These things which I found added in the Vulgate edition. Ch. 15.

And Mordecai commanded Esther without doubt, that she should go to the king and entreat him for her people and for her homeland. Remember, he said, the days of your lowliness, how you were nurtured in my hand: for Haman, who is second after the king, has spoken against us to bring us to death. Invoke the Lord and speak to the king for us, and deliver us from death. And the rest of what is recorded there. On the third day she laid aside the garments of her service and clothed herself in her glorious apparel. And when she was arrayed in royal robes, and had called upon the all-seeing God and Savior, she took two maids with her: and upon one she leaned, as if for delicacy and excessive tenderness of body she could not bear herself: the other maid followed her mistress bearing up her garments that flowed on the ground. But she, suffused with a rosy color in her face, and with gracious and sparkling eyes, concealed

her sorrowful heart and the great fear that gripped it. Entering through all the doors in order, she stood before the king, where he sat upon his royal throne, clothed in royal robes, glittering with gold and precious stones: and he was terrible to look upon. When he had raised his face, flushed with the fiercest anger, the queen sank down and grew pale, and fainted and leaned her head upon the maid who accompanied her. But God changed the spirit of the king to gentleness, and anxiously and fearfully he leaped from his throne, and held her in his arms until she recovered, soothing her with these words: What is the matter, Esther? I am your brother; do not fear. You shall not die; for this law is not made for you, but for all. Come near and touch the scepter. As she was silent, he took the golden scepter and laid it upon her neck and kissed her, and said: Why do you not speak to me? She answered: I saw you, my lord, as an angel of God, and my heart was troubled for fear of your majesty. For you are wonderful, my lord, and your face is full of grace. And as she spoke, she fainted again, and was barely revived. And the king was troubled, and all his servants comforted her. The text of the letter of King Artaxerxes which he sent to all the provinces of his kingdom on behalf of the Jews, which is also not found in the Hebrew volume. Ch. 16.

The great King Artaxerxes, to the rulers and governors of one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, who are subject to our command, sends greetings. Many men, the more they have been honored by the great generosity of their patrons, the more proud they have become: and they seek not only to oppress the subjects of kings, but, unable to bear the glory bestowed upon them, they also scheme against those who gave it to them. Nor are they content

· Esther ·

They do not give thanks for benefits and acts of kindness, nor do they refrain from violating the laws of humanity: but believing that they can escape the judgment of God who sees all things. And they break out into such great madness that they attempt to undermine with the tunnels of liars those who faithfully observe the offices entrusted to them and act so uprightly as to be worthy of the praise of all: while the ears of simple princes are deceived by the cunning fraud of those who, by nature, think less of others. This matter is attested both in ancient histories and in daily events: how the pursuits of kings are corrupted by the evil suggestions of certain men. Therefore provision must be made for the peace of all provinces. Nor should you think that if we command divine things, it proceeds from the levity of our mind: but according to the quality and necessity of the times, as the utility of the public good demands judgment. And that you may more clearly understand what we say: Haman, the son of Hammedatha, both in mind and race a Macedonian, alien to Persian blood, having stained our goodwill with his cruelty, was received among us as a foreigner: and having experienced such great humanity toward himself that he was called our father and was worshipped by all next to the king: he was so lifted up with arrogance that he endeavored to deprive us of our kingdom and our life. For Mordecai, by whose faith and benefits we live, and our consort of our kingdom, Esther, together with her entire people, he sought by certain new and unheard of schemes to deliver to death: thinking that by destroying those who were hostile to him he might transfer the kingdom of the Persians to the Macedonians. But we found the Jews, whom this most wicked of mortals had destined to death, to be in no fault whatsoever: but on the contrary, using just laws and being children of the most high and greatest living God, by whose benefit

both to our ancestors and to us the kingdom has been given and is preserved to this day. Know therefore that those letters which he sent under our name are null and void. For which crime, before the gates of this city, that is Susa, he himself who devised it, and all his kindred, hang on the gallows: not rendering to us but to God what he deserved. This edict which we now send out shall be posted in all cities: that the Jews may live by their own laws, to which you ought to give assistance, so that those who had prepared themselves to kill them may be killed on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is called Adar. For God Almighty has turned for them a day of mourning and grief into joy. Therefore you also, among other feast days, hold this day and celebrate it with all gladness: that both now and in the future all may know that those who faithfully serve receive worthy reward for their faith: but those who plot against their kingdom perish through their crime. And every province and city that refuses to participate in this solemnity shall perish by sword and fire: and shall be destroyed so that it shall be not only uninhabitable by men but even avoided by wild beasts forever: as an example of contempt and disobedience. Here begins the prologue to Job according to the translation of the interpreter.

I am compelled, for each book of Holy Scripture, to answer the slanders of adversaries, who accuse my translation by comparison with the Septuagint interpreters: as if even among the Greeks, Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion — whether word for word, or sense for sense, or a mixture of both in a middle manner — did not produce their own kind of translation: and as Origen marked all the books of the Old Testament with obeli and asterisks

· Prologue ·

distinguished — those either added or taken from Theodotion and inserted into the old translation — proving that what was added was lacking. Let my detractors therefore learn to receive the whole, not only in part, or to strip away my inspiration along with its asterisks. For it is possible that those whom they accept as having omitted many things did not also err in some matters — especially in Job — from which, if you remove what has been added under asterisks, a very large portion will be taken away, and this only among the Greeks. But among the Latins, before that translation which we recently published with asterisks and obeli, some seven hundred or eight hundred verses are missing — so that the book, mangled and torn and corrupted, makes a shameful display of itself to public readers. This translation follows none of the old interpreters, but draws from the Hebrew and Arabic text, with Kimhi, and sometimes in Syriac — rendering now words, now meanings, now both together. For the whole book among the Hebrews is considered oblique and slippery, and as the Greek rhetoricians call it, schematic — saying one thing while meaning another. Just as if you try to hold an eel or a small lamprey in a tight grip, the harder you squeeze, the more quickly it slips away. I remember that, to understand this volume, I redeemed at no small price a certain teacher named Lidbanus, who was considered the foremost among the Hebrews — whether his teaching profited me at all, I do not know. This one thing I know: I could not have translated what I had not first understood. From the beginning of the book up to the words of Job, the text among the Hebrews is prose. But from the words of Job in which he says "Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said a man is conceived" — up to the place near the end of the book where the text is written,

it is for this reason that I reproach myself and repent in dust and ashes — the verses are hexametric, running in dactyls and spondees, and because of the nature of the language frequently receiving other feet — not of the same syllables but of the same quantity. Sometimes also the rhythm itself, sweet and rising, flows in meters loosened by rule — which the metricians will understand better than the simple reader. From the aforementioned verse to the end of the book, the small remaining portion returns to prose. If it seems incredible to anyone that there should be meter among the Hebrews — like our Horace and the Greek Pindar and Alcaeus and Sappho or the Psalter or the Lamentations of Jeremiah or virtually all of the sacred writings — let him read Philo, Josephus, Origen, Eusebius of Caesarea, and by their testimony he will be convinced that I speak the truth. Let him hear therefore the reason why I have labored over this volume — not to criticize the ancient translation, but so that those things in it which are obscure, or omitted, or certainly corrupted through scribal error, might be made clearer by our translation — we who have learned the Hebrew language in part, and have been worn down in Latin almost from the cradle among grammarians, rhetoricians, and philosophers. For if among the Greeks, after the edition of the Seventy — now with the gospel of Christ shining forth — the Judaizing heretics Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion were received, who concealed many mysteries of the Savior through crafty translation, and are yet kept and expounded in the churches — how much more am I, a Christian, born of Christian parents, bearing the banner of the cross on my forehead, whose study it has been to recover what was omitted —

Job.

...so that they might come together to visit him and console him. And when they lifted up their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him. And crying out, they wept, and tearing their garments they sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven. And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him. For they saw that his grief was very great. Chapter 3.

After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth, and spoke. Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said that a man is conceived. Let that day be turned into darkness; let not God regard it from above, nor let the light shine upon it. Let darkness and the shadow of death cover it; let a cloud settle upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it. Let that night be solitary, let it not be joined unto the days of the year, nor let it come into the count of the months. Let it be a barren night; let no joyful voice come therein. Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to raise up Leviathan. Let the stars of its twilight be dark; let it wait for light, but have none; neither let it see the dawning of the day. Because it shut not up the doors of my mother's womb, nor hid sorrow from my eyes. Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? Why did the knees receive me? Why were there breasts for me to suck? For now I would lie still and be quiet; I would sleep with kings and counselors of the earth, who built themselves solitary places; or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver. Or as a hidden untimely birth I would not have been; as infants which never saw light. There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary are at rest; and those who were bound are at ease together. They do not hear the voice of the oppressor. The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master. Why is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto those who are bitter in soul? Who long for death, but it does not come; and who dig for it more than for hidden treasures; who rejoice greatly and are glad when they can find the grave. Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, and whom God has hedged in? For my sighing comes before I eat, and my roarings are poured out like the waters. For the thing which I greatly feared has come upon me, and that which I was afraid of has come to me. Was I not at peace? Had I not quiet? Had I not rest? Yet trouble came. Chapter 4.

Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: If one ventures a word to you, will you be offended? But who can keep from speaking? Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened weak hands. Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees. But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed. Is not your fear your confidence, your hope, and the integrity of your ways? Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off? As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed. The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, and the teeth of the young lions are broken. The lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered. Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it. In the troubled visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men, dread came upon me and trembling, and all my bones shook. A spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance; a form was before my eyes, and I heard...

Job.

...as if heard by a light ear. Can a man be justified in comparison with God, or can a man be purer than his maker? Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he found wickedness. How much more those who dwell in houses of clay, who have their foundation in the earth — they will be consumed as by a moth: from morning until evening they will be cut down, and because none understands, they will perish forever. And those who remain will be taken away from them: they will die, but not in wisdom. Chapter 5.
Call out then, if there is anyone who will answer you, and turn to some of the saints. Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the simple. I have seen the fool taking root, and I immediately cursed his dwelling. His children are far from safety, and they are crushed in the gate, and there is none to deliver them. The hungry shall eat his harvest, and the armed man shall seize it, and the thirsty shall drink his wealth. Nothing on earth happens without a cause, and sorrow does not spring from the ground. Man is born to labor, and a bird to flying. Therefore I will make my prayer to God, and to God I will set forth my cause: Who does great and unsearchable things, and marvels without number. Who gives rain upon the face of the earth, and waters the fields. Who sets the humble on high, and lifts the mourners to safety. Who frustrates the devices of the wicked, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they planned. Who catches the wise in their own craftiness, and overthrows the counsel of the wicked. In the daytime they run into darkness, and grope at noon as in the night. But he saves the poor from the sword of their mouth, and the needy from the hand of the violent. And there shall be hope for the poor, but wickedness shall shut its mouth. Blessed is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty,

...do not reject the Lord's correction: for he wounds, and he heals; he strikes, and his hands make whole. In six troubles he will deliver you, and in the seventh no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, and you shall not fear disaster when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and you shall not be afraid of the beasts of the earth. For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you. And you shall know that your tent is safe, and you shall visit your dwelling and not sin. You shall know also that your offspring shall be many, and your descendants as the grass of the earth. You shall come to your grave in full age, as a shock of grain comes in its season. Behold, this we have searched out; it is true. Hear it, and know it for your own good. Chapter 6.
Then Job answered and said: Oh that my grief were thoroughly weighed, and the calamity that I have suffered laid in the balance together — it would be heavier than the sand of the sea. Therefore my words are full of anguish, for the arrows of the Lord are in me, and my spirit drinks in their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me. Does the wild donkey bray when it has grass, or does the ox low over its fodder? Can that which is unsavory be eaten without salt? Or is there any taste in the white of an egg? My soul refuses to touch such things; they are like the food of my affliction. Oh that I might have my request, and that God would grant the thing I long for — that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off. Then I should still have comfort; yes, I would even exult in pain that spares nothing, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One. What strength do I have, that I should wait...

.Job.

Is my end such that I should act with patience? My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh made of bronze. Truly there is no help for me within myself, and my close friends have departed from me. He who withholds kindness from a friend forsakes the fear of the Lord. My brothers have passed by me like a torrent that rushes swiftly through the valleys. Those who fear the frost: snow shall fall upon them. At the time when they were scattered they perished, and when the heat comes they melt away from their place. The paths of their course are twisted; they walk into emptiness and perish. Consider the paths of Tema, the roads of Sheba, and wait a little while. They are confounded because I hoped. They came even to me and were covered with shame. Now you have come, and seeing my plague you said: Did I ask you to bring me something, or to give me of your substance, or to deliver me from the hand of the enemy and rescue me from the hand of the mighty? Teach me and I will be silent; and whatever I have ignorantly done, show me. Why do you speak against words of truth, when there is none among you who can refute me? You devise only to rebuke and utter words to the wind. You rush upon the fatherless and seek to undermine your own friend. Yet finish what you have begun. Give ear and see whether I speak falsely. Answer me, I pray, without contention, and speak what is just and I will judge it. You will not find iniquity in my tongue, nor will folly sound in my words. Chapter 7.
Is not the life of man upon earth a warfare, and his days like the days of a hired laborer? Like a servant who longs for the shade, and like a hired laborer who looks for his wages: so I also have had empty months, and I have numbered wearisome nights. If I lie down to sleep, I say: When shall I arise? And again I wait for the evening, and am filled with sorrows until darkness. My flesh is clothed with corruption and the filth of dust; my skin has dried up and shrunk. My days have passed more swiftly than a weaver cuts cloth, and they are spent without any hope. Remember that my life is but wind, and my eye shall not return to see good things; the eye of man shall not behold me. Your eyes are upon me, and I shall not exist. As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who goes down to the underworld shall not ascend; he shall return no more to his home, and his place shall know him no more. Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will discourse with the bitterness of my soul. Am I the sea or a whale, that you have enclosed me in prison? If I say: My bed shall comfort me and I shall find relief speaking with myself upon my couch: then you frighten me with dreams and terrify me with visions. So that my soul chooses strangling and death rather than my bones. I despair; I shall live no longer. Spare me, for my days are nothing. What is man that you magnify him, or that you set your heart upon him? You visit him early in the morning and suddenly you test him. How long will you not spare me, nor allow me to swallow my saliva? I have sinned. What shall I do for you, O keeper of men? Why have you set me as your adversary, so that I am a burden to myself? Why do you not remove my sin, and why do you not take away my iniquity? Behold, I shall sleep in the dust; and if you seek me in the morning, I shall not exist. Chapter 8.
Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: How long will you speak such things? The words of your mouth are like a strong wind. Does God pervert judgment, or does the Almighty subvert what is just?

Job.

Even if your sons have sinned against him and he has given them over to the power of their transgression: yet if you will arise early to God and make supplication to the Almighty; if you are pure and upright, surely now he will rouse himself for you and restore your righteous dwelling. And though your beginning was small, your latter days will be very great. For inquire, please, of bygone ages and consider what the fathers have searched out; for we are but of yesterday and know nothing, for our days on earth are a shadow, and they will teach you and tell you and utter words out of their understanding. Can papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Can reeds flourish where there is no water? While yet in flower and not cut down, they wither before any other plant. Such are the paths of all who forget God; the hope of the godless shall perish. His confidence is cut off; what he trusts in is a spider's web. He leans against his house, but it does not stand; he holds fast to it, but it does not endure. He is moist before the sun comes, and his shoots spread over his garden. His roots entwine the stone heap; he looks upon a house of stones. If he is destroyed from his place, then it will deny him, saying, I have never seen you. Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the earth others will spring. God will not reject a blameless man, nor take the hand of evildoers, till he fills your mouth with laughter and your lips with shouting. Those who hate you will be clothed with shame, and the tent of the wicked will be no more. Chapters 7 and 9.

Then Job answered and said: Truly I know that it is so: how can a man be in the right before God? If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times. He is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has hardened himself against him and succeeded? He who removes mountains and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger;

who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble; who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars; who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea; who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south; who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number. If he passes me, I will not see him; if he moves on, I will not perceive him. If he seizes the prey, who can turn him back? Who will say to him, What are you doing? God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab. How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him? Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser. Even if I called and he answered me, I do not believe he would listen to my voice. For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause; he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness. If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him? Though I am righteous, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse. Even if I am blameless, I do not know myself; I loathe my life. It is all one; therefore I say he destroys both the blameless and the wicked. When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges. My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away, they see no good. They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey. When I say I will forget my complaint...

· Job ·

You turn your face away from me and torment me. All my works were a terror to me, knowing you would not spare the sinner. But if I am wicked, why have I labored in vain? If I wash myself with waters of snow and my hands shine like the purest cloth, yet you would dip me in filth and my own garments would abhor me. For he is not a man as I am, that I should answer him, nor is there one who might contend with him equally in judgment. There is none who can argue both sides and lay his hand upon us both. Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his terror frighten me. Then I would speak and not fear him, for I cannot answer while I am afraid. (Ch. 10)
My soul is weary of my life; I will give free rein to my complaint against myself. I will speak in the bitterness of my soul; I will say to God: Do not condemn me. Tell me why you judge me so. Does it seem good to you to oppress me, to despise the work of your hands, while you smile on the counsel of the wicked? Do you have eyes of flesh, or do you see as a man sees? Are your days like the days of man, or your years like human years, that you search out my iniquity and probe my sin? You know that I am not guilty, yet there is no one who can deliver from your hand. Your hands shaped me and made me altogether, and yet you would suddenly destroy me? Remember that you made me like clay; and will you return me to dust? Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh and knit me together with bones and sinews. You granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit. Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose. If I sin, you watch me, and you will not acquit me of my iniquity.

Why then did you bring me out of the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me. I would have been as though I had not existed, carried from the womb to the grave. Are not my few days almost over? Leave me alone, that I may take a little comfort before I go — and I shall not return — to the land of darkness and deep shadow, the land of gloom and utter darkness, where even light is like darkness, and there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells. (Ch. 11)
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: Should not the multitude of words be answered, or should a man full of talk be justified? Should your boastings make men keep silent, and when you mock, shall no one shame you? For you have said: My speech is pure, and I am clean in your eyes. But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you, and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom — for wisdom is many-sided — that you might know that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves. Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty? It is higher than heaven — what can you do? Deeper than Sheol — how can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea. If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can hinder him? For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it? But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man. If you set your heart aright...

Job

Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth, and take my life in my own hands? Even if he kills me, I will hope in him. But I will defend my ways before him, and he himself will be my savior. For no hypocrite shall come before him. Hear my words, and receive my riddles with your ears. If I am put on trial, I know I shall be found just. Who is there to contend with me? Let him come. Why do I waste away in silence? Grant me only two things, and then I will not hide from your face: withdraw your hand from me, and let not your dread terrify me. Call me and I will answer you; or else I will speak and you reply to me. How many iniquities and sins have I? Show me my transgressions and my faults. Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy? You show your power against a leaf driven by the wind, and you pursue dry stubble. You write bitter things against me, and would consume me for the sins of my youth. You have put my feet in the stocks and watched all my paths, and examined the prints of my feet. I am like something that rots away, like a garment eaten by moths. Man born of woman, living but a short time, is filled with many miseries. He comes forth like a flower and is cut down; he flees like a shadow and does not remain in the same state. Do you think it fitting to open your eyes upon such a one, and to bring him into judgment with you? Who can make clean what is conceived of unclean seed? Is it not you who alone are? [Chapter 14.] The days of man are short; the number of his months is with you. You have set bounds which he cannot pass. Turn away from him a little, so that he may rest, until his wished-for day comes like that of a hireling.

...his days. A tree has hope. If it is cut down, it grows green again, and its boughs sprout. If its root grows old in the earth and its trunk dies in the dust, at the scent of water it will bud and bring forth leaves as when it was first planted. But when man dies and is laid bare and consumed, where, I ask, is he? Just as if the waters recede from the sea and a river drains away and dries up, so man when he sleeps shall not rise again. Until the heavens are worn away, he will not awake, nor will he rise from his sleep. Who will grant me this, that you would protect me in hell and hide me until your wrath passes, and that you would set me a time in which you would remember me? Do you think a dead man will live again? All the days in which I now serve, I will wait until my change comes. You will call me and I will answer you; you will stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands. You have indeed numbered my steps, but spare my sins. You have sealed up my offenses as it were in a bag, but you have taken care of my iniquity. A falling mountain crumbles away, and a rock is moved from its place. Waters wear away stones, and with flooding the earth is gradually consumed; and likewise you destroy men. You strengthened him for a little while, so that he passes away forever. You change his face and send him away. Whether his sons are noble or ignoble, he does not understand. But while his flesh is upon him, it shall grieve him, and his soul shall mourn over itself. [Chapter 15.] Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: Shall a wise man answer as if speaking into the wind, and fill his stomach with burning talk? You argue with words against someone who is not your equal, and you speak what does not profit you. As much as in you lies, you have done away with fear and diminished prayer before God. For he taught...

Job

Your iniquity speaks from your own mouth, and you imitate the tongue of blasphemers. Your own mouth will condemn you, not I; your own lips will testify against you. Were you the first man born, and were you formed before the hills? Have you heard the counsel of God, and is his wisdom less than yours? What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that we do not? Among us are the aged and the very old, far older than your father. Is it such a small thing that God should comfort you? But your own perverse words prevent it. What lifts up your heart, and why do you have eyes full of wonder as if thinking great things? What does your spirit stir up against God, that you should bring such words from your mouth? What is man, that he should be made pure, or that one born of woman should appear righteous? Behold, among his holy ones none is perfect, and the heavens are not pure in his sight — how much more abominable and worthless is a man who drinks iniquity like water. Listen to me and I will tell you what I have seen. Wise men have declared it, hiding nothing from their fathers, to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed through them. The wicked man is proud all his days, and the number of the years of his tyranny is uncertain. The sound of terror is always in his ears; even in peace he suspects ambushes. He does not believe he can return from darkness, knowing that a sword awaits him on every side, that he is appointed for the sword.
