He who mocks the poor reproaches his Maker, and he who rejoices at another's ruin shall not go unpunished. Children's children are the crown of old men, and the glory of children is their fathers. Fine words do not befit a fool, nor lying lips a ruler. A gift most welcome is an answer ready at hand; wherever it turns, it prospers. He who conceals a transgression seeks friendship, but he who repeats a matter separates friends. A rebuke does more good for a man of understanding than a hundred blows for a fool. The evil man always seeks strife, but a cruel messenger shall be sent against him. It is better to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool trusting in his own folly. He who returns evil for good: evil shall not depart from his house. He who releases water is the source of strife, and before a quarrel breaks out, he abandons judgment. He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the just:

both are abominable to the Lord. What good is wealth to a fool, since he cannot buy wisdom? He who builds his house high seeks ruin, and he who avoids learning shall fall into evil. He who loves is a friend at all times, and a brother is proved in adversity. A foolish man claps his hands when he has pledged for his friend. He who delights in discord loves strife, and he who exalts his mouth seeks ruin. He who is perverse of heart finds no good, and he who is twisted in tongue shall fall into evil. A fool is born to his own shame, and not even in old age will his shame leave him. A joyful spirit makes for a flourishing life; a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones. A wicked man accepts a bribe in secret to pervert the paths of justice. Wisdom shines on the face of the prudent; the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth. A foolish son is the anger of his father and the grief of his mother who bore him. It is not good to harm the just man, nor to strike the ruler who judges rightly. He who restrains his words is learned and prudent, and a man of understanding is of precious spirit. Even a fool, if he keeps silent, will be counted wise; and if he holds his lips, intelligent. Chapter 18.

He who seeks occasions wants to depart from a friend; in all things he will be found blameworthy. A fool does not receive the words of prudence, unless you say what is in his own heart. When the wicked man has come into the depths of sin, he shows contempt, but ignominy and disgrace follow him. The words of a man's mouth are deep waters, and the overflowing fountain is the source of wisdom. It is not good to accept the person of the wicked in judgment, to turn aside the truth of the judge. The lips of a fool involve him in strife, and his mouth provokes quarrels. A fool's mouth is his ruin, and his lips are the snare of his soul. The words of a double-tongued man seem simple, but they reach even to

Proverbs.

The wise will understand wisdom. He who mistreats his father and abandons his mother is shameful and wretched. Do not stop listening, my son, to instruction, and do not ignore the words of knowledge. A dishonest witness mocks justice, and the mouths of the wicked devour iniquity. Judgments are prepared for mockers, and blows for the backs of fools. Chapter 20.

Wine is a riotous thing, and drunkenness is tumultuous. Whoever is led astray by these will not be wise. Like the roaring of a lion, so is the terror of a king; whoever provokes him sins against his own soul. It is an honor for a man to keep himself from quarrels, but every fool will be meddling. Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; he will beg in harvest and have nothing. Counsel in the heart of a man is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. Many people are called merciful, but who can find a faithful man? The just man who walks in his integrity — blessed are his children after him. A king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters all evil with his eyes. Who can say, "I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin"? Differing weights and differing measures — both are an abomination to the Lord. Even a child makes himself known by his deeds, whether his work is pure and right. The hearing ear and the seeing eye — the Lord has made both of them. Do not love sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes and you will be satisfied with bread. "It is bad, it is bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts. There is gold and abundance of jewels, but the lips of knowledge are a precious vessel. Take a man's garment when he has given surety for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he does it for foreigners. Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel. Plans are established by counsel, and by wise guidance wage war.

Do not associate with one who reveals secrets, who walks deceitfully and spreads his lips wide. Whoever curses his father and his mother — his lamp will be put out in utter darkness. An inheritance gained hastily at the beginning will not be blessed in the end. Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the Lord, and he will save you. Differing weights are an abomination to the Lord, and a false balance is not good. A man's steps are directed by the Lord; how then can a man understand his own way? It is a snare for a man to devour what is holy, and after making vows to reflect. A wise king scatters the wicked and drives the wheel over them. The spirit of man is the lamp of the Lord, searching all his innermost parts. Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is upheld by mercy. The glory of young men is their strength, and the splendor of old men is their gray hair. Blows that wound cleanse away evil, and strokes reach the innermost parts. Chapter 21.

Like channels of water, so the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord; wherever he wishes, he turns it. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the Lord weighs the heart. To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice. Haughty eyes and a proud heart — the lamp of the wicked — are sin. The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death. The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do justice. The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright. It is better to live in a corner of a housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.

Proverbs

The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy from him. When a scoffer is punished, the simple become wiser; and if a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge. The righteous man considers the house of the wicked, casting the wicked down to ruin. Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard. A secret gift calms anger, and a bribe in the lap pacifies great fury. It is a joy to the just to do judgment, but ruin to the workers of iniquity. A man who strays from the way of wisdom will rest in the congregation of the dead. He who loves feasting will be in want; he who loves wine and rich food will not grow rich. The wicked shall be given in place of the righteous, and the treacherous in place of the upright. It is better to dwell in a desert land than with a contentious and fretful woman. A precious treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the wise, but a foolish man devours it. Whoever pursues righteousness and mercy will find life, righteousness, and glory. A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the strength of its confidence. Whoever guards his mouth and tongue keeps his soul from trouble. A proud and haughty man is called a scoffer; he who acts in arrogant anger. The desire of the slothful kills him, for his hands refuse to work. All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back. The sacrifices of the wicked are an abomination; how much more when brought with evil intent. A false witness will perish, but the man who obeys will speak victoriously. A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright corrects his ways. There is no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel against the Lord. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory belongs to the Lord. Chapter 22.

A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. The rich and the poor meet together; the Lord is the maker of them all. The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple pass on and suffer for it. The reward of humility and the fear of the Lord is riches, honor, and life. Thorns and snares are in the way of the perverse; he who guards his soul keeps far from them. Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. He who gives gifts gains victory and honor, but he who takes them away destroys souls. Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease. He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend. The eyes of the Lord keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the treacherous. The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!" The mouth of a forbidden woman is a deep pit; he with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it. Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him. Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty. My son, incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my teaching; for it will be pleasant if you keep it within you, and it will be ready on your lips, so that your trust may be in the Lord. I have made it known to you this day, even to you. Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge, to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you? Do not rob the poor because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate, for the Lord will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.

Proverbs

A glorious man who does not fulfill his promises. Patience soothes a prince, and a gentle tongue will break a hard resistance. You have found honey: eat only as much as is enough for you, lest you eat too much and vomit it. Withdraw your foot from your neighbor's house, lest having had enough of you he come to hate you. A dart and a sword and a sharp arrow is the man who speaks false witness against his neighbor. A rotten tooth and a weary foot is one who puts trust in a faithless man in the day of trouble, as one who takes off his garment in cold weather. Like vinegar on soda is one who sings songs to a heavy heart. As a moth to a garment and a worm to wood, so sadness harms the heart of a man. If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For doing so you will heap burning coals upon his head, and the Lord will reward you. The north wind drives away rain, just as a sorrowful face drives away a backbiting tongue. It is better to dwell in the corner of a housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome woman. Like cold water to a thirsty soul is good news from a far country. Like a muddied spring and a polluted well is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked. Like one who eats too much honey, so it is not good for a man to seek out his own glory. Like a city breached and without walls is a man who cannot control his own spirit.

Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, so honor for a fool is out of place. Like a fluttering sparrow or a darting swallow, an undeserved curse does not come to rest. A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools. Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be just like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes. Like cutting off one's feet and drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool.

Like beautiful legs on a lame man is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like one who binds a stone in a sling is the giving of honor to a fool. Like a thornbush brandished in the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools. A judge settles disputes, and one who silences a fool puts an end to strife. Like a dog that returns to its vomit is a fool who repeats his folly. Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him. A lazy person says, "There is a lion in the road, a lion in the streets!" As a door turns on its hinges, so the lazy person turns in his bed. A lazy person buries his hand in the dish, and it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth. A fool is wiser in his own eyes than seven people who can give a sensible answer. Like one who grabs a dog by the ears is someone who meddles in a quarrel that is not his own. Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death, so is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I was only joking!" Without wood, a fire goes out; and without a gossip, quarreling ceases. As charcoal to embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome person for kindling strife. The words of a gossip are like delicacies; they go down into the inner parts of the body. Like silver glaze on earthenware are fervent lips with a wicked heart. An enemy disguises himself with his lips while harboring deceit in his heart. When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for there are seven abominations in his heart. Though his hatred is concealed with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly. Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on the one who rolls it. A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.

Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring forth. Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips. A stone is heavy and sand is burdensome, but a fool's wrath is heavier than both. Wrath has no mercy, nor does the outburst of rage; and who can withstand a spirit provoked to anger? Open rebuke is better than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. A satisfied soul tramples on honeycomb, but to a hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet. Like a bird that wanders from its nest, so is a man who leaves his own place. Ointment and perfume delight the heart, and the sweetness of a friend comes from earnest counsel. Do not forsake your friend or your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity. A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away. Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me. A prudent man foresees evil and hides himself, but the simple pass on and are punished. Take the garment of him who is surety for a stranger, and hold it as a pledge when he is surety for a foreign woman. He who blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it will be counted as a curse to him. A continual dripping on a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike. Whoever restrains her restrains the wind, and grasps oil with his right hand. Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. Whoever tends the fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who looks after his master will be honored. As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. Hell and destruction are never full, and the eyes of man are never satisfied. As silver is refined in a crucible and gold in a furnace, so a man is tested by the praise he receives. The heart of the wicked seeks evil, but the heart of the upright seeks knowledge. Though you grind a fool in a mortar with a pestle among crushed grain, yet his foolishness will not depart from him. Know well the condition of your flocks, and pay attention to your herds; for riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to all generations. When the grass disappears and new growth is seen, and the herbs of the mountains are gathered, the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field. There will be enough goat's milk for your food, for the food of your household, and for the sustenance of your maidservants.

The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion. Because of the transgression of a land, many are its princes; but by a man of understanding and knowledge, order will be maintained. A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food. Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law contend with them. Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the Lord understand all things. Better is the poor man who walks in his integrity than one who is crooked in his ways, though he is rich. He who keeps the law is a wise son, but he who is a companion of gluttons shames his father. He who increases his wealth by interest and usury gathers it for him who will be gracious to the poor. He who turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination. Whoever causes the upright to go astray in an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will inherit good things. The rich man is wise in his own eyes, but the poor man who has understanding sees through him. When the righteous rejoice, there is great glory; but when the wicked rise, men hide themselves.

Proverbs.

He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them will find mercy. Blessed is the man who is always fearful of wrongdoing, but he who is hardened in heart will fall into evil. A roaring lion and a hungry bear — so is a wicked ruler over a poor people. A ruler who lacks understanding will oppress many through slander; but he who hates unjust gain will have long days. A man who unjustly sheds blood shall find no refuge, even to the grave. He who walks uprightly will be saved, but he who goes by crooked ways will fall all at once. He who works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who pursues idle pleasures will have poverty enough. A faithful man will be greatly praised, but he who makes haste to be rich will not go unpunished. He who shows partiality in judgment does not act well; such a man will forsake truth for a piece of bread. A man who hastens to grow rich and envies others does not know that poverty will come upon him. Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than one who flatters with the tongue. He who robs his father or his mother and says it is no sin is the companion of a murderer. He who is proud and boastful stirs up strife, but whoever trusts in the Lord will prosper. He who trusts in his own heart is a fool, but whoever walks wisely will be kept safe. He who gives to the poor will not lack, but he who ignores the needy will suffer want. When the wicked rise, people hide, but when they perish, the righteous increase. For the man of stiff neck who is often rebuked and refuses correction, destruction will come suddenly, and there will be no remedy. When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice; but when the wicked rule, the people groan. He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but he who keeps company with harlots

wastes his wealth. A foolish king oppresses his people, but a greedy man destroys the land. A man who flatters his neighbor with smooth words spreads a net for his feet. An evil man is snared by his sin, but the righteous sing and rejoice. The righteous man knows the cause of the poor; the wicked man does not understand such knowledge. Scoffers set a city aflame, but wise men turn away wrath. If a wise man contends with a foolish man — whether he is angry or laughs — there is no rest. Men of blood hate the upright, but the righteous seek his well-being. A fool vents all his spirit, but a wise man holds it back and restrains it. If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his servants will be wicked. The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the Lord gives light to the eyes of both. A king who judges the poor with truth will have his throne established forever. The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. When wickedness increases, transgression increases, but the righteous will see their downfall. Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your heart. Where there is no vision, the people perish, but he who keeps the law is happy. A servant cannot be corrected by words alone; though he understands, he will not respond. Do you see a man hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him. He who pampers his servant from childhood will find him stubborn in the end. A man given to anger stirs up strife, and one who is quick to become indignant is prone to sin. Pride goes before a fall, but a humble spirit will obtain honor. Whoever is partner to a thief hates his own soul; he hears the curse but says nothing. The fear of man brings a snare, but whoever trusts in the Lord

Proverbs                                                     Prologue.

wine: for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns: Let the poor drink and forget their poverty, and remember their misery no more. Give strong drink to those who are perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress. Let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their suffering no more. Open your mouth for the mute, and for the causes of all who are afflicted. Open your mouth, decree what is just, and defend the poor and needy. Aleph. Who can find a virtuous woman? Her price is far above rubies. Beth. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. Gimel. She does him good and not evil all the days of her life. Daleth. She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands. He. She is like the ships of the merchant, bringing her food from afar. Vav. She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and tasks for her maidens. Zayin. She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard. Heth. She girds herself with strength and makes her arms strong. Teth. She perceives that her merchandise is profitable, and her lamp does not go out by night. Yod. She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle. Kaph. She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy. Lamed. She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in double garments. Mem. She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple. Nun. Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land. Samech. She makes linen garments and sells them, and delivers sashes to the merchant. Ayin. Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. Pe. She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. Tzade.

She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness. Qoph. Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also praises her. Resh. Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all. Shin. Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised. Tav. Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates. Here begins the Prologue to Ecclesiastes.

Nearly five years ago, when I was still at Rome, and Ecclesiastes was being read to the blessed Blesilla so that I might draw her away from the contempt of this world and to consider all that is seen in the world as nothing: at her request, after the manner of a brief commentary, I undertook to explain the obscure passages so that she might understand what she was reading without my help. But she, whose work was cut short by sudden death before it was finished, and since we could not, O Paula and Eustochium, have such a companion in our life: struck dumb by so great a wound, I now at Bethlehem, that more august city, render to God both her memory and this work for you. I give notice briefly that I have followed no single authority, but translating from the Hebrew I have conformed myself chiefly to the usage of the Seventy translators in those places where they do not differ much from the Hebrew. Sometimes I have called to mind Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, so that I might neither discourage the reader's zeal by too great novelty, nor yet, abandoning the fountain of truth, follow mere streams of opinion.

Here ends the Prologue. Here begins the Book of Ecclesiastes.

The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. Vanity of vanities, says Ecclesiastes; vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.

Ecclesiastes

What more does a man have from all his labor with which he toils under the sun? One generation passes and another comes: but the earth endures forever. The sun rises and sets: and returns to its place; and rising there it turns through the south and turns toward the north. The wind goes round and round, and the wind returns to its circuits. All rivers run into the sea: yet the sea is not full. To the place from where the rivers come, they return, so that they may flow again. All things are difficult; a man cannot explain them. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. What is it that has been? The very same thing that is to be. What is it that has been done? The very same that will be done. There is nothing new under the sun: nor can anyone say, behold this is new. For it has already gone before in the ages that were before us. There is no remembrance of former things: nor indeed shall there be any remembrance of those things that are to come, with those that shall come in the last place. I, Ecclesiastes, was king of Israel in Jerusalem: and I applied my mind to seek and search out wisely concerning all things that are done under the sun. This sore travail has God given to the sons of men, to be exercised therewith. I have seen all the works that are done under the sun: and behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit. The perverse are hard to be corrected: and the number of fools is infinite. I spoke in my heart, saying, Behold I am great, and have surpassed in wisdom all that were before me in Jerusalem: and my mind has contemplated many things wisely, and I have learned: and I have applied my heart to know prudence and doctrine and errors and folly. And I perceived that in these things also there was labor and vexation of spirit: because in much wisdom there is much indignation: and he that adds knowledge adds also labor.

I said therefore in my heart: I will go and abound with delights, and enjoy good things.

And I saw that this also was vanity. I said of laughter: It is madness: and of mirth: What does it accomplish? I thought in my heart to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might turn my mind to wisdom and avoid folly, until I might see what was profitable for the children of men: what they should do under the sun the number of the days of their life. I made great works, I built myself houses and planted vineyards: I made gardens and orchards, and planted them with all kinds of fruit trees: and I made pools of water to water the wood of trees growing: I got servants and maids, and had a great family: and herds of oxen and great flocks of sheep, above all that were before me in Jerusalem. I heaped together for myself silver and gold, and the wealth of kings and provinces. I made singing men and singing women, and the delights of the children of men, cups and vessels to serve to pour out wine: and I surpassed in riches all that were before me in Jerusalem. Also my wisdom remained with me: and all things that my eyes desired I refused them not: and I withheld not my heart from any pleasure, for my heart rejoiced in all my labor: and this was my portion from all my labor. And when I turned myself to all the works which my hands had wrought, and to the labors in which I had toiled in vain: I saw in all things vanity and vexation of mind, and that nothing was lasting under the sun. I turned myself to consider wisdom, and errors and folly. What manner of man is he that can follow the king his maker? I saw that wisdom excels folly, as much as light excels darkness. The eyes of a wise man are in his head: the fool walks in darkness. And I learned that there is one end for both: and I said in my heart: If the end of the fool and mine shall be

Ecclesiastes.

The riches fall to strangers. And I found nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his own work, for that is his portion. For who can bring him to see what will be after him?

I turned to other things and saw (Chapter 4) the oppressions that are done under the sun: and the tears of the innocent, and no one to comfort them, and unable to resist their violence, destitute of all help. And I praised the dead more than the living, and I judged him happier than both who has not yet been born, and has not seen the evils that are done under the sun. Again I considered all the labors of men, and noticed that their industries are exposed to the envy of their neighbors. And in this also is vanity and vexation of spirit. The fool folds his hands together and eats his own flesh, saying: Better is a handful with rest, than both hands full with toil and vexation of mind. Considering, I found also another vanity under the sun. There is one, and he has not a second, no child, no brother, and yet he ceases not to labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with riches. For whom do I labor and deprive my soul of good things? In this also is vanity and a great affliction. It is better therefore that two should be together than one: for they have the advantage of their fellowship. If one falls, the other will lift up his companion. But woe to him that is alone, for when he falls, there is none to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they shall warm one another: how shall one alone be warmed? And if a man prevail against one, two shall withstand him. A threefold cord is not easily broken. Better is a child that is poor and wise than a king that is old and foolish, who knows not how to foresee for the future: because out of prison and chains sometimes a man comes forth to a kingdom, and another born king is consumed by poverty. I saw all the living that walk under the sun with the young man who shall succeed him. The number of the people of all who were before him is infinite: and they that shall come afterward shall not rejoice in him. But this also is vanity and vexation of spirit. Keep your foot when you go to the house of God, and draw near to hear. For much better is obedience than the victims of fools who know not what evil they do. (Chapter 5)

Speak not anything rashly, and let not your heart be hasty to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven and you upon earth: therefore let your words be few. Dreams follow many cares, and many words are found in folly. If you have vowed anything to God, defer not to pay it: for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him. But whatsoever you have vowed, pay it. It is much better not to vow than after a vow not to perform the things promised. Give not your mouth to cause your flesh to sin: and say not before the angel: There is no providence: lest God be angry at your words and destroy all the works of your hands. Where there are many dreams, there are many vanities and words without number: but do you fear God. If you see the oppressions of the poor and violent judgments and justice perverted in the province, wonder not at this; for he that is high has another higher, and there are others still higher than these: and moreover the king of all the earth commands the servant. A covetous man shall not be satisfied with money: and he that loves riches shall reap no fruit from them. And this also is vanity. Where there are many riches, there are many to eat them: and what does it profit the owner, but that he sees the riches with his eyes? Sweet is the sleep of the laboring man, whether he eat little or much: but the fullness of the rich will not suffer him to sleep. There is also another grievous evil which I have seen under the sun: riches kept to the hurt of the owner. For they are lost with very great affliction. He has begotten a son, and there is nothing at all in his hand.

Ecclesiastes

He will be in poverty. Just as he came naked from his mother's womb, so shall he return, and he shall take nothing from his labor. This is a grievous infirmity. Just as he came, so shall he return. What then does it profit him that he labored for the wind? All the days of his life he eats in darkness, and in much care, and in misery and sorrow. This therefore seemed good to me: that a man should eat and drink, and enjoy the fruit of his labor, with which he labored under the sun, all the days of his life which God has given him: and this is his portion. For every man to whom God has given riches and wealth, and has given him power to eat thereof, and to take his portion, and to rejoice of his labor: this is the gift of God. For he shall not much remember the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart. Chapter VI.

There is also another evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is common among men: A man to whom God has given riches and wealth and honor, and he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God does not give him power to eat thereof, but a stranger shall devour it. This is vanity and a great evil. If a man beget a hundred children, and live many years, and the days of his years be many, and his soul be not satisfied with good things, and also that he have no burial, I say that an untimely birth is better than he. For he comes in vanity and departs in darkness, and his name shall be covered with darkness. Moreover he has not seen the sun, nor known anything: this man has more rest than the other. Indeed, do not all go to one place? All the labor of man is for his mouth, yet the appetite is never filled. For what advantage has the wise man over the fool? What profit has the poor man, except to go where life is? Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of desire.

This is also vanity and vexation of spirit. Whatever exists has already been named, and it is known what man is: neither can he contend with one who is mightier than he. The more words there are, the more vanity there is.

Chapter VII. What need is it for man to seek things greater than himself, when he knows not what is good for him in life, all the days of his fleeting life, which passes like a shadow? For who can tell him what shall come after him under the sun? A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of birth. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men, and the living will take it to heart. Sorrow is better than laughter: for by the sadness of the face the heart is made better. The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. For like the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This also is vanity. Surely oppression destroys a wise man's reason, and a bribe corrupts the heart. Better is the end of a matter than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. Do not be quick in your spirit to become angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools. Do not say: "Why were the former days better than these?" For it is not wise to ask this. Wisdom with an inheritance is good, and profitable to those who see the sun. For wisdom is a defense, and money is a defense. But the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom gives life to those who have it. Consider the work of God: for who can make straight what he has made crooked? In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other, so that man should find no fault against him.

Ecclesiastes

These are the complaints I have seen in the days of my vanity. The just man perishes in his justice, and the wicked man lives long in his wickedness. Be not overly righteous, nor make yourself too wise, lest you be dumbfounded. Do not act wickedly too much, and do not be a fool, lest you die before your time. It is good to hold fast to the just man, but do not withdraw your hand from him either, for one who fears God neglects nothing. Wisdom strengthens the wise man more than ten rulers of a city. For there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins. Do not give heed to all the words that are spoken, lest you hear your servant cursing you. For your own conscience knows that you yourself have often cursed others. I have tested all things in wisdom. I said, I will become wise, but it went further from me than before. Deep indeed is it — who can find it out? I searched in my mind to know and to consider and to seek wisdom and reason, and to know the wickedness of folly and the error of the imprudent. And I found something more bitter than death: a woman who is a hunter's snare, and a net is her heart; her hands are chains. He who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is caught by her. Behold, this I have found, says Ecclesiastes, examining one thing after another to find the reason which my soul still seeks but has not found. One man among a thousand I have found; a woman among all these I have not found. Only this I found: that God made man upright, but he has entangled himself in countless questions. Who is as the wise man? And who knows the interpretation of things?
A man's wisdom illuminates his face, and the hardness of his countenance is changed. I keep the king's command and the oath sworn before God. Do not be in a hurry to leave his presence, and do not persist in an evil
matter, for he does whatever he pleases; his word is full of power, and no one can say to him, Why do you act thus? One who keeps the commandment will experience no evil. The wise man's heart knows the proper time and manner. For everything there is a time and a proper occasion, yet man's affliction is great because he does not know what is past and what is to come no one can tell him. It is not in man's power to restrain the spirit, nor does he have authority over the day of death; there is no discharge in war, and wickedness will not save the wicked. All this I observed, and I applied my heart to all the works done under the sun. Sometimes one man lords it over another to his own hurt. I saw the wicked buried; they even came and went from the holy place, and they were praised in the city for what they had done. This also is vanity. Because sentence against an evil deed is not executed swiftly, the hearts of the children of men are fully set to do evil. But I know that it will be well with those who fear God, who stand in awe before him. But it will not go well with the wicked, and his days will not be prolonged like a shadow, because he does not fear God. There is another vanity that occurs on earth: there are righteous people to whom what happens is as if they had done the works of the wicked, and there are wicked people to whom what happens is as if they had done the deeds of the righteous. I said this also is vanity. So I commended enjoyment, for man has nothing better under the sun than to eat and drink and be glad, for this will accompany him in his toil through the days of his life that God gives him under the sun. And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to understand the distinctions that are sought on earth. There is a man who day and night does not close his eyes in sleep. And I perceived that of all God's work one can find no explanation.

Ecclesiastes.

If a servant has been set free, this does not restore him as before, but with much labor he is sharpened again; and after diligence wisdom follows. If a serpent bites in silence, there is nothing better for one who slanders secretly. The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool will swallow him up. The beginning of his words is foolishness, and the end of his talk is wicked madness. A fool multiplies words. A man does not know what has come before him, and who can tell him what will come after? The toil of fools will afflict those who do not know how to go to the city. Woe to you, O land, when your king is a child, and your princes feast in the morning! Blessed are you, O land, when your king is of noble birth, and your princes eat at the proper time, for strength and not for drunkenness! Through laziness the roof sinks in, and through idleness of hands the house leaks. A feast is made for laughter, and wine makes life merry, and money answers everything. Even in your thoughts do not curse the king, nor in your bedroom curse the rich, for a bird of the air will carry your voice, and one with wings will report what you say. Chapter 11.

Cast your bread upon passing waters, for after many days you will find it again. Divide your portion among seven, or even eight, for you do not know what misfortune may occur on earth. If the clouds are full, they pour out rain upon the earth. Whether a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place the tree falls, there it will lie. Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever looks at the clouds will not reap. Just as you do not know how the spirit comes to the bones in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know the works of God who makes everything. In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand be idle, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or whether both will be equally good. Light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun. If a man lives many years and rejoices in them all, let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. All that comes is vanity. Rejoice, O young man, in your youth, and let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes. Yet know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. Chapter 11.

Remove anger from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh, for youth and the dawn of life are vanity. Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come and the years approach when you will say, "I have no pleasure in them"; before the sun and the light and the moon and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain. In the day when the guardians of the house tremble, and the strong men are bent, and the women who grind cease because they are few, and those who look through the windows grow dim; when the doors on the street are shut, as the sound of the grinding is low; when one rises at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low; when they are afraid of heights and terrors on the road; when the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper drags itself along, and the caper-berry no longer gives pleasure; because man is going to his eternal home, and mourners will go about the streets; before the silver cord is snapped, and the golden bowl is broken, and the pitcher is shattered at the fountain, and the wheel broken at the cistern; and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher; all is vanity. And because the Preacher was very wise, he taught the people knowledge, and he pondered and searched out and arranged many proverbs. He sought to find words of delight, and he wrote words of truth uprightly.

Song of Songs

they destroy the vineyards. But our vineyard has blossomed. My beloved is mine and I am his: he who feeds among the lilies until the day breathes and the shadows decline. Return: be like, my beloved, a roe or a young deer upon the mountains of Bethel. Chapter 3.
In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him and found him not. I will rise and go about the city, through the streets and the squares: I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him and found him not. The watchmen who go about the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves? Scarcely had I passed by them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her that bore me. I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the hinds of the field, that you stir not up nor awaken the beloved until she please. Who is this that comes up from the wilderness like a pillar of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, and with all the powders of the merchant? Behold the bed of Solomon: sixty valiant men surround it, of the most valiant of Israel: all holding swords, expert in war. Every man has his sword upon his thigh, because of fear in the night. King Solomon made himself a chariot of wood from Lebanon. He made the pillars thereof of silver, the seat of gold, the covering of purple: the interior furnished with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem. Go forth, O daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon in the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the joy of his heart.
How beautiful you are, my love: Chapter 4.
How beautiful you are. Your eyes are doves, beyond what is hidden within. Your hair is as a flock of goats that have come up from mount Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing. All of them bear twins, and none is barren among them. Like a thread of scarlet are your lips, and your speech is sweet. Like a piece of pomegranate are your temples, beyond what is hidden within. Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang upon it, all the armor of valiant men. Your two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline. I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. You are wholly beautiful, my love, and there is no spot in you. Come from Lebanon, my bride: come from Lebanon, come. You shall be crowned from the top of Amana, from the top of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards. You have ravished my heart, my sister, my bride; you have ravished my heart with one of your eyes, with one chain of your neck. How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride: your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices. Your lips, O my bride, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under your tongue, and the smell of your garments is like the smell of frankincense. A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed. Your plants are an orchard of pomegranates with pleasant fruits, with henna and nard; nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, streaming down from Lebanon. Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Chapter 5.
Let my beloved come into his garden and eat his pleasant fruits. I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey: I have drunk

Canticles . Wisdom .

like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies. Your two breasts are like two young roes that are twins. Your neck is like a tower of ivory; your eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon which looks toward Damascus. Your head upon you is like Carmel, and the hair of your head like purple; the king is held captive in its tresses. How beautiful and how delightful you are, my love, with all your charms. Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters. I said: I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit. And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine, and the fragrance of your breath like apples, and your mouth like the best wine. Worthy to be drunk by my beloved, flowing gently through the lips of those that are asleep. I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me. Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; let us stay in the villages. Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine has budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened, and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love. The mandrakes give a fragrance at our doors. All manner of pleasant fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved. O that you were like my brother, who nursed at my mother's breasts! If I should find you outside, I would kiss you; and no one would despise me. I would lead you, bring you into my mother's house: she would instruct me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranate. His left hand should be under my head, and his right hand should embrace me. I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, do not stir up nor awaken my love until she pleases. Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? I awakened you under the apple tree. There your mother was in labor; there she who bore you was in labor.

Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm: for love is as strong as death, jealousy as cruel as the grave. Its flames are flames of fire, a most vehement flame. Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it. If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would be utterly despised. We have a little sister, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for? If she is a wall, we will build upon her a turret of silver. If she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar. I am a wall, and my breasts like towers: therefore I was in his eyes as one that found peace. Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he let out the vineyard to keepers; every one was to bring for the fruit thereof a thousand pieces of silver. My vineyard, which is mine, is before me. You, O Solomon, may have the thousand, and those who tend its fruit two hundred. You who dwell in the gardens, the companions listen for your voice. Flee, my beloved, and be like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of spices. Here end the Song of Songs. Here begins the Book of Wisdom.

Love justice, you who judge the earth. Think of the Lord with goodness, and seek him with simplicity of heart: because he is found by those who do not tempt him, and he shows himself to those who have faith in him. For perverse thoughts separate from God: and his power, when tested, corrects the foolish. Because wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sin. For the holy spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be corrected when iniquity comes near.

Wisdom.

For the spirit of wisdom is kind and will not free the slanderer from his lips; because God is witness of his innermost feelings, and a true observer of his heart, and a hearer of his tongue. For the spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of every voice. Therefore no one who speaks unjust things can escape notice, nor will chastening judgment pass him by. For inquiry will be made into the thoughts of the ungodly, and the sound of his words will reach the Lord, to convict him of his wicked deeds. For the ear of jealousy hears all things, and the noise of grumblings is not hidden. Keep yourselves therefore from murmuring, which profits nothing, and from slander: refrain your tongue from detraction. For a secret word shall not pass away unpunished, and a lying mouth destroys the soul. Court not death by the error of your life, nor draw destruction upon yourselves by the works of your hands. For God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living. For he created all things that they might exist, and the nations of the world are wholesome, and there is no poison of destruction in them, nor has the kingdom of death any footing on earth. For justice is perpetual and immortal, but injustice is the acquisition of death. The ungodly called it to themselves with hands and words, thinking it a friend, and pined away, and made a covenant with it, because they deserve to be of its company.

For the ungodly said, reasoning with themselves, but not rightly: Our life is short and tedious, and in the death of a man there is no remedy, and no one has been known to have returned from the grave. For we were born of nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had never been. For our breath is as smoke in our nostrils, and a word is a spark to move our heart. For our body shall be reduced to ashes,

and our spirit shall be poured out as soft air. And our life shall pass away as the trace of a cloud, and shall be dispersed as a mist, which is driven away by the rays of the sun and overcome by its heat. And our name shall be forgotten in time, and no one shall have any remembrance of our works. For our time is as the passing of a shadow, and there is no going back of our end, for it is fast sealed, and no one returns. Come therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that are present, and let us speedily use the creatures as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments, and let not the flower of life pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let no meadow escape our wanton luxury. Let none of us go without his share in our revelry. Everywhere let us leave tokens of our joy, for this is our portion and this our lot. Let us oppress the poor righteous man; let us not spare the widow, nor respect the gray hairs of the aged. But let our strength be the law of justice, for that which is weak is proven useless. Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, because he is inconvenient to us and opposes our actions, and reproaches us for sins against the law, and charges us with sins against our training. He professes to have knowledge of God, and calls himself a child of God. He became for us a reproof of our thoughts. He is grievous to us even to behold, for his life is not like other men's, and his ways are of a different kind. We are considered by him as something base, and he avoids our ways as unclean; he calls the last end of the righteous happy, and boasts that God is his father. Let us see if his words are true, and let us test what will happen at the end of his life, and if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him and will deliver him from the hands of his adversaries. With insult and

Wisdom.

lest deceit ensnare his soul. For the bewitching of trivial things obscures what is good, and the instability of desire corrupts an innocent mind. Having been perfected in a short time, he fulfilled long years; for his soul was pleasing to God, and therefore He hastened to take him away from the midst of wickedness. The peoples saw and did not understand, nor did they take to heart such things: that grace and mercy are upon His holy ones, and He watches over His chosen ones. The just man who dies condemns the living wicked, and youth swiftly fulfilled condemns the many years of the unjust. For they shall see the end of the wise man, and shall not understand what God has purposed for him, or why the Lord has kept him safe. They shall see and despise him; but God shall laugh them to scorn. And after this they shall fall without honor, and be an outrage among the dead forever. For He shall burst them puffed up and speechless, and shall shake them from the foundations, and they shall be laid utterly waste, and shall be in sorrow, and their memory shall perish. Chapter 5.

Then the just shall stand with great confidence against those who have afflicted them and taken away their labors. Seeing this, they shall be troubled with terrible fear, and shall be amazed at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation, groaning in anguish of spirit: they shall say among themselves, repenting and groaning for anguish of spirit: These are they whom we once held in derision, and as a pattern of reproach. We fools esteemed their life as madness, and their end without honor. Behold how they are numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints. Therefore we have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shone for us, and the sun of understanding has not risen upon us. We were wearied in the way of wickedness and destruction, and we walked through difficult ways: but the way of the Lord we did not know. What has pride profited us? or what advantage has the boasting of riches brought us? All those things have passed away like a shadow, and like a swift messenger. Like a ship that passes through the waves, of which when it has passed, there is no trace to be found, nor path of its keel in the waves; or like a bird that flies through the air, of which no evidence of her passage is found, but only the sound of her wings beating the light air, and parting it by the force of her journey, moving her wings and flying through: and afterward no mark of her passage is found; or like an arrow shot at a mark, the air divided comes together again immediately, so that no one can know where it passed through. So we also, as soon as we were born, ceased to be; and had no mark of virtue to show, but were consumed in our wickedness. Such things the sinners said in hell: for the hope of the wicked is like dust which is blown away by the wind, and like a thin froth which is dispersed by the storm, and like smoke which is scattered by the wind, and like the remembrance of a guest of one day that passes by. But the just shall live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the care of them with the Most High. Therefore they shall receive a kingdom of glory, and a crown of beauty from the hand of the Lord: for with His right hand He shall cover them, and with His holy arm He shall defend them. And He shall take His zeal as armor, and shall arm the creature for the revenge of His enemies. He shall put on justice as a breastplate, and shall take judgment for a helmet. He shall take equity as an invincible shield; and He shall sharpen His severe wrath into a spear, and the whole world shall fight with Him against the unwise. Then shafts of lightning shall fly with true aim, and shall leap to the mark as from a well-drawn bow of clouds.

Wisdom.

They shall bend their bow of clouds and hurl their arrows to their mark. Dense hail shall be hurled from a stormy wrath, and the sea's water shall rage against them, and rivers shall flood together harshly. Against them shall stand the spirit of power, and as a whirlwind it shall divide them and scatter them, and it shall lay waste all the land of their iniquity, and wickedness shall overturn the seats of the mighty. Chapter VI.

Wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man is worth more than a strong one. Hear therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, O judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who hold multitudes in your power and take pride in the throngs of nations: for power was given to you by the Lord, and might by the Most High, who shall examine your works and search your thoughts. Because you were ministers of his kingdom and did not judge rightly, nor kept the law of justice, nor walked according to the will of God — he shall appear to you terribly and swiftly, because the most severe judgment is reserved for those in high places. For mercy is shown to the lowly, but the powerful shall be powerfully tormented. For God, who is Lord over all, will not withhold punishment from anyone, nor will he stand in awe of any man's greatness, since he made both small and great, and he cares equally for all. But a stricter examination awaits the stronger. Therefore, O kings, these are my words to you, that you may learn wisdom and not fall away. For those who keep just things justly shall be justified, and those who have learned them shall find what to answer. Desire therefore my words and love them, and you shall have instruction. Wisdom is bright and fadeless, and is easily seen by those who love her, and found by those who seek her. She anticipates those who desire her, making herself known first. He who rises early to seek her shall not labor, for he shall find her sitting at his door. To think of her is perfection of understanding, and whoever watches for her sake shall quickly be free from care. For she goes about seeking those worthy of her, and graciously appears to them in their paths, and comes to meet them in all their thoughts. The beginning of wisdom is the most true desire of instruction. Care for instruction is love of her, and love of her is the keeping of her laws. The keeping of her laws is the assurance of incorruption, and incorruption brings one close to God. So desire for wisdom leads to the everlasting kingdom. If then your delight is in thrones and scepters, O kings, honor wisdom so that you may reign forever. Love the light of wisdom, all you who lead nations. What wisdom is and how she came to be, I will tell you, and I will not hide from you the mysteries of God; but I will trace her out from the beginning of her birth, and bring the knowledge of her to light, and will not pass by the truth, nor indeed will I go in the way of consuming envy, for such a man shall not be a partaker of wisdom. The multitude of the wise is the welfare of the world, and a wise king is the strength of his people. Receive therefore instruction through my words, O children, and it shall profit you. Chapter VIII.

I myself also am a mortal man, like all others, and of the race of him that was first made of the earth, and in the womb of my mother was I fashioned to be flesh in the time of ten months, being compacted in blood of the seed of man and the pleasure of sleep. And when I was born, I drew in the common air, and fell upon the earth which is of like nature, and the first voice which I uttered was crying, as all others do. I was nursed in swaddling clothes, and with great cares. For there is no king that had any other beginning of birth. One entrance therefore there is for all into life, and

Wisdom

For this reason I prayed, and understanding was given to me; I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me. I valued her above kingdoms and thrones, and wealth I reckoned as nothing compared to her. I did not compare any precious stone to her, for all gold, compared to her, is but a little sand, and silver will be counted as clay beside her. I loved her more than health and beauty, and I chose to have her rather than light, because her radiance never ceases. All good things came to me along with her, and in her hands uncountable prosperity. I rejoiced in all these things, because wisdom leads them all, though I did not know that she was the mother of them all. What I learned without deceit, I share without envy; I do not hide her wealth. For she is an infinite treasure to men, and those who use her become the friends of God, commended by the gifts of her discipline. God has granted me to speak according to my thoughts and to conceive ideas worthy of the gifts I have received, because he is the guide of wisdom and the director of the wise. For in his hand are both we and our words, and all prudence and knowledge of works and discipline. For he himself gave me true knowledge of what exists: to know the structure of the world and the working of the elements; the beginning and end and middle of times, the alternations of the solstices and the changes of the seasons; the cycles of the year and the positions of the stars; the natures of animals and the tempers of beasts; the powers of winds and the thoughts of men; the varieties of plants and the virtues of roots; and all things hidden and unexpected I learned. For wisdom, the fashioner of all things, taught me. For in her there is a spirit that is intelligent, holy, unique, manifold, subtle,

eloquent, mobile, undefiled, certain, sweet, loving what is good, keen, unhindered in beneficence, humane, steadfast, sure, free from anxiety, all-powerful, overseeing all, and able to penetrate all spirits that are intelligent and pure and most subtle. For wisdom is more mobile than any motion; she reaches everywhere because of her purity. She is a breath of the power of God, and a pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty; therefore nothing defiled can enter into her. For she is the radiance of eternal light, a spotless mirror of the working of God, and an image of his goodness. Though she is one, she can do all things, and while remaining in herself, she renews all things; in every generation she passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets. For God loves nothing so much as the one who lives with wisdom. For she is more beautiful than the sun, and excels every constellation of the stars; compared with light she is found to be superior. For night succeeds light, but evil does not overcome wisdom.

She reaches therefore from one end to the other (chapter viii) mightily, and orders all things sweetly. I loved her and sought her from my youth; I desired to take her for my bride, and I became enamored of her beauty. She glorifies her noble birth by living with God, and the Lord of all has loved her. For she is an initiate in the knowledge of God and an associate in his works. If riches are a desirable possession in life, what is richer than wisdom, the active cause of all things? If understanding is effective, who, among all things, is a better craftsman than she? And if anyone loves righteousness, her labors are virtues, for she teaches self-control and prudence, justice and courage; nothing in life is more useful to men than these. And if anyone longs for wide experience, she knows the past and infers the future; she knows the subtleties of speeches

Wisdom.

By wisdom they were healed, all those who pleased you, O Lord, from the beginning.
This same wisdom watched over him who was formed first by God, the father of the world: when he alone had been created, she kept him safe, and delivered him from his sin. And she drew him out of the clay of the earth, and gave him the power to govern all things. But when the unrighteous man departed from her in his anger: he perished through his fratricidal rage. And when the flood destroyed the earth, wisdom again came to the rescue: guiding the righteous man by a despicable piece of wood. She was also present when the nations in their conspiracy of pride came together against the righteous man: she preserved him without blame before God, and kept a strong mercy toward his children. She delivered the righteous man from the ungodly who were perishing as he fled, from the descent of fire upon the five cities: as testimony to whose wickedness the desolate land still smokes, and where trees bearing fruit without season stand, and the incredible monument of a standing pillar of salt. For those who passed by wisdom were not only blinded so as not to know what was good, but they also left behind them for mankind a reminder of their folly, so that their sins could not remain hidden. But wisdom shall deliver from suffering those who serve her. She led the righteous man who fled from his brother's wrath by right paths, and showed him the kingdom of God, and gave him the knowledge of holy things. She prospered him in his toils, and multiplied the fruits of his labor. When those who oppressed him surrounded him with deceit, she stood by him and made him honorable. She guarded him from enemies, and protected him from those who would seduce him. She gave him a hard struggle so that he might overcome, and know that wisdom is mightier than all things. She did not forsake the righteous man when he was sold, but delivered him from sinners. She went down with him into the pit, and in chains she did not abandon him: until she brought him the scepter of a kingdom and power over those who had oppressed him.

She showed those who had mocked him to be liars, and gave him everlasting glory. She delivered the righteous man from the ungodly who oppressed him, once and for all without complaint from the nations. She entered into the soul of the servant of God and withstood fearsome kings with signs and wonders. She rendered to the righteous the reward of their labors, and led them by a marvelous path. She was a shelter to them by day, and a light of stars through the night. She brought them over the Red Sea and carried them through deep water. But their enemies she drowned in the sea, and from the depths of the abyss she raised the righteous. Therefore the righteous plundered the ungodly, and they sang praises to your holy name, O Lord, and praised with one accord your conquering hand. For wisdom opened the mouth of the mute, and made the tongues of infants speak clearly. Chapter XI.

She directed their works through the hand of a holy prophet. They journeyed through a desert where no man dwells, and pitched their tents in uninhabited places. They stood firm against their enemies and avenged themselves of their foes. They thirsted and called upon you, and water was given them out of a high rock, and rest for their thirst out of hard stone. For by the very things through which their enemies were punished, lacking water to drink, the children of Israel were made glad. By those same things, when they were in need, it went well with them. Instead of a fountain of an ever-flowing river, you gave human blood to the unrighteous. When they sought to kill the infant children, you gave your people water beyond all hope, showing through the thirst they then endured how you would exalt your own and destroy their enemies. For when they were tried, though only with mercy's discipline, they learned how the ungodly, being judged with wrath, were tormented. You tested us as a father warns his children.

Wisdom

But those you condemned, as if by a harsh king's questioning. Those absent and present alike were tormented. For a double grief had overtaken them: and they groaned at the memory of things past. For when they heard that through their own torments these things were being remembered, they gave thanks to the Lord, marveling at the end of their departure. For him who had been cast down in wicked reproach, they marveled at in the end. You will not deal similarly with the unjust: for through senseless deliberations they wandered, worshipping walls and tombs set above empty things; you sent against them a multitude of irrational animals in vengeance, so that they might know that through whatever things a man sins, through those same things he is punished. For it was not impossible for your almighty hand, which created the world from formless matter, to send against them a multitude of bears or fierce lions, or unknown beasts of a new kind full of rage, or to breathe out fiery vapor, or to discharge foul-smelling smoke, or to flash horrible sparks from their eyes, which not only could destroy them by their harm but also kill them by the very sight through fear. Indeed, even without these things, they could have been struck down by a single breath, persecuted by their own deeds, and scattered by the breath of your power; but you arranged all things by measure and number and weight. For to be of great power is yours alone always: and who shall resist the strength of your arm? For the whole world before you is like the turning of a balance, and like a drop of morning dew that falls upon the earth. But you have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of men for the sake of repentance. For you love all things that exist and hate nothing that you have made; for you would not have made anything if you had hated it. How could anything have endured, unless you had willed it? Or how would anything not called by you have been preserved? You spare all things, because they are yours, O Lord, you who love souls.

O how good and sweet is your spirit, O Lord, in all things. Therefore you correct those who err little by little, and you warn them about the things in which they sin, and speak to them, so that abandoning evil they may believe in you, O Lord. For those ancient inhabitants of your holy land, whom you abhorred for doing hateful deeds through sorceries and wicked sacrifices, and those who killed their own children without mercy, and devoured the flesh of men and drank blood, and initiates of secret rites, and parents who murdered helpless lives - you willed to destroy them by the hands of our ancestors, so that the land most precious to you might receive a worthy colony of the children of God. But even with these you dealt gently, sending hornets as forerunners of your army, to destroy them little by little. Not that you were unable to subdue the ungodly to the just in battle, or to destroy them at once by terrible beasts or by one stern word, but judging them by degrees you gave them space for repentance, not being ignorant that their nation was wicked and their malice natural, and that their way of thinking could never be changed. For their very root was cursed from the beginning. Neither did you spare anyone: you granted pardon to the sins of some, for who shall say to you, what have you done? Or who shall stand against your judgment? Or who shall come before you to plead for the wicked? Or who shall accuse you if the nations perish which you made? For there is no other God besides you who cares for all, that you should show that you do not judge unjustly. Neither king nor tyrant shall dare to question you concerning those whom you have destroyed. Therefore, being just, you order all things justly...

[Header: Wisdom (chapter) 13-14]

For you condemn those who ought not to be punished, and you reckon eternity as nothing compared to your power. For your power is the beginning of justice: and because you are Lord of all, you spare all. For you show your power when men will not believe you to be absolute in strength: and you reprove those who know this insolence. But you, being master of power, judge with calmness, and with great forbearance you govern us. For power is at your disposal whenever you wish. And by such works you have taught your people that the just man must be kind, and you have made your children to have good hope: because when you judge you give leave for repentance for sins. For if you punished the enemies of your servants, and those deserving death, with such great care, giving them time and opportunity to be changed from their wickedness: with how great care did you judge your sons, to whose fathers you swore covenants and made good promises. When therefore you correct us, you scourge our enemies many times, so that we may think on your goodness when we judge, and when you judge us we may look for mercy. Hence also those who lived in folly and unrighteousness in their lives, you tormented through their own abominations. For they went astray for long in the ways of error, taking for gods those things that even among animals are superfluous, living in the manner of senseless infants. Therefore you gave them foolish judgment as to children. But those who were not corrected by mockeries and rebukes experienced worthy judgment of God. For even those things by which they were afflicted they suffered with indignation: for them that were patient, seeing the one they once denied they knew, they acknowledged the true God. Therefore the full condemnation for their own guilt came upon them.

But all people were vain in whom there was not the knowledge of God: and who from the visible good things could not understand him who is: neither by attending to works did they acknowledge the artisan: but deemed either fire, or wind, or swift air, or the circle of the stars, or water, or the sun and moon to be the gods that govern the world. With whose beauty, if they being delighted took them to be gods: let them know how much better the Lord of them is than they: for the first author of beauty made all those things. Or if they admired their power and their effects, let them understand from them that he who made these things is mightier than they: for from the greatness of the beauty and of the creature, the Creator of them may be seen and known. But yet as to these there is less blame: for they perhaps err seeking God and desiring to find him. For being conversant among his works they search, and are persuaded that things are good which they see. But yet they are not to be pardoned: for if they were able to know so much as to make judgment of the world, how did they not more easily find out the Lord thereof? But unhappy are they, and their hope is among the dead, who have called gods the works of the hands of men, gold and silver, the inventions of art, and the resemblances of beasts, or an unprofitable stone the work of an ancient hand. Or if an artificer, a carpenter, has cut down a straight tree in the wood, and skillfully stripped all its bark, and with his skill fashioned a vessel fit for the service of life; and used the chips from his work for the preparation of food; and the residue of them which is good for nothing, being a crooked piece of wood and full of knots, he carves with the diligence of his leisure time, and by the skill of his knowledge fashions it, and makes it like the image of a man, or makes it like some beast, laying it over with vermilion...

Wisdom.

rubric: and you shall color his face with red paint, and cover every blemish that is in it with earth; and make for it a fitting dwelling place, and setting it in the wall and fastening it with iron so that it might not fall; knowing that it cannot help itself. For it is an image and has need of help. And concerning his substance, and his children, and his marriage, he inquires by making a vow. He does not blush to speak to that which has no life, and prays for health to that which is weak; and for life he entreats that which is dead, and for aid he calls upon that which cannot help; and for a journey he petitions that which cannot walk; and for acquiring, and working, and for the outcome of all things he asks of one that is unable to do anything. Chapter VIII.

Again, another person planning to sail, and through fierce waves, calls upon a piece of fragile wood to bear him, more fragile than the wood that carries him. For the desire of gain invented it, and the craftsman built it by his skill. But your providence, O Father, governs from the beginning, because you have made a path in the sea, and a most secure way among the waves; showing that you are able to save out of all things, even if a man were to go to sea without a raft. Nevertheless, so that the works of your wisdom should not be idle, men trust their lives even to a small piece of wood, and passing over the sea by a raft are saved; and from the beginning, when the proud giants perished, the hope of the world, taking refuge on a raft, guided by your hand, left to the world the seed of a new generation. For blessed is the wood by which justice is wrought; but cursed is the handmade idol, and he who made it; because that man worked, but that thing, though fragile, is called a god. Likewise, the ungodly and his ungodliness are equally hateful to God.
