The Lord will cut off the man that does this, the master and the scholar, out of the tabernacles of Jacob, and him that offers an offering to the Lord of hosts. And this have you done again: you have covered the altar of the Lord with tears, with weeping, and with crying out, so that he does not regard the offering any more, or receive it with good will at your hand. Yet you say, For what reason? Because the Lord has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously: yet she is your companion and the wife of your covenant. And did not he make one? Yet he had the residue of the spirit. And why one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. For the Lord God of Israel says that he hates putting away: for one covers violence with his garment, says the Lord of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that you deal not treacherously. You have wearied the Lord with your words. Yet you say: In what have we wearied him? In that you say: Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and such

Prologue to Maccabees.

Here begins the prologue of the blessed Jerome, priest, on the Books of Maccabees. The two Books of Maccabees record the wars of the Hebrew leaders against the Persian peoples, the battles on the Sabbath, and the noble triumphs of Judas Maccabeus, from whose name the books themselves also take their title. This history contains the manifest and clear deeds of the Maccabean brothers, who under King Antiochus endured terrible torments for the sake of the sacred laws. Their pious mother, though they were pressed with various punishments, not only did not weep, but rejoicing urged them on toward the glory of martyrdom. Here ends the prologue. Here begins the first Book of Maccabees, Chapter 1.

And it came to pass that Alexander, son of Philip the Macedonian, who first reigned in Greece, having gone out from the land of Cittim, struck down Darius king of the Persians and the Medes; he fought many battles and seized the strongholds of all, and killed the kings of the earth. And he advanced to the ends of the earth, and took the spoils of many nations; and the earth was silent before him. And he gathered a very strong army, and his heart was exalted and lifted up; and he seized the regions of nations and their rulers, and they became his tributaries. And after these things he fell sick upon his bed, and realized that he was dying. And he called his noble servants, who had been raised with him from his youth, and he divided his kingdom among them while he was still living. And Alexander reigned twelve years, and then he died. And his servants took possession of his kingdom, each one in his own place; and all put on crowns after his death, and their sons after them for many years; and evils multiplied upon the earth. And there came out of them a root of sin: Antiochus,

the illustrious son of Antiochus the king, who had been a hostage in Rome, and he reigned in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks. In those days there went out from Israel certain wicked men, and they persuaded many, saying: Let us go and make a covenant with the nations that are around us, for since we departed from them many evils have befallen us. And the proposal seemed good in their eyes. And some of the people volunteered and went to the king; and he gave them authority to practice the customs of the nations. And they built a gymnasium in Jerusalem according to the laws of the nations; and they made themselves uncircumcised, and departed from the holy covenant; and they allied themselves with the nations, and were sold to do evil. And when the kingdom was established before Antiochus, he resolved to reign over the land of Egypt, that he might rule over two kingdoms. And he entered into Egypt with a great multitude, with chariots and elephants and horsemen and with a great fleet. And he made war against Ptolemy king of Egypt; and Ptolemy was afraid before him and fled; and many were killed. And he seized the fortified cities in the land of Egypt and took the spoils of the land of Egypt. And after Antiochus had struck Egypt, in the one hundred and forty-third year, he turned back and went up against Israel and went up to Jerusalem with a great multitude. And he entered into the sanctuary with pride, and took the golden altar and the lampstand for the light, with all its vessels, and the table of showbread, and the libation vessels and the cups and the golden mortars, and the veil and the crowns, and the golden ornamentation on the front of the temple, and he stripped it all away. And he took the silver and the gold and the precious vessels; and he took the hidden treasures which he found; and carrying all away he departed to his own land. And he made a great slaughter of people, and he spoke with great arrogance.

Maccabees.

There was great mourning, and a great lamentation arose in Israel, and in every place among them. The rulers and elders groaned; young men and maidens were made feeble, and the beauty of the women was altered. Every bridegroom took up lamentation, and she who sat in the marriage chamber mourned. The land was shaken for those who dwelt in it, and the whole house of Jacob put on shame. After two full years, the king sent a chief collector of tribute to the cities of Judah, and he came to Jerusalem with a great company. He spoke words of peace to them in deceit, and they trusted him. Then he fell suddenly upon the city and struck it with a great blow and destroyed many of the people of Israel. He took the spoils of the city and burned it with fire. He pulled down its houses and its walls on every side, and they led away the women and children captive, and the cattle they took for themselves. Then they built the city of David with a great and strong wall and strong towers, and it became their stronghold. They placed there a sinful nation, wicked men, and they grew strong in it. They stored up arms and provisions, and gathered together the plunder of Jerusalem and laid it up there; and it became a great snare. This became an ambush against the sanctuary and a wicked adversary to Israel continually. They shed innocent blood on every side of the sanctuary and defiled it. The inhabitants of Jerusalem fled because of them, and she became a dwelling of strangers; she became strange to her own offspring, and her children forsook her. Her sanctuary was desolate like a wilderness; her feasts were turned into mourning, her sabbaths into reproach, and her honor into contempt. According to her glory, so was her dishonor multiplied, and her high estate was turned into mourning. Then king Antiochus wrote to his whole kingdom that all should be one people,

and each should give up his own customs. And all the nations accepted the command of the king. And many of Israel consented to his worship and sacrificed to idols and profaned the sabbath. And the king sent letters by the hand of messengers to Jerusalem and to all the cities of Judah, that they should follow the laws of the surrounding nations and forbid burnt offerings and sacrifices and drink offerings in the temple of God, and that they should profane the sabbaths and feasts, and defile the sanctuary and the holy people of Israel. He commanded that altars and temples and shrines of idols should be built, and that swine's flesh and unclean animals should be sacrificed, and that they should leave their sons uncircumcised, and defile their souls with all manner of uncleanness and abomination, so that they should forget the law and change all the ordinances of God. And whoever would not do according to the word of king Antiochus should be put to death. According to all these words he wrote to his whole kingdom, and he appointed overseers over all the people, and he commanded the cities of Judah to sacrifice. Then many of the people gathered to them, everyone who had forsaken the law, and they did evil things in the land. And they drove Israel into hiding and into secret places of refuge. On the fifteenth day of the month Casleu, in the one hundred and fifty-fifth year, king Antiochus built the abomination of desolation upon the altar of God, and in all the cities of Judah round about they built altars, and before the doors of the houses and in the squares they burned incense and sacrificed. And they burned the books of the law of God with fire, tearing them to pieces, and whoever was found with a book of the covenant of the Lord, and whoever observed the law of the Lord, was put to death according to the king's decree. By their might they did these things to Israel, who

Maccabees

He himself fled with his sons into the mountains, and they left behind whatever they had in the city. Then many who sought justice and righteousness went down into the wilderness and settled there, they and their sons and their wives and their cattle, because evil had pressed hard upon them. And it was reported to the king's men and to the army that was in Jerusalem, the city of David, that certain men who had defied the king's commandment had gone down into the hiding places in the wilderness. And many pursued after them, and having overtaken them, they set battle against them on the Sabbath day. And they said to them: "Enough, come out now, and do according to the word of king Antiochus, and you shall live." But they said: "We will not come out, nor will we obey the king's word, to profane the Sabbath day." And they gave battle to them. But they answered them not, neither did they cast a stone at them, nor stopped up the secret places, saying: "Let us all die in our simplicity, and heaven and earth shall be witnesses for us, that you put us to death wrongfully." So they rose up against them in battle on the Sabbath, and they were slain, with their wives and their children and their cattle, to the number of a thousand souls. And Mattathias and his friends heard of it, and they mourned greatly for them. And one said to another: "If we all do as our brethren have done, and do not fight against the heathens for our lives and our laws, they will quickly destroy us from the earth." And they decided on that day, saying: "Whoever shall come against us to battle on the Sabbath day, we will fight against him, and we shall not all die as our brethren died in their hiding places." Then there gathered to them a company of the Hasideans, mighty men of Israel, every one that offered himself willingly for the law. And all those who fled from the troubles joined them, and became a support to them. They mustered an army and struck down sinners in their anger and wicked men in their wrath; and the rest fled to the nations to save themselves. And Mattathias and his friends went about and pulled down the altars, and circumcised by force the uncircumcised boys that they found within the borders of Israel. And they pursued after the sons of pride, and the work prospered in their hands. So they recovered the law out of the hand of the Gentiles and out of the hand of the kings, and they did not let the sinner triumph. Now the days drew near that Mattathias should die, and he said to his sons: "Pride and rebuke have now grown strong, and a time of destruction and furious anger has come. And now, O my sons, be zealous for the law, and give your lives for the covenant of your fathers. And remember the deeds they did in their generations, and you shall receive great glory and an everlasting name. Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness? Joseph in the time of his anguish kept the commandment, and became lord of Egypt. Phinehas our father, in his great zeal, received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. Joshua, when he fulfilled the word, became a leader in Israel. Caleb, for bearing witness before the congregation, received an inheritance. David in his mercy obtained the throne of an everlasting kingdom. Elijah, zealous for the law, was taken up into heaven. Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, who believed, were saved from the flame. Daniel in his simplicity was delivered from the mouth of the lions. And so consider this from generation to generation, that all who hope in him shall not fail. And do not fear the words of a sinful man, for his glory is dung and worms. Today he is lifted up—

First

And he will be found no more, for he has returned to his own land, and his thought has perished. You therefore, O sons, take courage and be strong in the law, for by it you shall be glorified. And behold Simon your brother, I know that he is a man of counsel; listen to him always, for he shall be a father to you. And Judas Maccabeus, mighty in strength from his youth, shall be your leader in war, and he shall wage the war of the people. And you shall gather to you all the doers of the law, and avenge the wrong of your people. Repay the Gentiles their due and hold fast to the commandment of the law. And he blessed them and was gathered to his fathers. And he died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year and was buried by his sons in the sepulchres of his fathers at Modin, and all Israel mourned for him with great lamentation.

Then Judas, who was called Maccabeus, rose up in his father's place, and all his brothers helped him, and all those who had joined themselves to his father, and they fought Israel's battle with gladness. And he extended the glory of his people, and put on a breastplate like a giant, and girt about him his warlike armor in battle, and he set the camp in order with his sword. He was like a lion in his deeds, and like a lion's whelp roaring in the hunt. And he pursued the lawless men seeking them out, and those who troubled his people he burned with fire, and the enemies of his people were driven back in fear of him. And all the workers of iniquity were confounded, and salvation prospered in his hand. And he embittered many kings and made Jacob glad by his deeds, and his memorial is blessed forever. And he went through the cities of Judah, and drove out the ungodly from them, and turned away wrath from Israel. And he was renowned to the uttermost part of the earth.

And he gathered together those who were perishing. And Apollonius gathered together the Gentiles and a large and mighty force from Samaria to make war against Israel. And Judas perceived it and went out to meet him, and smote him and killed him; and many fell slain, and the rest fled. And they took their spoils; and Judas took the sword of Apollonius and fought with it all his days. And Seron, the commander of the army of Syria, heard that Judas had gathered a great assembly and a congregation of faithful men with him. And he said, I will make myself a name and get glory in the kingdom; I will make war against Judas and those who are with him, who despise the word of the king. And he prepared himself, and the camp of the ungodly went up with him, strong auxiliaries, to help him take vengeance on the children of Israel. And they drew near to Bethhoron, and Judas went out to meet them with a small force. But when they saw the army coming to meet them, they said to Judas: How shall we, being so few, be able to fight against so great and strong a multitude? And we are exhausted from fasting today. And Judas said: It is easy for many to be shut up in the hands of a few, and there is no difference in the sight of the God of heaven to deliver by many or by few. For victory in battle does not come from the size of the army, but strength comes from heaven. They come against us in great pride and iniquity, to destroy us and our wives and children and to plunder us. But we are fighting for our lives and our laws, and the Lord himself will crush them before us; as for you, do not be afraid of them. And when he had ceased speaking, he rushed upon them suddenly, and Seron and his army were routed before him. And they pursued him down from Bethhoron to the plain, and eight hundred men of them fell, and the rest fled.

Maccabees

into the land of the Philistines. And the fear of him and dread of him fell upon all the nations round about, and the report of him came to the king; and all the nations told of the battles of Judas. But when king Antiochus heard these words, he was angry in mind; and he sent and gathered all the forces of his kingdom, a very strong army. And he opened his treasury and gave his soldiers pay for a year, and commanded them to be ready for every need. And he saw that the money in his treasuries was failing, and that the tributes from the region were small, because of the dissension and disaster he had brought upon the land, in removing the laws that had been in force from the earliest times. He feared that he might not have enough, as had happened once and twice, for the expenses and gifts that he had previously given with a generous hand, surpassing the kings before him. He was greatly perplexed in mind, and thought to go to Persia to collect the tributes of those regions and gather much money. And he left Lysias, a man of noble birth of the royal family, to oversee the king's affairs from the river Euphrates to the borders of Egypt, and to bring up his son Antiochus until his return. And he entrusted to him half of his forces and the elephants, and gave him instructions about all he wanted done concerning the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem: to send an army against them to crush and destroy the strength of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem, and to wipe out their memory from the place, and to settle foreigners in all their territory and distribute their land by lot. And the king took the remaining part of his forces and departed from Antioch, the city of his kingdom, in the one hundred and forty-first year, and crossed the river Euphrates and went through the upper provinces. And Lysias chose Ptolemy the son of

Dorymenes, and Nicanor, and Gorgias, mighty men and friends of the king, and sent with them forty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry, to go into the land of Judah and destroy it according to the king's command. And they set out with all their forces, and came and encamped near Emmaus in the plain. And the merchants of the region heard of their fame, and took silver and gold in great quantity, along with slave dealers, and came to the camp to buy the children of Israel for slaves; and forces from Syria and the land of the Philistines joined themselves to them. And Judas and his brothers saw that evils had multiplied, and that the armies were encamping in their territory; and they learned the king's orders which he had given to destroy and utterly annihilate the people. And they said each man to his neighbor: Let us raise up the ruin of our people, and let us fight for our people and for the sanctuary. And the assembly gathered to be ready for war, and to pray and seek mercy and compassion. And Jerusalem was not inhabited, but was like a desert; none of her children went in or out, and the sanctuary was trampled down. And foreign men were in the citadel, and it was a lodging place for Gentiles. Joy was taken away from Jacob, and the flute and the harp ceased to play. And they gathered and came to Mizpah, opposite Jerusalem, because Israel formerly had a place of prayer at Mizpah. And they fasted that day, and put on sackcloth and ashes on their heads, and tore their garments. And they opened the book of the law, to find those things about which the Gentiles consulted the likenesses of their idols. And they brought the priestly vestments and the first fruits and the tithes, and they stirred up the Nazirites who had completed their days; and they cried out to heaven with a loud voice saying: What shall we do

Maccabees

praised God in heaven, for he is good, and his mercy endures forever. And there was a great deliverance in Israel on that day. But those foreigners who had escaped came and reported to Lysias everything that had happened. When he heard these things, he was confused and discouraged, because things had not gone in Israel as he had wished, nor had happened as the king had commanded. So the following year he gathered sixty thousand chosen men and five thousand cavalry to subdue them. They came into Judea and set up camp at Bethoron, and Judas met them with ten thousand men. When they saw the great army, he prayed and said: Blessed are you, O Savior of Israel, who broke the power of the mighty through your servant David, and delivered the camp of the foreigners into the hand of Jonathan the son of Saul and his armor-bearer. Shut up this army in the hand of your people Israel, and let them be put to shame with their troops and their horsemen. Strike them with fear, and let the boldness of their strength melt away, and let them be shaken by their own downfall. Strike them down with the sword of those who love you, and let all who know your name praise you. And they joined battle, and about five thousand of Lysias's men fell. When Lysias saw that his men had been routed and that the Jews were ready to live or die bravely, he went to Antioch and recruited mercenaries, so that he might return to Judea with a larger force. Then Judas and his brothers said: Now that our enemies are crushed, let us go up to cleanse the sanctuary and rededicate it. So all the army assembled and went up to Mount Zion. They found the sanctuary desolate and the altar profaned, the gates burned, shrubs growing in the courts as in a thicket or on some mountain, and the priests' chambers torn down. They tore their garments and mourned greatly, and put ashes on their heads, and fell on their faces to the ground, and sounded the signal on the trumpets, and cried to heaven. Then Judas detailed men to fight against those in the citadel until the sanctuary was cleansed. He chose priests without blemish, devoted to the law, and they cleansed the sanctuary and removed the defiled stones to an unclean place. They deliberated about the altar of burnt offerings which had been profaned, what to do with it. A good plan occurred to them: to tear it down, lest it be a reproach to them, because the Gentiles had defiled it. So they tore down the altar and stored the stones in a convenient place on the temple hill until a prophet should come to tell what to do with them. Then they took unhewn stones, as the law directs, and built a new altar like the former one. They also rebuilt the sanctuary and the interior of the temple and consecrated the courts. They made new holy vessels and brought into the temple the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table. They burned incense on the altar and lit the lamps on the lampstand, and they gave light in the temple. They placed bread on the table and hung up the curtains, and all the work they had undertaken was finished. Early in the morning on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, which is the month of Chislev, in the one hundred and forty-eighth year, they rose and offered sacrifice according to the law on the new altar of burnt offerings which they had built. At the very season and on the very day that the Gentiles had profaned it, it was rededicated with songs and harps and lutes and cymbals. All the people fell on their faces and worshiped and blessed Heaven, who had prospered them. And they celebrated the dedication of the altar for eight days.

First.

They offered burnt offerings with joy, and thanksgiving offerings. They decorated the front of the temple with golden crowns and small shields, and they rededicated the gates and the side rooms and hung new doors on them. There was very great joy among the people, and the disgrace brought on them by the Gentiles was removed. Judas and his brothers and the whole congregation of Israel decreed that the days of the dedication of the altar should be celebrated every year with joy and gladness for eight days, beginning on the twenty-fifth of the month of Chislev. They built high walls and strong towers around Mount Zion at that time, so that the Gentiles could not come and trample it down as they had done before. Judas stationed a garrison there to defend it and fortified Beth-zur to guard it against Idumea. Chapter 5.

When the surrounding nations heard that the altar had been rebuilt and the sanctuary rededicated as before, they were greatly angered, and they resolved to destroy the descendants of Jacob who lived among them, and they set out to kill and eliminate them. But Judas attacked the sons of Esau in Idumea, and those in Arabathane, because they were besieging the Israelites, and he struck them with a great blow. He also remembered the wickedness of the sons of Bean, who were a trap and a snare to the people on the road. He shut them up in towers and besieged them, and he devoted them to destruction by fire, burning the towers with all who were in them. Then he crossed over to the Ammonites, where he found a strong and large force, with Timothy as their commander. He fought many battles with them and they were crushed before him; he struck them down. He seized Jazer and its villages, then returned to Judea. The nations in Gilead gathered together against the Israelites who were in their territory to destroy them, but these fled to the stronghold of Dathema, and they sent a letter to Judas and his brothers saying: "The surrounding nations have gathered against us to wipe us out. They are preparing to come and seize the stronghold to which we have fled, and Timothy is the commander of their forces. Come now and save us from their hands, for many of us have fallen. All our kindred who were in the region of Tob have been killed; the enemy has carried off their wives, their children, and their goods and has destroyed about a thousand men there." While the letter was still being read, other messengers arrived from Galilee with their garments torn, bringing a similar report that people from Ptolemais, Tyre, and Sidon and all of Galilee of the Gentiles had assembled against them to destroy them. When Judas and the people heard these words, a great assembly was called together to consider what they should do for their kindred who were in distress and being attacked by enemies. Judas said to his brother Simon: "Choose your men and go to rescue our kindred in Galilee; I and my brother Jonathan will go to Gilead." He left Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah as leaders of the remaining forces in Judea to guard it, and he gave them these orders: "Take charge of this people, but do not engage in battle with the Gentiles until we return." Three thousand men were assigned to Simon to go to Galilee, and eight thousand to Judas for Gilead. Simon went to Galilee and fought many battles against the Gentiles, who were crushed before him. He pursued them to the gate of Ptolemais; about three thousand of the Gentiles fell, and he collected their spoils. He took with him those who had been in Galilee and in Arbatta, with their wives

Maccabees.

and to their wives and children and all who were with them; and he brought them back to Judea with great rejoicing. And Judas Maccabeus and Jonathan his brother crossed the Jordan and traveled three days' journey through the desert. And the Nabateans met them and received them peaceably, and told them all that had happened to their brothers in the land of Gilead: that many of them were shut up in Bozrah, Bosor, Alema, Chaspho, Maked, and Carnaim — all these cities were strong and large — and that others were held in the remaining cities of Gilead. And they had planned the next day to move against these cities and to seize and destroy them all in one day. Then Judas and his army suddenly turned and marched through the desert to Bozrah, and he took the city and killed every male by the edge of the sword, and took all their spoils and burned it with fire. He arose from there by night and they marched until they reached the stronghold. When morning came and he looked up, there was a multitude beyond counting, carrying ladders and siege machines to capture the stronghold and attack them. And Judas saw that the battle had begun, and the sound of the battle rose up to heaven like a trumpet, and there was a great uproar from the city. And he said to his army: "Fight today for your brothers!" He came upon them with three companies behind them, and they sounded their trumpets and cried out in prayer. And the camp of Timothy recognized that it was Maccabeus and fled from him. And they struck them with a great blow, and in that day nearly eight thousand men fell. Then Judas turned to Mizpah and attacked it and captured it, and killed every male there, and took its spoils and burned it with fire. From there he went on and captured Chalebon, Maged, Bosor, and the remaining cities of Gilead.

After these events, Timothy assembled another army and set up camp opposite Raphon, across the stream. And Judas sent scouts to observe the army, and they reported back to him saying that all the nations around them had assembled to him, and the army was very great. And the Arabs had come to help them, and they had camped across the stream, ready to come out against him in battle. And Judas went out to meet them. And Timothy said to the commanders of his army: "When Judas and his army approach the stream, if he crosses first we will not be able to withstand him, for he is strong enough to prevail against us. But if he is afraid and camps on the other side of the river, we will cross over to them and we will be able to prevail against him." Now when Judas drew near to the stream, he stationed the officers of the army by the stream and commanded them saying: "Let no one remain behind; let all come forward into battle." And he crossed over to them first, and all the people after him. All the nations were shattered before them and threw down their arms and fled to the temple at Carnaim. And Judas took that city and burned the temple with fire, with all that was in it. So Carnaim was subdued and could no longer withstand Judah. Then Judas gathered all the Israelites who were in Gilead, from the least to the greatest, together with their wives and children and their very large army, to come to the land of Judah. And they came as far as Ephron, which was a great city situated on the road, very strongly fortified; and there was no way to turn aside to the right or to the left; the road went straight through it. And those who were in the city shut themselves in and blocked up the gates with stones. And Judas sent to them with words

speaking peacefully: "Let us pass through your land to reach our own land, and no one will harm you; we will only pass through on foot." But they refused to open to them. Then Judas commanded in the camp that each man should attack from wherever he was. The men of valor drew near and he attacked that city all day and all night, and the city was delivered into his hand. He put every male to the sword, and plundered it and took its spoils, and passed through the whole city over the slain. They crossed the Jordan into the great plain before Beth-shan. And Judas was gathering the stragglers and encouraging the people all along the road until they came into the land of Judah. They went up to Mount Zion with joy and gladness and offered burnt offerings, because not one of them had fallen until they returned in peace. Now while Judas and Jonathan were in the land of Gilead, and Simon his brother was in Galilee before Ptolemais, Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah, commanders of the forces, heard of the brave deeds and the fighting that had been done, and said: "Let us also make a name for ourselves, and let us go fight against the Gentiles around us." So they gave orders to those in their forces and marched toward Jamnia. Gorgias and his men came out of the city to meet them in battle. Joseph and Azariah were put to flight and were pursued to the borders of Judea, and about two thousand of the people of Israel fell that day. A great defeat came upon the people because they had not listened to Judas and his brothers, thinking to do something brave. They were not of the family of those men through whom deliverance was given to Israel. The men of Judah were greatly honored and held in high regard in the sight of all Israel and all the nations wherever their name was heard, and people gathered to them with joyful acclamations.

Then Judas and his brothers went out and fought the sons of Esau in the land toward the south; he struck Hebron and its villages and tore down its walls and burned its towers all around. Then he marched off to go into the land of the Philistines and passed through Samaria. On that day some priests fell in battle, having gone out to fight boldly but without counsel, going out to battle rashly. And Judas turned aside toward Azotus in the land of the Philistines; he tore down their altars and burned with fire the carved images of their gods and plundered the spoils of their cities, and he returned into the land of Judah. Chapter VI.

King Antiochus was passing through the upper provinces and heard that there was a city called Elymais in Persia, very renowned and rich in silver and gold, and that there was a temple in it very full of wealth, with golden shields and breastplates and weapons left there by Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian king who reigned first over the Greeks. He came and sought to take the city and plunder it, but he could not because the plan had become known to those in the city, and they rose up against him in battle; so he fled and departed from there in great grief and returned to Babylon. Then someone came to him in Persia and reported that the armies that had gone into the land of Judah had been put to flight, and that Lysias had gone first with a strong force but had been driven back before the Jews; and that they had grown strong in arms and resources and in the abundant spoils they had taken from the armies they had cut down, and that they had torn down the abomination which he had built upon the altar in Jerusalem, and had surrounded the sanctuary with high walls as before, and also Bethzur, his city. When the king heard these words, he was struck with fear and greatly shaken; he fell upon his bed and sank into sickness from grief, because things had not turned out as he had planned.

Maccabees.

Just as he had been thinking. And he was there many days, because a great sorrow had been renewed in him, and he thought he would die. And he called all his friends and said to them: Sleep has departed from my eyes and my heart has failed from worry. And I said in my heart: Into what great tribulation have I come, and into what a flood of sorrow, in which I now find myself, who was once joyful and beloved in my power. But now I remember the evils I did in Jerusalem, from which I carried away all the golden and silver vessels that were there, and sent men to destroy the inhabitants of Judea without cause. I know therefore that these evils have found me because of this, and behold I perish with great grief in a foreign land. And he called Philip, one of his friends, and set him over all his kingdom. And he gave him his crown and his robe and his ring, so that he might bring up his son Antiochus and raise him to rule. And king Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year. And Lysias learned that the king was dead, and he appointed Antiochus his son, whom he had brought up from childhood, to reign, and he called his name Eupator. And those who were in the citadel had shut up Israel around the sanctuary, and were always seeking evil against them to strengthen the Gentiles. And Judas thought to destroy them, and called all the people together to besiege them. And they came together and besieged them in the one hundred and fiftieth year, and they made siege engines and war machines. And some of those who were besieged came out, and certain ungodly men of Israel joined them, and went to the king and said: How long do you not execute judgment and avenge our brethren? We were content to serve your father and to walk in his ordinances and to obey his edicts. And for this reason our own children were alienating themselves from us. And whoever was found among us was killed, and our inheritances were plundered. And not only against us did they extend their hand, but also against all our borders. And behold, they have come today to take the citadel in Jerusalem and have fortified Bethsura. Unless you come quickly, they will do greater things than these, and you will not be able to stop them. And the king was angry when he heard this, and he gathered all his friends and the commanders of his army and those who were over the cavalry. And also from other kingdoms and from the maritime islands came hired armies to him. The number of his army was one hundred thousand foot soldiers and twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two elephants trained for battle. And they came through Idumea and approached Bethsura, and they fought many days and made war machines. But the Jews sallied out and burned them with fire and fought bravely. And Judas departed from the citadel and moved his camp to Bethzacharan, opposite the king's camp. And the king rose before dawn and moved his army in force along the road to Bethzacharan, and the armies prepared for battle and sounded the trumpets. And they showed the elephants the juice of grapes and mulberries to provoke them to fight. And they divided the beasts among the legions, and stationed by each elephant a thousand men in coats of mail with bronze helmets on their heads, and five hundred chosen horsemen were assigned to each beast. These were ready before the beast wherever it went; and wherever it moved, they moved with it and did not leave it. And there were also wooden towers of strength upon them, fastened upon each beast with devices, and upon each were thirty-two strong men who fought from above, and

[Chapter heading: Primus]

...the master of the beast was inside. And the remainder of the army he stationed here and there in two divisions: to move the army with trumpets, and to purge those constrained in their legions. And when the sun shone upon the golden and bronze shields, the mountains gleamed with them and shone like torches of fire. And half the king's army was spread over the high mountains, and the other half over the low ground, and they advanced steadily and in order. And all the inhabitants of the land were shaken by the noise of their multitude and the marching of the company and the rattling of arms; for the army was very great and strong. And Judas and his army drew near for battle, and six hundred men of the king's army fell. And Eleazar, the son of Saura, saw one of the beasts armed with royal armor, and it was taller than all the other beasts; and he supposed that the king was upon it. And he gave his life to save his people and to win everlasting renown. He ran boldly toward it in the midst of the legion, killing on the right hand and on the left, so that they fell back from him on both sides. He crept under the elephant, stabbed it from beneath, and killed it; and it fell to the ground upon him, and he died there. And when they saw the power of the king and the fierceness of his forces, they turned away from them. The king's army went up to Jerusalem, and they camped against Judea and Mount Zion. And he made peace with those who were in Bethsura, for they came out of the city because they had no food there to endure the siege, for it was a sabbath year for the land. And the king took Bethsura and stationed a garrison there to hold it. Then he encamped before the sanctuary for many days and set up there artillery and engines of war and fire-throwers and stone-casters and scorpions to shoot arrows and slings. And the besieged also made engines of war against theirs, and they fought for many days. But there was no food in the city because it was the seventh year, and those who had fled to Judea from the Gentiles had consumed the last of the stores. And few men were left in the sanctuary because famine had prevailed among them, and they had been scattered, each to his own place.

And Lysias heard that Philip, whom King Antiochus had appointed while he still lived to raise his son Antiochus to be king, had returned from Persia and Media with the army that had gone with him, and that he was seeking to take over the government. So he hastened to depart and said to the king and the commanders of the army: "We grow weaker day by day, our food supply is scant, the place we are besieging is strong, and it is urgent that we settle the affairs of the kingdom. So now let us come to terms with these men and make peace with them and with all their nation, and agree to let them live by their laws as they did before; for it is on account of their laws which we abolished that they were angered and did all these things." The speech pleased the king and the commanders, and he sent word to make peace with them, and they accepted the terms. The king and the commanders swore to them, and they evacuated the stronghold. Then the king entered Mount Zion and saw the strength of the place, and he broke the oath he had sworn and gave orders to tear down the surrounding wall. Then he departed quickly and returned to Antioch, where he found Philip in control of the city, and he fought against him and took the city by force.

Chapter III.

In the one hundred and fifty-first year, Demetrius the son of Seleucus came up from Rome and landed with a few men at a city on the sea and began to reign there. And it came to pass, as he entered the palace of his ancestors...

Annua.

near Rapharsalama. And about five thousand men of Nicanor's army fell, and they fled to the city of David. After these events Nicanor went up to Mount Zion, and some of the priests came out from the sanctuary to greet him peaceably and to show him the burnt offerings that were being offered for the king. But he mocked them and defiled them and spoke arrogantly, and swore in anger, saying: Unless Judas and his army are delivered into my hands, when I return victorious I will burn this house. And he left in great anger. Then the priests went in and stood before the altar and the temple, and weeping they said: You, O Lord, chose this house to bear your name, to be a house of prayer and supplication for your people. Take vengeance on this man and his army, and let them fall by the sword. Remember their blasphemies and let them not endure. So Nicanor left Jerusalem and encamped at Beth-horon, and the Syrian army met him. And Judas encamped at Adasa with three thousand men. And Judas prayed and said: O Lord, when the messengers of the king of Assyria blasphemed you, your angel went out and struck down one hundred eighty-five thousand of them; so crush this army before us today, so that the rest may know that Nicanor has spoken wickedly against your sanctuary, and judge him according to his wickedness. So the armies met in battle on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and Nicanor's army was crushed, and he himself fell first in the battle. When his army saw that Nicanor had fallen, they threw down their arms and fled. The Jews pursued them a full day's journey from Adasa as far as Gazara, blowing the trumpets after them as a signal. And men came out from all the villages of Judea round about and outflanked them, and they turned them back to the pursuers, and they all fell by the sword. Not one of them was left. Then they took the spoils and the plunder, and they cut off Nicanor's head and the right hand which he had stretched out so arrogantly, and they brought them and displayed them just outside Jerusalem. The people rejoiced greatly and celebrated that day with great gladness. And they decreed that this day should be observed every year on the thirteenth of Adar. And the land of Judah had rest for a few days. Chapter 8.

Now Judas heard of the fame of the Romans, that they were very strong, and that they agreed to all who joined them, and that all who came to them they made friends with, and that they were very powerful. He was also told of their wars and the brave deeds that they were doing in Gaul, how they had conquered it and brought it under tribute. And he learned what they had done in the land of Spain to get control of the silver and gold mines there, and how they had gained control of the whole region by their planning and patience, even though the place was very far from them. And the kings who came against them from the ends of the earth they crushed and inflicted great defeat on them. And the rest paid them tribute every year. They had also defeated Philip and Perseus king of the Macedonians, and those who had taken up arms against them. And Antiochus the Great, king of Asia, who had gone to fight against them with one hundred twenty elephants and with cavalry and chariots and a very large army, had been defeated by them: and they took him alive, and agreed that he and those who should reign after him should pay a large tribute and give hostages. And the regions of Media and Lydia and the finest of their territories

Maccabees.

And having received these things from them, they returned to King Eumenes. And because those who were at Elladam wanted to go and remove them, word came to them of this and they sent one commander against them, and they fought against them, and many of them fell; and they carried off their wives and children as plunder, and plundered them, and possessed their land, and tore down their walls, and reduced them to slavery unto this day. And the remaining kingdoms and islands which had at any time resisted them they destroyed and brought under their power. But with their friends and those who relied on them they kept friendship; and they conquered kingdoms both near and far, because whoever heard their name was afraid of them. Those whom they wished to help to a kingdom reigned; but those whom they wished to depose they deposed, and they were greatly exalted. Yet for all this, none of them wore a crown or put on purple to be magnified thereby. And they had made for themselves a senate house, and every day three hundred and twenty men sat in council, deliberating continually on behalf of the people, to do what was right. And they entrust the government to one man every year, to rule over all their country, and all obey that one, and there is no envy or jealousy among them.

And Judas chose Eupolemus the son of John, the son of Accos, and Jason the son of Eleazar, and sent them to Rome to establish friendship and alliance with them, and to ask them to take the yoke of the Greeks off them, for they saw that the kingdom was oppressing Israel with slavery. And they went to Rome, a very long journey, and entered the senate house and said: "Judas Maccabeus and his brothers and the people of the Jews have sent us to you to make an alliance and peace with you, and that we might be enrolled as your allies and friends."

The proposal was pleasing in their sight. And this is the copy of the letter which they wrote back on bronze tablets and sent to Jerusalem to be there as a memorial of peace and alliance: "May it go well with the Romans and with the nation of the Jews at sea and on land forever, and may the sword and the enemy be far from them. But if war comes first upon Rome or any of her allies throughout her dominion, the nation of the Jews shall fight along with them as allies wholeheartedly, as the occasion may direct. And to those who wage war they shall not give nor supply grain, arms, money, or ships, as Rome has decided; and they shall keep their obligations without receiving anything in return. In the same way, if war comes first upon the nation of the Jews, the Romans shall willingly aid them as occasion may allow; and to those aiding them there shall not be given grain, arms, money, or ships, as Rome has decided; and they shall keep these obligations and do so without deceit. According to these terms the Romans make this agreement with the Jewish people. But if after these things either party shall determine to add or delete anything, they shall do so at their discretion, and whatever they add or delete shall be valid." And concerning the wrongs which King Demetrius is doing against them, we have written to him saying: "Why have you made your yoke heavy upon our friends and allies the Jews? If therefore they appeal to us again against you, we will defend their cause and fight against you by sea and by land."

Chapter 10.

Now when Demetrius heard that Nicanor and his army had fallen in battle, he sent Bacchides and Alcimus into Judea again, with the right wing of his army. And they went by the road that leads to Gilgal, and camped against Mesaloth in Arbela, and they captured it and killed many people. In the first month of the one hundred and [fiftieth] year...

Pinus.

The fifty-second joined the army at Jerusalem, and they rose up and went to Berea with twenty thousand men on foot and two thousand horsemen. And Judas had encamped at Laisa, with three thousand chosen men. And they saw the multitude of the army, for they were many, and they were greatly afraid; and many slipped away from the camp, so that only eight hundred men remained. And Judas saw that his army had melted away and the battle pressed upon him, and he was distressed in heart because he had no time to gather them together, and he was disheartened. And he said to those who remained: Let us arise and go up against our enemies; perhaps we are able to fight against them. And they tried to dissuade him, saying: We are not able; but let us save our lives now, and return with our brethren, and then we will fight against them; for we are too few. And Judas said: Far be it from me to do this thing, to flee from them. And if our time has come, let us die bravely for our brethren, and let us not leave a stain upon our glory. And the army moved from the camp and they stood to meet them. And the horsemen were divided into two parts, and the slingers and the archers went before the army, and all the mighty men were in the front of the battle. But Bacchides was on the right wing, and the legion drew near from both sides, and they sounded their trumpets. And those on the side of Judas also cried out, and the earth shook at the noise of the armies, and the battle was joined from morning until evening. And Judas saw that the stronger part of Bacchides' army was on the right side, and all the stouthearted men came together with him, and the right side was broken by them, and he pursued them to the mountain Azotus. And those who were on the left wing saw that the right wing was broken, and they followed after Judas and those who were with him, from behind. And the battle became severe, and many fell wounded on both sides. And Judas fell, and the rest fled. And Jonathan and Simon took Judas their brother and buried him in the sepulchre of his fathers in the city of Modin. And all Israel wept for him with great lamentation, and mourned many days, and said: How is the mighty man fallen, who saved Israel. And the rest of the acts of Judas, and his wars, and the brave deeds which he did, and his greatness, have not been written down, for they were very many. And it came to pass after the death of Judas that the wicked arose in all the borders of Israel, and all the workers of iniquity rose up. In those days there was a very great famine, and the whole region surrendered to Bacchides with them. And Bacchides chose wicked men and made them lords of the country; and they sought out and persecuted the friends of Judas, and brought them to Bacchides, and he took vengeance on them and mocked them. And there was great tribulation in Israel, such as had not been since the day when a prophet was not seen in Israel. And all the friends of Judas came together and said to Jonathan: Since your brother Judas has died, there is no man like him to go out against our enemies, Bacchides and those who are enemies of our nation. Now therefore we choose you this day to be our ruler and leader, to fight our battle. And Jonathan accepted the leadership at that time, and rose up in the place of his brother Judas. And Bacchides knew it, and sought to kill him. And Jonathan and his brother Simon and all who were with him learned of it, and they fled into the desert of Tekoa and settled by the water of the lake of Asphar. And Bacchides learned of it, and on the sabbath day he came himself

First.

And Bacchides learned of this and gathered all his forces, and notified those who were in Judea. He came and pitched camp against Bethbasi and besieged it for many days and built siege machines. Jonathan left his brother Simon in the city and went out into the countryside; with a force he struck down Odaras and his brothers and the sons of Phasiron in their encampments, and they began to multiply and grow in strength. Simon and his men went out from the city and burned the siege machines, and they fought against Bacchides and he was crushed by them. They afflicted him greatly, for his plan and his enterprise had come to nothing. He was furious with the lawless men who had advised him to come into the country, and he killed many of them. He then decided to go back with the rest to his own land. Jonathan learned of this and sent envoys to him to make peace and arrange for the return of the captives. He agreed gladly and did as Jonathan asked, swearing he would do him no harm for the rest of his life. He restored to him the captives he had previously taken from the land of Judah, and he turned and went back to his own land and never again came into their territory. The sword ceased from Israel. Jonathan dwelt in Michmash and began to judge the people and destroyed the ungodly out of Israel.

In the one hundred and sixtieth year, Alexander son of Antiochus, surnamed the Noble, came up and seized Ptolemais; he was received there and began to reign. Demetrius the king heard of it and assembled a very large army and went out to meet him in battle. Demetrius sent a letter to Jonathan in peaceful terms, to honor him.

For he said: Let us make peace with him before he makes one with Alexander against us; for he will remember all the wrongs we have done to him and to his brothers and to his nation. So he gave Jonathan authority to raise an army and to manufacture weapons, and ordered that the hostages in the citadel be handed over to him. Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letters in the hearing of all the people and of those in the citadel. They were very afraid, because they heard that the king had given him authority to raise an army. The hostages were handed over to Jonathan and he restored them to their parents. Jonathan settled in Jerusalem and began to rebuild and restore the city. He directed those doing the work to build the walls and encircle Mount Zion with squared stones for fortification, and so they did. The foreigners who were in the strongholds that Bacchides had built fled; each one left his post and returned to his own land. Only in Bethsura did some remain who had forsaken the law and the commandments of God, for it served as a refuge for them.

King Alexander heard of the promises that Demetrius had sent to Jonathan, and they told him of the battles and acts of valor that Jonathan and his brothers had performed and the hardships they had endured. He said: Shall we find another such man? Let us now make him our friend and ally. He wrote a letter and sent it to him with these words: King Alexander to his brother Jonathan, greetings. We have heard of you, that you are a man mighty in strength and worthy to be our friend. We now appoint you today as high priest of your nation and to be called Friend of the King. He sent him a purple robe and a golden crown, that you may hold what is ours in common with us and maintain friendship with us.

Maccabees.

friendships with us. And Jonathan put on the holy vestment in the seventh month of the one hundred and sixtieth year, on the feast of Tabernacles. And he gathered an army and made ready an abundance of arms. And Demetrius heard these words and was greatly troubled. And he said: What have we done, that Alexander has gotten ahead of us in securing the friendship of the Jews as a support for himself? I too will write to them words of entreaty and offer honors and gifts, so that they may be my help. And he wrote to them in these words: King Demetrius to the people of the Jews, greeting. Since you have kept faith with us and remained in our friendship and have not gone over to our enemies, we have heard this and rejoiced. Now continue to keep faith with us, and we will repay you with good things for what you have done for us; we will grant you many exemptions and give you gifts. And now I free you and all the Jews from tribute; I remit the salt tax and the crown taxes. And the third of the grain and the half of the fruit of the trees which is my share, I relinquish to you from this day forward, so that it shall not be taken from the land of Judea, nor from the three cities that are added to it from Samaria and Galilee, from this day and for all time. And let Jerusalem be holy and free with all its borders, and let its tithes and revenues be its own. I also yield up authority over the citadel in Jerusalem and give it to the high priest, that he may station in it men of his own choosing to guard it. And every Jew who has been taken captive from the land of Judah into any part of my kingdom, I set free without ransom, so that all shall be exempt from tribute, even on their own livestock. And let all feast days, sabbaths, new moons, appointed days, and three days before a feast and three days after a feast

be days of immunity and remission for all Jews in my kingdom. And no one shall have authority to do anything or to bring proceedings against any of them in any matter. And let there be enrolled among the king's forces thirty thousand men from among the Jews, and they shall be given pay as all the king's forces require; and some of them shall be stationed in the great fortresses of the king. And some shall be appointed over the affairs of the kingdom that are to be managed faithfully; let their officers and leaders be from among them, and let them live by their own laws, as the king has commanded in the land of Judah. And the three cities that have been added to Judea from the region of Samaria shall be considered part of Judea, and shall be subject to one authority and shall obey none except the high priest. Ptolemais and its surrounding territory I have given as a gift to the sanctuary in Jerusalem to meet the necessary expenses of the sanctuary. And I will give fifteen thousand shekels of silver each year from the royal revenues, whatever is due to me; and all the surplus that the administrators of revenues had not paid in years before, from now on they shall give for the works of the Temple. And in addition, five thousand shekels of silver which were received from the account of the sanctuary each year, this shall belong to the priests who perform the ministry. And whoever takes refuge in the Temple in Jerusalem and in all its precincts, because they owe something to the king in any matter, shall be released, and all that they possess in my kingdom shall be free. For the building or restoration of the works of the sanctuary, the cost shall be met from the king's revenues; and likewise for the rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem and the fortification of its circuit, the cost shall be met from the king's revenues; and for building walls in Judea. Bc

Maccabees.

He had so great an army in the plain where there was neither stone nor rock nor any place to flee. And Jonathan heard the words of Apollonius, and was moved in his mind, and he chose ten thousand men and set out from Jerusalem. Simon his brother met him to help him. They pitched camp at Joppa, and he shut Apollonius out of the city, because a garrison of Apollonius was at Joppa, and they fought against it. And those in the city opened to him, and Jonathan took Joppa. And Apollonius heard of it, and he gathered three thousand horsemen and a great army. And he went to Azotus as if he were making a journey, and immediately he went out into the plain, because he had a multitude of horses and trusted in them. And Jonathan pursued him to Azotus, and they joined battle. And Apollonius had left in the camp a thousand horsemen behind them in secret. And Jonathan learned that there was an ambush behind him, and they surrounded his camp and cast javelins at the people from morning until evening. But the people stood as Jonathan commanded, and their horses grew weary. And Simon led out his force and engaged the legion. The horsemen were exhausted and were broken by him and fled. Those who were scattered through the plain fled to Azotus and entered into Bethdagon their idol's temple to save themselves there. And Jonathan burned Azotus and the towns around it and took their spoils, and he burned with fire the temple of Dagon and all who had fled into it. And those who had fallen by the sword together with those who were burned came to eight thousand men. And Jonathan moved his camp from there and applied it to Ascalon, and the people of the city came out to meet him with great glory. And Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his people, bearing spoils.

And it came to pass that when Alexander the king heard these things, he continued to honor Jonathan still more. And he sent him a golden buckle, such as is customarily given to kinsmen of kings. And he gave him Accaron and all its territory as a possession. Chapter XI. And the king of Egypt gathered an army as great as the sand along the seashore, and many ships, and sought to take Alexander's kingdom by deceit and add it to his own. He went into Syria with words of peace, and the cities opened to him and met him, because Alexander the king had ordered that they should go out to meet him, since he was his father-in-law. But as Ptolemy entered the cities he stationed garrisons of soldiers in each city. And when he came near to Azotus they showed him the temple of Dagon that had been burned, and Azotus and its surroundings demolished and bodies thrown about, and the mounds of those slain in battle that he had made along the road. And they told the king that Jonathan had done these things, to make him resent him. But the king said nothing. And Jonathan met the king at Joppa with glory, and they greeted one another, and he slept there. And Jonathan went with the king as far as the river called Eleutherus, and then returned to Jerusalem. But king Ptolemy took control of the coastal cities as far as Seleucia, and he devised evil plans against Alexander. He sent envoys to Demetrius saying: Come, let us make a pact between us, and I will give you my daughter whom Alexander has, and you shall reign in the kingdom of your father. For I repent that I gave her to him, for he has sought to kill me. And he slandered him because he coveted his kingdom. And he took back his daughter and gave her to Demetrius, and he alienated himself from Alexander, and their enmity was made manifest.

[Chapter heading] First.

And Ptolemy entered Antioch and placed two crowns upon his head, one of Egypt and one of Asia. But Alexander the king was in Cilicia at that time, because those who were in those places were rebelling. And Alexander heard of it and came against him in battle. And Ptolemy brought out his army and met him with a strong force and routed him. And Alexander fled into Arabia to find protection there. And king Ptolemy was exalted, and Gaddeel the Arab cut off the head of Alexander and brought it to Ptolemy. And king Ptolemy died on the third day, and those who were in the fortresses were killed by those who were inside the camps. And Demetrius reigned in the one hundred and seventy-seventh year. In those days Jonathan gathered those who were in Judea to attack the citadel that is in Jerusalem, and they built many siege engines against it. And certain lawless men who hated their own nation went to king Demetrius and reported to him that Jonathan was besieging the citadel. When he heard this he was angry, and immediately came to Ptolemais and wrote to Jonathan that he should not continue the siege but should come to meet him at once. But when Jonathan heard this, he ordered the siege to continue. And he chose elders of Israel and priests and put himself in danger. And he took gold and silver and clothing and many other gifts and went to the king at Ptolemais and found favor in his sight. And certain lawless men of his own people brought accusations against him. But the king treated him as those before him had treated him. And he exalted him in the presence of all his friends, and confirmed him in the high priesthood and in all the honors he had previously held, and made him chief among his friends. And Jonathan asked the king to make Judea and the three districts — that is, Samaria and its borders — free from tribute, promising him three hundred talents. And the king consented and wrote letters to Jonathan about all these matters, in the following terms: "King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan and to the nation of the Jews, greetings. We send you a copy of the letter we have written to Lashthenes our kinsman about you, so that you may know its contents. King Demetrius to Lashthenes his father, greetings. We have decided to do good to the nation of the Jews, who are our friends and who keep their obligations to us, because of their goodwill toward us. We therefore confirm for them the borders of Judea and the three cities of Apherema, Lydda, and Ramathaim, which were added to Judea from Samaria, and all their territories, to be set apart from all the sacrificial dues at Jerusalem in place of the royal revenues which the king formerly received from them each year from the produce of the land and the orchards. And the other things due to us — the tithes and taxes — and the salt pits and the crown taxes which were paid to us, all of these we now grant them; and not one of these decrees shall be invalidated from now and forever. Now therefore take care to have a copy of this made and given to Jonathan and placed on the holy mountain in a prominent place." And when king Demetrius saw that the land was quiet before him and nothing resisted him, he disbanded his entire army, each man to his own place, except for the foreign troops he had recruited from the islands of the nations; and all the armies of his fathers were hostile to him. Now Tryphon had previously been a supporter of Alexander, and he saw that all the army was murmuring against Demetrius, so he went to Malchuel the Arab who was raising Antiochus, the son of Alexander, and pressed him to hand the boy over to him so that he might reign in his father's place. And he reported to him all that Demetrius had done and the hostility that...

Maccabees.

He kept his army against him, and stayed there for many days. Jonathan sent word to King Demetrius asking him to remove those who were in the citadel in Jerusalem, and those who were in the garrisons, because they were attacking Israel. Demetrius sent word to Jonathan saying: Not only will I do this for you and your people, but I will greatly honor you and your nation when the opportunity arises. So you will do well now if you send men to help me, for all my army has deserted. Jonathan sent three thousand valiant men to Antioch, and they came to the king, and the king rejoiced at their arrival. Then the citizens of the city gathered together, about a hundred and twenty thousand men, and wanted to kill the king. The king fled into the palace, and those who were from the city seized the streets of the city and began to fight. The king called the Jews to his aid, and they all gathered together to him. They spread through the city and killed a hundred thousand men that day. They set fire to the city and seized much plunder that day, and rescued the king. Those who were in the city saw that the Jews had taken control of the city as they wished, and their resolve weakened, and they cried out to the king with these words: Grant us peace, and let the Jews stop fighting against us and our city. They laid down their arms and made peace. The Jews were honored in the sight of the king and in the sight of all who were in his kingdom, and they were well known throughout the kingdom. They returned to Jerusalem with much plunder. Demetrius the king sat upon his royal throne, and the land was quiet before him. But he lied about everything he had promised, and he became estranged from Jonathan, and did not repay him according to the benefits he had received from him, and he treated him harshly. After these things, Trypho returned,

with Antiochus, who was still a young boy, and he made him king and placed a crown upon him. All the forces that Demetrius had scattered gathered to him, and they fought against Demetrius, who fled and was routed. Trypho took the war elephants and captured Antioch. Young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan saying: I confirm you in the high priesthood and appoint you over four cities, so that you shall be among the king's friends. He sent him golden vessels of service and gave him the right to drink from gold cups and to wear purple and to bear a golden brooch. He appointed his brother Simon as commander from the border of Tyre to the borders of Egypt. Jonathan went out and traveled through the cities beyond the river, and all the army of Syria gathered to him as allies. He came to Ashkelon, and the people of the city came out to meet him honorably. He went from there to Gaza, but the people of Gaza shut themselves in, so he besieged it and burned the surrounding area and plundered it. The men of Gaza made petition to Jonathan and he gave them his right hand; he took their sons as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem, and he traveled through the region as far as Damascus. Jonathan heard that the commanders of Demetrius had come to Kadesh in Galilee with a large army, intending to remove him from his office, so he went to meet them, leaving his brother Simon within the country. Simon advanced against Beth-zur and fought against it for many days and shut them in. They asked him to grant them peace terms, and he granted them. He drove them out and took the city and placed a garrison in it. Jonathan and his army encamped by the waters of Gennesaret, and before dawn they marched into the plain of Hazor. And behold, the army of the foreigners met them in the plain and set an ambush for him in

Maccabees.

He met them in the region of Amath. For he had not given them room to enter his territory. He sent spies into their camp, and when they returned they reported that the enemy had planned to attack by night. When the sun had set, Jonathan commanded his men to keep watch and to remain under arms throughout the night. He posted sentinels all around the camp. When the adversaries heard that Jonathan and his men were ready for battle, they were afraid and filled with dread. They lit fires in their camp. But Jonathan and his men did not know it until morning, for they saw the lights burning. Jonathan pursued them, but he did not overtake them, for they had crossed the river Eleutherus. Then Jonathan turned against the Arabs called Zabadeans, struck them, and took their spoils. He then marched on to Damascus and traveled throughout that whole region. Simon went out and advanced as far as Ashkelon and to the nearby strongholds, then turned toward Joppa and seized it. For he had heard that they intended to hand over the stronghold to the men of Demetrius. He placed a garrison there to hold it. Jonathan returned and called together the elders of the people, and planned with them to build strongholds in Judea, to heighten the walls of Jerusalem and to raise a great barrier between the citadel and the city, to separate the citadel from the city so that it would stand alone, and so that no one could buy or sell. They gathered to build up the city, and part of the wall along the eastern valley fell down, and he repaired it. Simon also built Adida in the Shephelah; he fortified it and set up gates with bars. When Trypho planned to become king of Asia and to put on the diadem and to stretch out his hand against King Antiochus, he was afraid that Jonathan would not permit him but would fight against him, so he looked for a way to seize and kill him. He set out and came to Beth-shan. Jonathan went out to meet him with forty thousand picked fighting men, and he came to Beth-shan. When Trypho saw that Jonathan had come with a large army, he was afraid to stretch out his hand against him. He received him with honor and commended him to all his friends and gave him gifts, and he commanded his forces to obey him as they would himself. He said to Jonathan, "Why have you put all these men to such trouble when we are not at war? Send them home. Choose a few men to stay with you, and come with me to Ptolemais; I will hand it over to you along with the remaining strongholds and other troops and all the officials, and I will turn around and go. That is why I am here." Jonathan trusted him and did as he said. He dismissed his troops, and they returned to the land of Judah. He kept three thousand men with him, two thousand of whom he sent to Galilee, while one thousand accompanied him. When Jonathan entered Ptolemais, the men of Ptolemais closed the gates and seized him, and they killed with the sword all who had come in with him. Trypho sent troops and cavalry into Galilee and the great plain to destroy all Jonathan's men. But when these men learned that Jonathan had been seized and had perished, and that all who were with him had been killed, they encouraged one another and marched out ready to fight. When their pursuers saw that they were ready to fight for their lives, they turned back. All of Jonathan's men then returned safely to the land of Judah. They mourned deeply for Jonathan and those who were with him, and all Israel grieved bitterly.

First.

There was great celebration. And all the nations that were around them sought to crush them. They said: "They have no leader, so now let us fight against them and wipe out the memory of them from among men." Chapter 13.
And when Simon heard that Trypho had assembled a large army to come into the land of Judah and destroy it, seeing that the people were trembling and fearful, he went up to Jerusalem and gathered the people together and encouraged them, saying: "You know how much I and my brothers and my father's house have fought for the laws and the sanctuary, and what tribulations we have seen. For this cause all my brothers have perished for the sake of Israel, and I alone am left. Now far be it from me to spare my own life in any time of tribulation, for I am not better than my brothers. I will therefore avenge my nation and the sanctuary and our wives and children, for all the nations have gathered together to destroy us out of hatred." When the people heard these words, the spirit was kindled among them, and they answered with a loud voice, saying: "You are our leader in place of Judas and Jonathan your brother. Fight our battle, and whatever you say to us, we will do." So he gathered together all the men of war and hastened to finish the walls of Jerusalem and to fortify it all around. He sent Jonathan the son of Absalom with a fresh army to Joppa, and having driven out those who were in it, he remained there.

Then Trypho moved from Ptolemais with a large army to enter the land of Judah, and Jonathan was with him under guard. Simon encamped at Adida, facing the plain. When Trypho learned that Simon had risen up in the place of his brother Jonathan, and that he was about to join battle with him, he sent envoys to him saying: "We have detained your brother Jonathan on account of the money he owed to the king's treasury in connection with the matters he handled. Now send a hundred talents of silver and two of his sons as hostages, so that when released he will not revolt against us, and we will release him." Simon knew that he was speaking deceitfully, but he ordered the money and the children to be sent, lest he bring great hatred upon himself among the people of Israel, who might say that Jonathan perished because he did not send the silver and the children. So he sent the children and the hundred talents; but Trypho broke his word and did not release Jonathan. After this Trypho came to invade and devastate the country, and he went around by the way that leads to Adora, and Simon and his army marched opposite him in every place wherever he went. The men in the citadel sent envoys to Trypho urging him to come quickly by way of the desert and to send them provisions. Trypho made ready all his cavalry to come that night, but there was very much snow and he did not come to Gilead. When he approached Baskama, he killed Jonathan and his sons there. Then Trypho turned back and went to his own land. Simon sent and took the bones of Jonathan his brother, and buried them in Modin, the city of his fathers. All Israel bewailed him with great lamentation, and mourned for him many days. Simon built a monument over the tomb of his father and his brothers; he made it high to the sight, with polished stone at front and back. He erected seven pyramids opposite one another, for his father and mother and four brothers. And around these he set great columns, and upon the columns he placed suits of armor for a permanent memorial, and beside the armor he carved ships, so that they could be seen by all who sail the sea. This is the tomb which he made at Modin, to this day.

Maccabees.

until this day. And Trypho, while making a journey with the young king Antiochus, killed him by treachery and reigned in his place. He put on himself the crown of Asia and inflicted a great plague upon the land. Simon built up the strongholds of Judea, fortifying them with high towers and great walls and gates and bars, and he stored provisions in the fortresses. Simon chose men and sent them to King Demetrius to obtain a remission for the region, because all the acts of Trypho had been carried out by plunder. King Demetrius answered him in these words and wrote a letter of this kind: King Demetrius to Simon, the high priest and friend of kings, and to the elders and to the nation of the Jews, greetings. We have received the golden crown and the garland which you sent, and we are ready to make great peace with you and to write to the king's officers to grant you the remissions we have allowed. Whatever we have established for you stands firm. The fortifications you have built shall remain yours. We forgive all oversights and offenses up to this day, and we forgive the crown you owed. And if anything else was subject to tribute in Jerusalem, let it no longer be. And if any among you are fit to be enrolled among our forces, let them be enrolled, and let there be peace between us. In the one hundred and seventieth year the yoke of the nations was lifted from Israel. And the people of Israel began to write in their records and public documents: In the first year of Simon, the great high priest, commander and leader of the Jews. In those days Simon marched against Gaza and besieged it with his forces and built siege engines; he pressed against the city and captured one tower. Those who were inside the siege engines and the city were thrown into great confusion. The men in the city went up onto the walls with their wives and children, with their garments torn,

crying out in a loud voice, begging Simon to grant them terms of peace, saying: Do not deal with us according to our wickedness, but according to your mercy, and we will serve you.
