Weeping, Simon did not attack them, but drove them out of the city and cleansed the houses in which the idols had been, and then he entered it with hymns, blessing the Lord. Having removed all uncleanness from it, he settled there men who observed the law and fortified it and made for himself a dwelling there. Those who were in the citadel of Jerusalem were prevented from going out and coming in to the region, and from buying and selling; they were very hungry, and many of them perished from famine. They cried out to Simon to accept their surrender, and he gave them terms. He expelled them from there and cleansed the citadel from its pollutions. They entered it on the twenty-third day of the second month, in the one hundred and seventy-first year, with praise and palm branches and with harps and cymbals and lyres and hymns and songs, because a great enemy had been crushed in Israel. And he ordained that every year these days should be celebrated with gladness. He fortified the temple mount which was beside the citadel, and he and his men dwelt there. Simon saw that his son John had become a man of war, and he made him commander of all the forces, and he dwelt in Gazara. Chapter 13.

In the one hundred and seventy-second year, King Demetrius assembled his army and marched into Media to gather help for himself so that he might fight against Trypho. Arsaces, king of Persia and Media, heard that Demetrius had invaded his territory, and he sent one of his princes to take him alive and bring him back. He went and attacked the camp of Demetrius, and captured him and brought him

1 Maccabees

And the enemies wanted to trample the holy places and ravage their region, and stretch out their hands against the sanctuary. Then Simon stood firm and fought for his people; he spent large sums of money and armed the fighting men of his nation, paying them wages. He fortified the cities of Judea, and Bethsura which lay on the borders of Judea, where the enemy had previously kept their arms, and he placed a garrison of Jewish men there. He also fortified Joppa which lay by the sea, and Gazara which was on the borders of Azotus, where the enemy had formerly dwelt. He settled Jews there and provided whatever was needed for their restoration. When the people saw Simon's deeds and the glory he sought to bring to his nation, they made him their leader and high priest, because he had done all these things, and for the justice and loyalty he had maintained toward his nation, and he sought in every way to exalt his people. In his days things prospered in his hands, so that the Gentiles were expelled from the land, and those in the city of David in Jerusalem in the citadel, from which they had gone out and defiled everything around the sanctuary, inflicting great harm. He placed Jewish men there for the defense of the region and the city, and raised the walls of Jerusalem higher. And King Demetrius confirmed him as high priest. According to these things he made him his friend and honored him greatly. For he had heard that the Jews had been called friends, allies, and brothers by the Romans, and that the Romans had received the envoys of Simon with honor; and that the Jews and their priests had agreed that Simon should be their leader and high priest forever, until a faithful prophet should arise, and that he should be their commander, and should have charge of the sanctuary, and should appoint officers over the works and over the country, and over the arms and over the strongholds; and that he should be obeyed by all, and that all contracts in the country should be written in his name; and that he should be clothed in purple and wear gold. And no one among the people or among the priests shall be permitted to nullify any of these things or to oppose what he says, or to call any assembly in the country without him, or to be clothed in purple, or wear a gold buckle. Whoever acts contrary to these things or nullifies any of them shall be liable to punishment. All the people agreed to grant Simon the right to act in accordance with these words. Simon accepted and agreed to serve as high priest, to be commander and ruler of the Jewish nation and priests, and to have authority over all. They ordered this document to be placed on bronze tablets and set up in a prominent place in the precincts of the sanctuary, and copies to be placed in the treasury, so that Simon and his sons might have them. Chapter 15.

And King Antiochus, son of Demetrius, sent letters from the islands of the sea to Simon, the priest and ruler of the Jewish nation, and to all the people. The content was as follows: King Antiochus to Simon the great priest and to the nation of the Jews, greetings. Whereas certain pestilent men have seized the kingdom of our fathers, I intend to reclaim the kingdom and restore it to its former state; I have raised a large army and built warships. I want to march through the country to take vengeance on those who have ruined our country and laid waste many cities in my kingdom. Now therefore I confirm to you all the tax remissions which the kings before me granted you, and whatever other gifts they remitted to you, and I authorize you to mint your own coinage in your own region. Jerusalem the holy...

first

to be and to hold: and all the arms which have been made, and the strongholds which you have built shall remain yours. And all the debts owed to the king, and those which shall be owed to the king in the future, shall be remitted to you henceforth. And when we shall have obtained our kingdom, we will glorify you and your nation and the temple with great glory, so that your glory shall be made manifest in all the earth. In the one hundred and seventy-fourth year Antiochus returned to the land of his fathers, and all his armies came together to him, so that few were left with Trypho. And Antiochus the king pursued him, and he came to Dora fleeing along the seacoast. For he knew that troubles had gathered upon him, and his army had forsaken him. And Antiochus camped against Dora with a hundred and twenty thousand warriors and eight thousand horsemen. And he surrounded the city, and ships came from the sea, and they pressed the city by land and sea, and suffered none to go out or come in. Then came Numenius and those who had been with him from the city of Rome, having letters written to the kings and countries, in which were contained these things: Lucius, consul of the Romans, to king Ptolemy, greeting. The ambassadors of the Jews our friends came to us renewing the old friendship and alliance, sent by Simon the high priest and the people of the Jews. They also brought a golden shield of a thousand pounds. It pleased us therefore to write to kings and countries, that they should do them no harm, nor fight against them, their cities or countries, and that they should give no aid to those who fight against them. And it seemed good to us to receive the shield from them. If therefore any pestilent persons have fled from their country to you, deliver them to Simon the high priest, that he may punish them according to their law. These same things were written to king Demetrius, and to Attalus, and to Ariarathes,

and to Arsaces, and to all the countries: and to Sampsames, and to the Spartans, and to Delos, and to Myndos, and to Sicyon, and to Caria, and to Samos, and to Pamphylia, and to Lycia, and to Halicarnassus, and to Rhodes, and to Phaselis, and to Cos, and to Side, and to Aradus, and to Gortyna, and to Cnidus, and to Cyprus, and to Cyrene. A copy of these things they wrote to Simon the high priest and to the people of the Jews. But Antiochus the king came again to Dora the second time, attacking it continually, and making engines of war, and he shut up Trypho from going any whither. And Simon sent to him two thousand chosen men to aid him, and silver and gold and abundance of supplies: but he would not receive them, but broke all the covenants he had made with him before, and became estranged from him. And he sent to him Athenobius one of his friends to treat with him saying: You hold Jaffa and Gazara and the citadel which is in Jerusalem, cities of my kingdom. Their borders you have wasted and made great havoc in the land, and have possessed many places in my kingdom. Now therefore deliver up the cities which you have seized, and the tributes of the places which you have possessed outside the borders of Judea; or else give me for them five hundred talents of silver, and for the destruction you have made and the tributes of the cities, other five hundred talents: otherwise we will come and fight against you. And Athenobius the king's friend came to Jerusalem, and saw the glory of Simon and his magnificence in gold and silver and his great attendance, and he was astonished, and reported to him the king's words. And Simon answered and said to him: We have not taken foreign land, nor do we hold what belongs to others, but we have taken back the inheritance of our fathers, which was unjustly possessed for a time by our enemies. Now that we have opportunity, we maintain the inheritance of our fathers. For as to Jaffa and Gazara which you demand, they were doing great harm

Seds

and he gave them silver and gold and gifts. And he sent others to occupy Jerusalem and the mount of the temple. And some runners announced to John in Gazara that his father and his brothers had perished, and that he had sent men to kill him too. And when he heard it, he was greatly troubled, and seized the men who had come to kill him, and slew them. Now John knew that they sought to kill him. As for the rest of the acts of Simon and of John, and his wars, and the brave deeds which he performed, and the building of the walls, and all his doings: behold, these things are written in the book of the days of his priesthood, from the time he was made high priest after his father.

Here begins the Second Book of Maccabees, Chapter 1.

To their brothers who are among the Jews throughout Egypt, greetings. The brothers who are in Jerusalem and in the land of Judea send greeting and peace. May God be gracious to you and remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, his faithful servants, and give you all a heart to worship him and to do his will with a great heart and a willing soul. May he open your heart to his law and his commandments, and may he grant you peace. May he hear your prayers and be reconciled to you, and may he not forsake you in time of evil. And now here we are, praying for you. In the reign of Demetrius, in the year one hundred and sixty-nine, we Jews wrote to you, in the tribulation and assault that came upon us in those years, when Jason departed from the holy land and from the kingdom. They set the gateway on fire and shed innocent blood. We prayed to the Lord and were heard, and we offered sacrifice and fine flour, and we lit the lamps and

set out the loaves of bread. And now keep the feast of tabernacles in the month of Chislev. In the one hundred and eighty-eighth year, the people who are in Jerusalem and in Judea, and the senate, and Judas, to Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy, who is of the family of the anointed priests, and to the Jews who are in Egypt: greeting and health. Having been delivered from great dangers by God, we give him great thanks, seeing that we fought against such a king. For he made those who fought against us and against the holy city come out from Persia. For when their leader was in Persia, and with him an immense army, they fell in the temple of Nanea, having been deceived by the counsel of the priests of Nanea. For Antiochus came to the place, as if to marry her, and his friends came with him to receive a large dowry in her name. When the priests of Nanea set it out, and he entered with a small retinue into the inner court of the temple, they shut the temple. And when Antiochus came in, they opened a secret door in the ceiling and threw stones and struck down the leader, and those who were with him, and cut them limb from limb and threw their heads outside. Blessed in all things is God, who delivered the impious. Therefore, since we are about to celebrate the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Chislev, we thought it necessary to inform you, so that you also may keep the feast of tabernacles and the feast of fire, which was given when Nehemiah offered sacrifice after building the temple and the altar. For when our fathers were led into Persia, the priests who were then devout took fire secretly from the altar and hid it in a valley where there was a deep dry well, and they kept it safe there, so that the place was unknown to all. Now when many years had passed, it pleased God to send

Maccabees 7.

Nehemiah, sent by the king of Persia, sent the descendants of the priests who had hidden the fire to find it; and as they reported to us, they did not find fire but thick water. He commanded them to draw it out and bring it to him; and the priest Nehemiah commanded that the sacrificial offerings be sprinkled with it, along with the wood and the things placed upon it. When this was done, and the time came when the sun shone out, which had previously been hidden in clouds, a great fire blazed up so that all marveled. The priests made prayer while the sacrifice was being consumed, Jonathan beginning and the rest responding. And Nehemiah's prayer was in this manner: "O Lord God, Creator of all things, terrible and strong, just and merciful, you who alone are the good King, you alone are bountiful, you alone are just and almighty and eternal, who delivers Israel from all evil, who chose our fathers and sanctified them: accept the sacrifice for all your people Israel, and guard your portion and sanctify it. Gather together our scattered people; free those who serve among the Gentiles; look upon those who are despised and abhorred, that the Gentiles may know that you are our God. Afflict those who oppress us and who insolently wrong us. Plant your people in your holy place, as Moses said." The priests meanwhile sang hymns until the sacrifice was consumed. When the sacrifice was consumed, Nehemiah commanded that the remaining water be poured upon great stones. When this was done, a flame blazed up, but it was consumed by the light that shone back from the altar. When the matter became known, it was reported to the king of Persia that in the place where the exiled priests had hidden the fire, water had appeared, and that Nehemiah and those with him had used it to purify the sacrifices. The king considered the matter and had a temple enclosure built there, to mark what had happened. And when it pleased him, he gave the priests many good gifts and various other presents, and receiving them with his own hand, he distributed them. Nehemiah called this place Nephthar, which is interpreted as purification; but by many it is called Nephi.

Now it is found in the records of Jeremiah the prophet that he commanded those who were going into exile to take fire, as has been described, and that he gave them the Law, lest they forget the commandments of the Lord; and that they should not be led astray in their minds when they saw images of gold and silver and their ornaments and other such things. And with such words he exhorted them not to let the Law depart from their heart. It was also in the same writing how the prophet, by divine response made to him, commanded that the tabernacle and the ark should accompany him, until he came to the mountain where Moses had gone up and had seen the inheritance of God. And coming there, Jeremiah found a hollow cave, and he brought in there the tabernacle, and the ark, and the altar of incense, and stopped up the entrance. Some of those who followed to mark the way were unable to find it. When Jeremiah learned of it, he rebuked them and declared that the place would remain unknown until God gathers his people together and shows them mercy. And then the Lord will disclose these things, and the glory of the Lord will appear, and so will the cloud, as it was revealed to Moses, and as when Solomon asked that the great God sanctify the place, these things were made manifest. For he dealt wisely with wisdom: and as one having wisdom he offered the sacrifice of dedication and completion of the temple. As Moses prayed to the Lord, so fire came down from heaven.

Seds.

And he consumed the burnt offering, and Moses said that what had been for sin was not eaten, for it had been consumed. Likewise Solomon celebrated the dedication for eight days. And in the records and commentaries of Nehemiah these same things were found: and how he, having founded a library, gathered together the books about the kings and prophets, and the writings of David, and letters of kings concerning votive offerings. And likewise Judas also gathered together for us all those writings that had been scattered because of the war that came upon us, and they are now in our possession. If therefore you have need of these things, send those who will bring them to you. We therefore, as we are about to celebrate the purification, have written to you. You will do well, therefore, if you observe these days. Now God, who saved all his people, and restored the inheritance to all, and the kingdom and the priesthood and the holiness, even as he promised in the Law, we hope that he will shortly have mercy upon us and will gather us together from every land under heaven into the holy place. For he hath delivered us out of great troubles and hath purified the place. Now as concerning Judas Maccabaeus and his brethren, and the purification of the great temple, and the dedication of the altar, and the wars against Antiochus the Noble and his son Eupator, and the illuminations that came from heaven to those who behaved themselves manfully to their honour for Judaism, so that being but a few, they recovered the whole country, and put to flight the barbarous multitude, and recovered again the temple renowned all the world over, and freed the city, and upheld the laws which were going down, the Lord being gracious unto them with all favour: all these things, I say, which have been declared by Jason of Cyrene in five books, we will assay to abridge in one volume. For considering the infinite number of books and the difficulty which they find that desire to look into the narrations of history, for the variety of the matter,

we have been careful to please those that are willing to read, that it might be a delight to those who wish to occupy their minds, easy for those who are eager to memorize, and profitable to all readers. And for us indeed who have undertaken the toil of abbreviating, it is no light matter but a thing of difficulty and labor of vigilance. As they that prepare a banquet and seek to satisfy the taste of others, for the sake of the gratitude of many do willingly undergo the labor: so we undertaking this thankful task, though it be not easy, do take upon us willingly the sweat of it, leaving to the author the exact handling of every particular, and laboring to follow the rules of an abridgement. For as the master builder of a new house must have care of the whole building; but he that undertaketh to decorate and paint it, must seek out the things fit for the adorning thereof: so I think it is with us. To collect everything belonging to understanding and arrangement belongs to the author of the history; but to be brief in expression and to avoid a full discussion of every particular, is to be allowed to him that maketh the abridgement. Here therefore shall we begin the narration: let it be enough to have said this much by way of preface; for it is foolish to be prolix before the history and to be brief in the history itself.

Chapter III. Now when the holy city was inhabited with all peace, and the laws were kept very well, because of the godliness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness, it came to pass that even the kings themselves did honour the place and glorify the temple with their best gifts, and that Seleucus king of Asia of his own revenues bore all the costs belonging to the service of the sacrifices. But one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city,

Seda.

...who, having entered the treasury with many runners and attendants, was being carried out with no one able to help him, God's power having been made manifest. And he indeed lay mute through divine power, deprived of all hope and health. But these men blessed the Lord, because He had glorified His place; and the temple, which a little before was full of fear and tumult, was filled with joy and gladness at the appearance of the Almighty Lord. Then some of Heliodorus's friends quickly begged the high priest to invoke the Most High to grant life to him who was at his last breath. The high priest, considering that the king might suspect that some foul play had been done by the Jews against Heliodorus, offered a sacrifice for the recovery of the man. And while the high priest was making atonement, the same young men appeared again to Heliodorus, clothed in the same garments, and said: "Give great thanks to Onias the priest, for the Lord has granted you life. And you, having been scourged by God, proclaim to all men the great works and power of God." Having said these things, they appeared no more. So Heliodorus, after he had offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made great vows to him who had spared his life, and having given thanks to Onias, returned with his army to the king. And he testified before all men the works of the great God which he had seen with his own eyes. And when the king asked Heliodorus who would be a fit man to be sent once more to Jerusalem, he said: "If you have any enemy or traitor to your kingdom, send him there, and you will receive him back well scourged, if he indeed escapes at all; for there is certainly some power of God about that place. For he who dwells in heaven is the overseer and protector of that place, and he strikes and destroys those who come to do evil." Thus the matter concerning Heliodorus and the keeping of the treasury stands. Chapter 4.

But Simon, who had betrayed the money and his country, spoke evil of Onias, as if he had incited Heliodorus to these things, and had been the originator of all the evils. He dared to call a benefactor of the city, a guardian of his people, and a zealot for the laws of God, a plotter against the government. But when his enmity went so far that murders were committed by some of Simon's associates, Onias, considering the danger of this contention and that Apollonius, as the commander of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was furthering Simon's malice, went to the king — not to be an accuser of his fellow citizens, but having in view the welfare of all the people, both public and private. For he saw that without the king's intervention it was impossible to have peace again, and that Simon would not stop his folly. But after Seleucus departed from life and Antiochus, called the Noble, took the kingdom, Jason, the brother of Onias, ambitiously sought the high priesthood; going to the king, he promised him three hundred and sixty talents of silver, and from another source of revenue eighty talents. Besides this he promised to pay a hundred and fifty more if he were given authority to set up a gymnasium and an ephebeum there, and to enroll the people of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch. The king agreed and, having obtained the office, he immediately began to convert his fellow countrymen to the Greek way of life; setting aside the royal concessions to the Jews granted out of humanity, through John the father of Eupolemus (who later went on the embassy to the Romans about friendship and alliance), he was breaking down the lawful ways of living and was introducing customs contrary to the law. For he dared to set up a gymnasium right under the citadel, and to bring the noblest of the young men...

Maccabees.

to put them in the brothel. But this was not a beginning but an increase and advancement of the Gentile and foreign way of life, on account of the wicked and unlawful deeds of the impious Jason, who was no true priest — a crime so monstrous and unheard of that the priests were no longer devoted to the service of the altar, but despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened to share in the unlawful exercises of the wrestling ground, and to take part in its practices, caring nothing for their ancestral honors but valuing Greek glories above all. For this reason a dangerous rivalry gripped them and they emulated those customs, eagerly desiring to be in all things like those who had made them their enemies and oppressors. For acting impiously against the divine laws does not go unpunished, as the time that followed would show. When the quinquennial games were being held at Tyre and the king was present, the vile Jason sent men from Jerusalem, sinners, carrying three hundred silver drachmas for the sacrifice of Hercules, which those who had brought them requested should not be used for sacrifice — since it would be improper — but be set aside for other expenses. But these offerings, though sent by their sender for the sacrifice of Hercules, were used instead for the construction of triremes. When Apollonius, son of Menestheus, was sent to Egypt for the first audience of King Ptolemy Philometor, Antiochus, learning that the king was now hostile to his affairs, consulting his own interests, went from there to Joppa and from there to Jerusalem. He was received magnificently by Jason and the city, welcomed with torchlight and cheering, and then led his army into Phoenicia. After a period of three years Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the aforementioned Simon, carrying money to the king and to bring answers on necessary matters of government. But he, having commended himself to the king and having made an impression by his show of authority, turned it to his own advantage, outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver for the high priesthood. Having received royal authorization he came, possessing nothing worthy of the high priesthood, but with the heart and fury of a cruel tyrant and wild beast. And Jason, who had betrayed his own brother, was himself deceived, driven out as a fugitive into the region of the Ammanites. Menelaus thus obtained the office, but paid nothing of the money he had promised the king, while Sostratus, the commander of the citadel, who was responsible for collecting revenue, pressed him for it — and for this reason both were summoned before the king. Menelaus was removed from the priesthood, and his brother Lysimachus succeeded him, while Sostratus was made governor of Cyprus. While these things were happening, the people of Tarsus and Mallus broke into revolt because they had been given as a gift to the king's concubine. The king therefore hastened to settle the matter, leaving one of his officers, Andronicus, in his place. Menelaus, thinking he had found a convenient opportunity, stole some golden vessels from the temple and gave them to Andronicus; he had also sold others at Tyre and in the neighboring cities. When Onias had learned of this with certainty, he confronted him, having taken refuge in a safe sanctuary at Daphne near Antioch. Then Menelaus approached Andronicus and urged him to kill Onias. Andronicus came to Onias and, giving deceitful assurances with an oath — though Onias remained suspicious — persuaded him to leave sanctuary. Then immediately, without any regard for justice, he put him to death. For this reason not only the Jews but also many people of other nations were filled with indignation and grief.

The nations were indignant and grieved bitterly at the unjust death of so great a man. But when the king returned from Cilicia, the Jews together with the Greeks came to him at Antioch, complaining about the unjust death of Onias. Antiochus was grieved in spirit on account of everything, and moved to pity he shed tears, remembering the sobriety and modesty of the deceased. Inflamed in spirit, he ordered Andronicus to be stripped of his purple robe and led through the whole city, and in the same place where he had committed the impiety against Onias, to be deprived of his life, the Lord rendering to him the punishment he deserved. Many acts of sacrilege committed in the temple by Lysimachus with the counsel of Menelaus became known, and when a rumor spread, the multitude gathered against Lysimachus, the mule already loaded with gold. As the crowds rose up and their minds were filled with anger, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and resorted to unjust violence, led by a certain tyrant, as old in age as he was foolish in mind. But when they perceived the attempt of Lysimachus, some seized stones, others stout clubs, some threw ashes at Lysimachus. Many were wounded, some were struck down, and all were put to flight. The sacrilegious man himself they killed beside the treasury. An accusation was therefore brought against Menelaus. And when the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the elders brought the matter before him. When Menelaus was losing his case, he promised Ptolemy many sums of money to persuade the king. So Ptolemy, under pretense of taking some rest in a certain colonnade, approached the king and turned him from his purpose, acquitting Menelaus of the charges of wickedness. But those who had spoken on behalf of the city and people and the sacred vessels — though they would have been found innocent even before any court — he condemned to death. So those who had pleaded the cause of the city, the people, and the sacred vessels received unjust punishment. Therefore even the Tyrians, indignant, provided magnificently for their burial. Menelaus, however, through the greed of those in power, remained in his position, growing worse in malice and plotting against the citizens.

At the same time Antiochus was preparing a second expedition into Egypt. It happened that throughout the whole city of Jerusalem, for forty days there were seen in the air horsemen riding in golden garments and carrying spears, like bands of armed men, and troops of horsemen drawn up in order, and charges and countercharges made on this side and on that, and the brandishing of shields, and a multitude of men in armor, and the drawing of swords, and the shooting of arrows, and the gleaming of golden ornaments, and armor of every sort. Therefore all prayed that this vision might prove a good omen. But when a false rumor arose that Antiochus had died, Jason took no fewer than a thousand men and made a sudden attack upon the city. As the citizens crowded to the walls, the city was at last taken, and Menelaus fled into the citadel. Jason slaughtered his own citizens without mercy, not realizing that success won against one's own kindred is the greatest of misfortunes, imagining he was gaining a trophy over enemies and not over fellow citizens. He did not gain control of the government, however, and in the end received only disgrace as the result of his treachery, and again took refuge as a fugitive in the country of the Ammonites. At last he was shut up in Egypt, condemned by the Arab tyrant, fleeing from city to city, an outcast, hated by all, a fugitive from the laws, an abomination, loathed as an enemy of his country and his fellow citizens; he was driven into Egypt — he who had driven many from their native land.

Second

The altar too was full of illicit things, which were forbidden by the laws. The sabbaths were not kept, nor were the traditional feasts observed, nor did anyone openly confess himself a Jew. They were led by bitter necessity to the king's birthday sacrifices, and when the feast of Bacchus was celebrated, they were compelled to go in procession in honor of Bacchus, wearing wreaths of ivy. At the suggestion of the people of Ptolemais, a decree went out to the neighboring Greek cities that they should act in the same way against the Jews and compel them to sacrifice, and those who would not cross over to Greek customs should be put to death. One could see therefore great misery. For two women were denounced for having circumcised their children; and when they had led them publicly around the city with their infants hanging at their breasts, they cast them down headlong from the wall. Others who had gathered in nearby caves to celebrate the sabbath secretly, being betrayed to Philip, were burned together, because their respect for the law led them to scruple to defend themselves. Now I urge those who read this book not to be discouraged by these misfortunes, but to recognize that these punishments were designed not for the destruction but for the correction of our nation. For it is a sign of great kindness not to let the impious alone for long but to punish them at once. For indeed with other nations the Lord patiently holds back his judgment until they have filled up the measure of their sins: but with us he has determined to deal differently, so that he may not have to punish us more severely later when our sins have reached their height. Therefore he never withdraws his mercy from us, and though he disciplines us with adversity, he does not abandon his own people. Let this suffice by way of reminder for readers; we must now proceed with our narrative.

So Eleazar, one of the leading scribes, a man already advanced in age and of noble bearing, was forced to open his mouth and eat pork. But he, welcoming death with honor rather than life with pollution, went forward of his own accord to the instrument of torture. He considered how he ought to approach the matter, and decided patiently that he would not do anything unlawful for love of life. Those who stood by, moved by an unreasonable pity for the long acquaintance they had with the man, took him aside privately and urged him to bring meat of his own provision, such as was lawful for him to use, and to pretend that he was eating the king's required sacrifice, so that by this device he might escape death and be treated kindly for an old friendship. But making a high resolve, worthy of his years and the dignity of his old age, and the gray hairs he had reached with such distinction, and his excellent upbringing from childhood, and still more in keeping with the holy legislation given by God, he declared his mind accordingly, telling them to send him at once to the underworld. For it is not worthy of our time of life, he said, to pretend, so that many of the young might suppose that Eleazar in his ninetieth year had gone over to an alien religion; and so through my pretense, for the sake of living a brief moment longer, they should be led astray because of me, and I would bring defilement and dishonor upon my old age. Even if for the present I should avoid the punishment of men, yet whether I live or die I shall not escape the hands of the Almighty. Therefore by bravely giving up my life now, I will show myself worthy of my old age, and leave to the young a noble example of how to die willingly and generously for the revered and holy laws. When he had said these words, he went immediately

Maccabees

They were being led to punishment. Those who were leading them, who had shortly before been junior officers, were moved to anger on account of the words he had spoken, which they regarded as uttered out of arrogance. But when he was dying under the blows, he groaned and said: "Lord, you who have holy knowledge, you know full well that, though I could have been freed from death, I endure these terrible bodily pains; yet in my soul I willingly bear these things out of fear of you." And so he departed this life in this way, leaving behind not only for the young but for all people the memory of his death as an example of virtue and fortitude. Chapter VII.

It happened that seven brothers together with their mother were arrested and tortured with whips and scourges by the king, to force them to eat unlawful pork. One of them, the first to speak, said: "What do you seek? What do you wish to learn from us? We are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers given by God." The king in his rage commanded that pans and brazen cauldrons be heated. When these were immediately heated, he commanded that the tongue of the one who had spoken first be cut out, and then that his head be scalped and his hands and feet cut off, while the rest of his brothers and his mother looked on. When he was now utterly helpless, the king ordered fire to be brought near and him to be fried alive in the pan. While the vapor from the pan spread widely, the rest together with their mother encouraged one another to die nobly, saying: "The Lord God will look upon the truth and will take comfort in us, as Moses declared in the song of testimony: and he will take comfort in his servants." After the first had died in this manner, they brought the second for their mockery, and having torn the skin of his head together with his hair—

He asked him whether he would eat before his whole body was punished limb by limb. He answered in the language of his fathers and said: "I will not do it." So this one also in his turn received the same tortures as the first, and at the point of death he said: "You, most wicked man, are destroying us from this present life, but the King of the world will raise us up, who die for his laws, in the resurrection of eternal life." After him the third was made sport of, and when he was called upon he quickly put out his tongue and courageously stretched forth his hands, and said with confidence: "From heaven I received these; and for the sake of his laws I now despise them; and from him I hope to receive them again." So that the king and those around him marveled at the young man's spirit, that he counted the sufferings as nothing. After he too had died, they tortured the fourth in the same way. And when he was near death he said: "It is better, being put to death by men, to look for hope from God to be raised up again by him; for as for you, you shall have no resurrection to life." Next they brought the fifth and abused him. But he looking at the king said: "You have power over men, and though you are corruptible, you do what you will; but do not think that our nation is forsaken by God. Just wait patiently and you will see his great power, how he will torment you and your descendants." After him they brought the sixth, and when he was about to die he said: "Do not deceive yourself in vain. For we suffer these things because of ourselves, having sinned against our God, and worthy of great wonder are the things that have happened to us. But do not think that you shall go unpunished, having attempted to fight against God." But above all was the mother worthy of admiration and of honorable memory, who, seeing her seven sons perish within the space of one day, bore it with good courage because of her hope in God; and of each one she—
