But he exhorted them with the voice of their fathers, bravely, filled with wisdom, and instilling a manly spirit into his reasoning, he said to them: I do not know how you appeared in my womb. It was not I who gave you breath and life, nor I who arranged each of your members. It was the Creator of the world who formed the nature of man and found the origin of all things: and he will restore to you breath and life again with mercy, as you now disregard yourselves for the sake of his laws. Now Antiochus, feeling himself despised, and stung by the tone of her reproach, yet she was still the youngest — not only urged with words but also swore with an oath that he would make him rich and blessed, and would take him from his ancestral laws and count him his friend and provide him with what was needful. But as the young man would not be moved by this, the king called the mother and urged her to counsel the youth to save himself. After he had urged her with many words, she agreed to persuade her son. So she leaned toward him and, mocking the cruel tyrant, spoke in her native tongue: My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb nine months, nursed you for three years, and brought you to this age. I beg you, child, look at the heaven and the earth, and at all that is in them, and know that God made them out of nothing, and the human race as well. So do not be afraid of this executioner, but be worthy of your brothers and accept death, so that in that mercy I may receive you again with your brothers. While she was yet speaking, the young man said: What are you waiting for? I do not obey the command of the king, but the command of the law that was given to us by Moses. And you, who have devised all manner of evil against the Hebrews, shall not escape the hand of God. For we suffer these things for our own sins.

And if our living Lord is angry with us for a little while to rebuke and correct us, yet he will again be reconciled with his servants. But you, O most wicked of all men, do not be lifted up in vain with empty hopes, puffed up against his heavenly servants. For you have not yet escaped the judgment of Almighty God who sees all things. My brothers, after enduring a brief pain, have now drunk of overflowing life under God's covenant; but you, by the judgment of God, shall receive just punishment for your arrogance. I, like my brothers, give up body and soul for the laws of our fathers, calling upon God to be soon merciful to our nation, and to make you confess by trials and torments that he alone is God. With me and my brothers may the Almighty's wrath, which has been justly brought upon our whole nation, come to an end. Then the king, inflamed with anger, treated him worse than all the others, bitterly resenting the scorn. And so he too died undefiled, putting his whole trust in the Lord. Last of all, after her sons, the mother died. Let this, then, suffice concerning the sacrificial feasts and the extreme cruelties. Chapter VIII. But Judas Maccabeus and those who were with him went secretly into the villages, and summoned their kinsmen and friends and enrolled those who had remained in the Jewish faith, and gathered together about six thousand men. And they called upon the Lord to look upon the people who were oppressed by all, and to have mercy on the temple that had been profaned by the impious. They prayed that he would have mercy on the ruined city that was soon to be leveled to the ground, that he would hearken to the blood that cried out to him, that he would remember the unjust deaths of the innocent children and the blasphemies committed against his name, and that he would show his hatred of wickedness. Now Maccabeus assembled...

Maccabees.

The wrath of the Lord had turned to mercy. And appearing suddenly at castles and towns he would attack them, and seizing favorable positions he put not a few of the enemy to flight. He carried out these raids especially at night, and news of his valor spread everywhere. Seeing that Philip was gradually making progress, and that things were prospering for him more and more, Ptolemy, governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, wrote to ask for the king's help in his affairs. Ptolemy quickly sent Nicanor, son of Patroclus, one of the king's chief friends, giving him no fewer than twenty thousand armed men from various nations, to wipe out the whole race of Judea. With him he sent Gorgias, a general of experience and distinction in military matters. Nicanor planned to raise for the king the tribute of two thousand talents owed to the Romans by selling Jewish captives into slavery. So he immediately sent to the coastal cities, inviting them to come and buy Jewish slaves, promising to deliver them at ninety slaves to the talent, not reckoning with the vengeance that was to follow him from the Almighty. When Judas learned of this, he told the Jews who were with him about Nicanor's advance. Some of them were cowardly and distrustful of God's justice and fled; others had sold all they had left and begged God to deliver them from the wicked Nicanor who had sold them before they even came to him. They prayed that if not for their sakes, then for the sake of the covenants made with their ancestors and the invocation of his holy and glorious name upon them, God would act. Maccabeus gathered seven thousand men who were with him and urged them

not to be reconciled with the enemy, nor to fear the great multitude of those who were unjustly coming against them, but to fight bravely, keeping before their eyes the outrage that had been unlawfully done to the holy place, and likewise the mockery of the city that had been dishonored, and also the overthrow of their ancestral way of life. For they, he said, trust in their weapons and bold deeds; but we trust in the Almighty God, who is able with a single nod to strike down those coming against us and even the whole world. He also reminded them of the help given by God to their ancestors: how in the time of Sennacherib one hundred and eighty-five thousand had perished, and of the help given to them in Babylon in the battle against the Galatians — how they, only eight thousand strong, had together with four thousand Macedonians, when their Macedonian allies were at a loss, destroyed one hundred and twenty thousand, because of the help they received from heaven, and had received very great blessings because of this. With these words they were greatly encouraged and ready to die for their laws and their country. He appointed his brothers as officers of the divisions — Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan, each in command of fifteen hundred men. Furthermore, after reading to them from the holy book and giving them the watchword, "God's help," he himself took command of the first division and joined battle with Nicanor. With the Almighty as their ally, they killed more than nine thousand of the enemy, and wounded and disabled the greater part of Nicanor's army, and forced them all to flee. They captured the money of those who had come to buy them as slaves, and pursued them for some distance, but then had to return because the hour was late. For it was the day before the Sabbath and so they could not continue the pursuit. When they had collected the arms of the enemy and stripped them of their spoils, they kept the Sabbath, giving great praise and thanks to the Lord, who had saved them on that day and poured out his mercy upon them.

Seds

They brought devastation upon them. After the Sabbath they distributed the spoils among the weak, the orphans, and the widows, keeping the rest for themselves. After these things were done, and after they had all made common supplication, they begged the merciful Lord to be reconciled with his servants at the end. They fought against those who were with Timothy and Bacchides, and killed more than twenty thousand of them, and took possession of some very high strongholds, and divided many spoils, giving equal shares to the weak, orphans and widows, and also to the elderly. When they had carefully collected their weapons, they stored everything in convenient places. The remaining spoils they carried to Jerusalem, and they killed Philarches, who was with Timothy, a very wicked man who had greatly afflicted the Jews. While they were celebrating the festival of victory in Jerusalem, they burned those who had set fire to the sacred gates, including Callisthenes, who had fled into a certain house; so he received a fitting reward for his impieties. The most wicked Nicanor, who had brought a thousand merchants to purchase the Jews, was humbled with the help of the Lord by those he had regarded as of no account; laying aside his glorious garments, he fled through the interior of the country and came alone to Antioch, having met with the greatest misfortune through the destruction of his army. And he who had promised to provide a tribute to the Romans from the captives of Jerusalem now proclaimed that the Jews had God as their defender, and that because of this they could not be harmed, since they followed the laws he had established.

At about that same time Antiochus was returning in disgrace from Persia. He had entered the region called Persepolis and attempted to plunder a temple and oppress the city; but the multitude ran to arms and put him to flight.

And so it happened that Antiochus returned in shame after his flight. When he had come near Ecbatana, he learned what had happened to Nicanor and Timothy. Carried away with anger, he thought he could make the Jews pay for the injury inflicted by those who had put him to flight; and so he ordered his chariot to be driven without stopping, pressing on his journey, the judgment of heaven urging him on. For he had spoken so arrogantly, saying that he would come to Jerusalem and make it a grave for Jews. But the Lord God of Israel, who sees all things, struck him with an incurable and invisible blow. As soon as he had finished speaking thus, he was seized with a relentless pain in his bowels and bitter internal torments — and rightly so, since he had tortured the bowels of others with many new forms of cruelty, though he himself had not ceased his wickedness in the least. Beyond this, being filled with arrogance and breathing fire against the Jews in his mind, and urging that the journey be hastened, it happened that he fell from his chariot as it rushed along, and every part of his body was badly mangled by the fall. Thus he who had just thought himself able to command the waves of the sea, being so arrogantly lifted up above human condition, and to weigh the heights of mountains in a balance, was now laid low on the ground and had to be carried in a litter, making the power of God manifest to all. So much so that worms swarmed from the body of this impious man, and while he was still living, his flesh fell away in agony and pain, and the stench of his corruption was so unbearable that the whole army was overwhelmed by it. And the man who, a little while before, had thought to touch the stars of heaven, could not be endured by anyone because of his unbearable stench. Then at last, broken from his great pride, he began to come to self-knowledge under the lash of God's affliction, as his pains grew greater from moment to moment. And when he could no longer endure his own stench, he said: "It is just..."

Maccabees

He held that it was right to be subject to God, and that no mortal should think himself equal to God. But this wicked man prayed to the Lord from whom he was not to receive mercy; and the city toward which he hastened he had intended to level to the ground and make a mass grave — now he wishes to make it free. The Jews, whom he had said were not even worthy of burial but would be thrown out to be devoured by birds and beasts, along with their children he had threatened to destroy — these same he now promises to make equal to the Athenians. The holy temple, which he had previously plundered, he promises to adorn with the finest gifts, and to multiply the sacred vessels, and to defray the costs of the sacrifices from his own revenues; and besides all this, he promises to become a Jew himself and to travel through every land on earth and proclaim the power of God. But as his pains did not cease — for the just judgment of God had come upon him — despairing of his life, he wrote to the Jews in the manner of a letter of supplication, containing the following. "To the worthy citizens of the Jews, hearty greetings and wishes for health and prosperity: King and Prince Antiochus. If you are well, and your children, and all things are going well for you, we give the greatest thanks. I am laid up with illness, but remembering you with goodwill, I returned from the regions beyond, and being seized with grave sickness I thought it necessary to take thought for the common good; not despairing of myself, but having great hope of escaping my illness. Reflecting that my father also, at the times when he led his army in the upper regions, indicated who should take up the rule after him, so that if anything contrary or difficult should arise, those living in those regions would know to whom the conduct of affairs had been entrusted, and would not be troubled — taking these things into account, and having regard for the nearest powers and neighbors,

who at various times lay in wait and watched for opportunity — I have appointed my son Antiochus as king, whom I have often commended to most of you when I visited the upper kingdoms; and I have written to him the things set out below. I urge you, therefore, bearing in mind the public and private benefits you have received, that each of you maintain your goodwill toward me and toward my son. For I am confident that he will conduct himself with moderation and kindness, following my policy, and will be favorable to you." So the murderer and blasphemer, having suffered most grievously, even as he had treated others, died a miserable death in a foreign land among the mountains. Philip, his foster-brother, conveyed the body; and fearing the son of Antiochus, he went away to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt. Chapter 10.
Now Maccabeus and his companions, under the Lord's guidance, recovered the temple and the city. They demolished the altars that the foreigners had built in the public squares, as well as the sacred precincts. Having purified the temple, they built a new altar; and striking fire from flints, they offered sacrifices after an interval of two years, with incense and lamps and the bread of the Presence. When they had done all this, they fell prostrate on the ground and begged the Lord that they might never again fall into such evils; and that if they should ever sin again, he himself would chastise them with forbearance, and not hand them over to blasphemous and barbarous pagans. Now it happened that on the same day on which the temple had been profaned by foreigners, the purification of the temple took place, on the twenty-fifth of the same month, which is Chislev. And they celebrated it for eight days with gladness, like the feast of Tabernacles, remembering how, not long before, they had spent the feast of Tabernacles wandering like wild animals in the mountains and in caves. Therefore bearing wands wreathed with leaves and fair branches and palms, they offered hymns of praise to him who had prospered the cleansing of his own holy place. And they decreed by common resolution

Maccabees

They were blaspheming beyond measure and hurling shameful words; but when the fifth day began to dawn, the young men who were with Maccabeus, inflamed in spirit because of the blasphemies, bravely attacked the wall, and with fierce courage they climbed up; and likewise others climbed the towers and the gates, and set about burning the blasphemers alive. After two continuous days, having laid waste the garrison, they found Timotheus hiding in a certain place and killed him; and they also killed his brother Chaereas and Apollophanes. When this was done, they praised with hymns and thanksgivings the Lord who had done great things for Israel and given them the victory. Chapter 11.

But a short time afterward, Lysias, the king's guardian and kinsman and chancellor, greatly displeased at what had happened, gathered together about eighty thousand infantry and all his cavalry and marched against the Jews, intending to make the city a home for Greeks and to levy tribute on the temple as he did on the other sacred places of the Gentiles, and to put the high priesthood up for sale every year. He had no regard whatever for the power of God, but was elated with his tens of thousands of infantry and his thousands of cavalry and his eighty elephants. Invading Judea, he approached Beth-zur, which was a fortified place about five stadia from Jerusalem, and pressed it hard. When Maccabeus and his men learned that Lysias was besieging the strongholds, they and all the people, with lamentations and tears, prayed the Lord to send a good angel to save Israel. And Maccabeus himself was the first to take up arms, and he urged the others to join him in risking their lives to help their kindred.

And with ready hearts they set out together, and while they were still near Jerusalem, a horseman appeared at their head, clothed in white and brandishing weapons of gold. Then they all praised the merciful God together, and took heart, ready to assault not only men but the most ferocious beasts and walls of iron. They advanced in battle order, having in heaven a champion and the Lord who showed mercy to them. Rushing upon their enemies like lions, they struck down eleven thousand infantry and sixteen hundred cavalry, and forced all the rest to flee. Most of them were wounded and escaped without weapons. And Lysias himself escaped only by shameful flight. But as he was not without intelligence, he considered what defeat he had suffered, and realized that the Hebrews were invincible because the mighty God fought on their side. So he sent to them and persuaded them to settle everything on just terms, promising that he would persuade the king to be their friend. Maccabeus, having regard for the common good, agreed to all that Lysias urged. And whatever Maccabeus wrote to Lysias about the Jews, the king granted. For there were letters written to the Jews from Lysias, containing the following: "Lysias to the people of the Jews, greetings. John and Absalom, who were sent by you, delivered your petition and asked about the matters indicated in it. I have reported to the king whatever needed to be brought before him, and he has agreed to what was possible. If you will maintain your goodwill toward the government, I will endeavor in the future to help promote your welfare. And concerning these matters and their details, I have ordered these men and my own representatives to confer with you. Farewell. In the year one hundred and forty-eighth, the twenty-fourth of Dioscorus." And the king's letter contained these words:

Second [part].

Antiochus the king greeted his brother Lysis. Since our father has been translated among the gods, we, wishing those who are in our kingdom to conduct themselves without disturbance and to attend to their own affairs, have heard that the Jews have not consented to our father's wish to be transferred to the Greek rite, but wish to keep their own customs and request that their lawful practices be granted to them. Wishing therefore that this nation too should be at peace, we have decided and judged that their temple should be restored to them, so that they may conduct themselves according to the custom of their ancestors. You will therefore do well if you send word to them and give them the right hand of friendship, so that, knowing our will, they may be of good spirit and attend to their own concerns. To the Jews the king's letter was as follows: King Antiochus to the senate of the Jews and to the other Jews, greeting. If you are well, it is as we wish; we ourselves are also well. Menelaus came to us saying that you wish to come down to your own people who are with us. Therefore, for those who travel up until the twentieth day of the month of Xandicus, we grant safe conduct, so that the Jews may use their own foods and laws as before, and no one shall trouble them in any way for things that were done in ignorance. We have also sent Menelaus to speak with you. Farewell. In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, the fifteenth day of the month of Xandicus. The Romans also sent a letter in these words: Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, legates of the Romans, to the people of the Jews, greeting. Concerning what Lysis, the king's kinsman, has granted you, we also grant. But concerning those matters which he judged should be referred to the king, send someone promptly after you have conferred among yourselves, so that we may decide as is best for you. We are now going to Antioch. Therefore hasten to write back so that we also may know what your wishes are. Farewell. In the one hundred and forty-eighth year, the fifteenth day of the month of Xandicus.

After these things had been done, Lysis went to the king, and the Jews attended to their farming. But those who were left behind — Timothy and Apollonius son of Genneus, and also Jerome and Demophon, and Nicanor the commander of Cyprus — would not allow them to live quietly and in peace. The people of Joppa committed a great outrage. They asked the Jews who lived among them to board boats which they had prepared, together with their wives and children, as if there were no ill will between them. Following a public decree of the city, and the Jews consenting to it and suspecting nothing, as they were seeking peace — when they had gone out into the deep water, they drowned no fewer than two hundred of them. When Judas learned of this cruelty done to his people, he ordered the men who were with him, and calling upon the just judge God, he came against the murderers of his brothers: he set fire to the harbor by night, burned the boats, and put to the sword those who had fled from the fire. When he had done these things he withdrew, as if intending to return and utterly destroy all the people of Joppa. But learning that the people of Jamnia also intended to do the same thing to the Jews who lived among them, he attacked the Jamnites by night and set fire to the harbor and the fleet, so that the light of the flames was visible from Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stades away. From there, when they had already marched nine stades on the way against Timothy, five thousand Arabs with five hundred horsemen attacked him. After a hard battle, which by God's help turned out successfully, the remaining Arabs asked Judas to grant them the right hand of friendship,

Maccabees.

promising that they would provide pastures and would be profitable in other matters. Judas, considering them truly useful as mules, agreed to peace, and having accepted the terms they withdrew to their tents. But he attacked a certain fortified city surrounded by walls and gates, which was inhabited by a multitude of peoples of various nations, called Chasphim. Those who were inside, trusting in the strength of the walls and in their supply of provisions, behaved very arrogantly, reviling and blaspheming and saying things that were not lawful. But Maccabeus, having invoked the great Lord of the world who without battering rams and siege engines threw down Jericho in the time of Joshua, rushed fiercely upon the walls, and having taken the city by the will of God, made an innumerable slaughter, so that the adjacent lake, two furlongs wide, appeared to be overflowing with blood. Then they marched seven hundred and fifty furlongs and came to Characa to those called the Tubianean Jews. They did not find Timotheus in those places, for he had departed without accomplishing anything, leaving behind a garrison in a certain very strong position. Dositheus and Sosipater, who were captains under Maccabeus, slew those left by Timotheus in the garrison, ten thousand men. But Maccabeus arranged six thousand men around himself and set them in cohorts, and advanced against Timotheus, who had with him a hundred and twenty thousand foot soldiers and two thousand five hundred horsemen. When Timotheus learned of the approach of Judas, he sent away the women and children and the rest of the baggage to a place called Carnion, which was very difficult to besiege and hard to approach because of the narrowness of the passes. When Judas's first cohort appeared, the enemy was struck with terror by the presence

of God who sees all things, and they fled in every direction, often harming one another, struck by their own swords. Judas pressed on vigorously, punishing the profane, and killed thirty thousand of them. Timotheus himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater, and he begged with many entreaties to be let go alive, because he had the parents and brothers of many of the Jews, and it might happen that they would be deceived by his death. When he had given his pledge to restore them according to the agreement, they let him go for the sake of saving their brethren. Judas returned from Carnion, having killed twenty-five thousand. After this flight and slaughter, he marched to Ephron, a strongly fortified city, where a great multitude of peoples of various nations lived, and strong young men standing before the walls resisted vigorously. There were many war machines and a supply of missiles. But when they invoked the Almighty who with his power crushes the strength of enemies, they took the city and killed twenty-five thousand of those who were within. From there they went to the city of the Scythians, which was six hundred furlongs from Jerusalem. The Jews who lived among the Scythopolitans testifying that they were treated kindly by them, and that even in times of misfortune they had dealt gently with them, they gave thanks to them and exhorted them also for the future to be well-disposed toward their people, and came to Jerusalem, as the feast of Weeks was at hand. After Pentecost they marched against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea. He came out with three thousand foot soldiers and four hundred horsemen. When they engaged, it happened that a few of the Jews fell. But Dositheus, a certain horseman of Bacenor's company, a valiant man, was holding Gorgias, and when he was about to

Sds.

A certain horseman from Thrace rushed upon him and cut off his shoulder, and thus Gorgias fled to Marissa. But those who were fighting alongside Heldrin invoked the Lord, and Judas called upon him as helper and leader of the battle, raising his voice in the ancestral tongue, and drove Gorgias's forces into flight. Then Judas gathered his army and came to the city of Adullam. When the seventh day arrived, they purified themselves according to custom in the same place and observed the Sabbath. On the following day Judas came with his men to collect the bodies of the fallen and to place them in their ancestral tombs. Under the tunics of the dead they found votive offerings to the idols of Jamnia, which the law forbids to Jews. It was therefore evident to all that this was the reason they had perished. All therefore blessed the just judgment of the Lord, who had made hidden things manifest. They turned to prayer and besought that the sin committed might be wholly blotted out. The noble Judas urged the people to keep themselves free from sin, having before their eyes what had happened because of the sins of those who had fallen. He then took up a collection, amounting to two thousand silver drachmas, which he sent to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering — a thoroughly good and noble act, in which he was thinking of the resurrection. For if he had not hoped that the fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead. And because he considered that those who had fallen asleep in godliness had excellent grace stored up for them, it was a holy and pious thought. Therefore he made atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin. r.rui.

In the year one hundred and forty-nine, Judas learned that Antiochus the emperor was coming with a great multitude against Judea, and with him Lysias, his guardian and administrator of affairs, having one hundred and ten thousand infantry, and also thousands of cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots fitted with scythes. Menelaus also joined them, and with great deceitfulness urged Antiochus on — not for the welfare of the country, but hoping to be established in authority. But the King of kings stirred up the mind of Antiochus against the sinner, and when Lysias informed him that Menelaus was the cause of all the trouble, he ordered that he be seized and executed in the manner of that place. There was in that place a tower of fifty cubits height, filled with ashes, and it had a device for tipping toward the precipice. From there he ordered the sacrilegious man to be cast into the ashes, with all pushing him toward his doom. And by such a law it came about that the transgressor of the law died, and did not even receive burial in the earth. Justly enough indeed. For because he had committed many sins against the altar of God, whose fire and ashes were sacred, he met his death in ashes. The king, enraged in mind, was coming to show himself even worse to the Jews. But Judas, learning of this, ordered the people to call upon the Lord day and night, as always, to help them — those who were now about to be deprived of their law and their country and their holy temple — and not to allow those who had just recently begun to revive to fall under the blasphemous nations again. When all had done this together and implored the Lord's mercy with weeping and fasting, prostrate for three continuous days, Judas exhorted them to prepare themselves. Then he himself consulted with the elders before the king could move his army against Judea and take the city, and committed the outcome of the matter to the judgment of the Lord, giving authority therefore

Maccabees

All this he arranged in honor of God, creator of the world, urging his men to fight bravely and to stand firm unto death for the laws, the temple, the city, the country and the institutions, around Modein he deployed his force. And giving his men the signal of divine victory, with the bravest young men chosen, he attacked the royal pavilion in the camp by night and killed fourteen thousand men, and also the greatest of the elephants with those upon them. And filling the enemy camp with great terror and confusion, they withdrew having accomplished their mission successfully. This was done at daybreak, with the protection of the Lord's aid. But the king, having had a taste of the boldness of the Jews, attempted to take difficult positions by strategy: he moved against Bethsura which was a strong Jewish garrison, but was driven back repeatedly. Meanwhile Judas was supplying those within with necessities. But one Rhodocus from the Jewish army revealed secrets to the enemy; he was sought out, captured, and imprisoned. The king again treated with those in Bethsura, gave pledges, received pledges, withdrew, attacked Judas, and was defeated. Then he heard that Philip had revolted in Antioch, whom he had left in charge of affairs; dismayed, he appealed to the Jews, submitted to their terms, swore to observe all their rights, was reconciled, offered sacrifice, honored the temple and gave gifts, embraced Maccabeus, and made him commander and governor from Ptolemais to the land of the Gerrenians. But when he came to Ptolemais, the people of Ptolemais were indignant over the treaty, being angry that the agreement might be broken. Then Lysias went up to the tribunal and explained the situation, calmed the people, and returned to Antioch. And so the king's campaign and return ended thus. Chapter XIII.

Now after a period of three years Judas and his companions learned that Demetrius son of Seleucus had sailed into the harbor of Tripolis with a strong army and a fleet, and had taken possession of the country, having made away with Antiochus and his guardian Lysias. Now one Alcimus, who had been high priest but had willingly defiled himself in the times of mingling with the Gentiles, realizing that there was no way for him to be safe or to have access to the holy altar anymore, came to King Demetrius in the one hundred and fifty-first year, presenting him with a gold crown and a palm, and also some of the customary olive branches from the temple. On that day he kept silent. But having found the right moment for his madness, summoned by Demetrius and asked about the state and plans of the Jews, he answered: "Those of the Jews called Hasideans, whose leader is Judas Maccabeus, are keeping up war and stirring up sedition, and will not let the kingdom attain peace. For I too, though deprived of my ancestral glory — I mean the high priesthood — have come here, first of all for the genuine interests of the king, and secondly to seek the good of my own people, since the entire nation is suffering no little harm from the foolish conduct of those men. Please look into each of these matters, O king, and take care of our country and our people in accordance with the gracious goodness you show to all, for as long as Judas survives, it is impossible for the government to find peace." After he had said these things, the rest of the king's friends, who were hostile to Judas, quickly inflamed Demetrius further. He immediately chose Nicanor, who had been in command of the elephants, and sent him to Judea, with orders to seize Judas himself alive, to scatter those with him, and to install Alcimus as high priest of the great temple. And the Gentiles from Judea who had fled from Judas —

Seds.

They were mingling with Nicanor separately, considering the miseries and disasters of the Jews as their own prosperity. When the Jews heard of Nicanor's arrival and the gathering of nations, they sprinkled earth on themselves and prayed to him who established his own people forever, that he might protect them; their portion he adorned with evident signs. The commander ordered them to move out at once, and they gathered at the castle of Dessau. Simeon had left his brother behind with Nicanor, but the army was suddenly attacked by the advance of flatterers. Yet Nicanor, hearing of the valor of Judas's companions and their great courage which they had for the contests of the fatherland, feared to decide the matter by bloodshed. Therefore he sent Posidonius and Theodotus and Mattathias to give and receive pledges; and when they had deliberated long about these matters, and the leader had referred back to the multitude, the unanimous opinion was to agree to the friendship. So they appointed a day on which to meet privately, and separate seats were set out and placed. Judas ordered armed men to be in convenient places, lest perhaps some evil should suddenly arise from the enemy. And they held a friendly conference. Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem and did nothing unjust, and dismissed the crowds of people that had gathered. He kept Judas always dear to his heart, and was inclined toward the man. He urged him to marry a wife and have children. He married; lived quietly; they shared life in common. But Alcimus, seeing their affection for one another and their agreements, came to Demetrius and said that Nicanor was serving foreign interests and had appointed Judas, the destroyer of his kingdom, as his successor. The king, exasperated by the accusations of this criminal, wrote to Nicanor saying that he was very displeased about the treaty of friendship, and ordered him to send Maccabeus bound to Antioch. When Nicanor learned this he was troubled, and he was deeply distressed that he should break what had been agreed, having suffered no harm from the man; but since he could not oppose the king, he watched for an opportunity to carry out the order. But Maccabeus, noticing that Nicanor was treating him more sternly and behaving more harshly in their customary meetings, understanding that this harshness boded no good, gathered a few of his men and hid himself from Nicanor. When Nicanor realized this, and that the man had boldly eluded him, he went to the great and holy temple, and while the priests were offering the customary sacrifices, he ordered them to hand over the man. When they swore with oaths that they did not know where the man he sought was, he stretched out his hand toward the temple and swore, saying: "Unless you hand over Judas bound to me, I will raze this sanctuary of God to the ground and tear down the altar, and I will consecrate this place to Bacchus." And having said this, he left. The priests stretched out their hands to heaven and called upon him who is always the protector of their nation, saying these things: "Lord of all, who need nothing, you were pleased to have a temple for your dwelling among us. Now, O Lord, holy of holies, keep undefiled forever this house that has lately been cleansed." Now a certain Razias, one of the elders of Jerusalem, was accused before Nicanor, a man who was a lover of his city and highly esteemed, and who because of his goodwill was called father of the Jews. He had for many years maintained his purpose in Judaism, and had resolved to risk his body and life for it. Nicanor, wishing to make evident the hatred he bore toward the Jews, sent five hundred soldiers to arrest him, thinking that if he captured him

Seds [Second]

He had these things for those who were about to engage in battle. And now when all hoped for the judgment of the future, and these were present, and the exercise was arranged — the beasts and cavalry positioned in a suitable place — Maccabeus, considering the coming multitude and the varied display of arms and the ferocity of the beasts, stretching his hands toward heaven, called upon the Lord who works wonders, knowing that victory is given not by arms but as it pleases God to grant it to the worthy. He called upon him in this way: "You, O Lord, who sent your angel under King Hezekiah of Judea and destroyed one hundred and eighty-five thousand from the camp of Sennacherib; and you, O Ruler of the heavens, now send a good angel before us, to bring fear and trembling; that those who come with blasphemy against your holy people may be struck with terror." And with this prayer he ended. But Nicanor and those with him advanced with trumpets and battle songs. Judas and those with him, calling upon God with prayers, engaged them with their hands fighting, yet with their hearts praying to God: and they struck down no fewer than thirty-five thousand men, greatly gladdened by the presence of God. When the engagement ended and they were returning with joy, they recognized that Nicanor had fallen in full armor. Then, raising a shout and great commotion, they blessed the Almighty Lord in their native tongue. And Judas, who was prepared to die in body and soul for his fellow citizens, commanded that Nicanor's head and his hand with the shoulder be cut off and carried to Jerusalem. When he arrived there, he called together his countrymen and the priests before the altar; and calling also those who were in the citadel, he showed them the head of the wicked Nicanor, and the hand of that blasphemer which he had stretched out against the holy house of the Almighty God, and glorified him greatly. And he commanded that Nicanor's tongue be cut out and given piece by piece to the birds, and that the hand of the madman be hung up opposite the temple. Then all blessed the Lord of heaven, saying: "Blessed is he who has kept his own place undefiled." He hung Nicanor's head from the citadel, that it might be an evident and manifest sign of the help of God. And all decreed by common consent never to let this day pass without celebration, but to celebrate the thirteenth day of the twelfth month — which is called Adar in the Syrian language — the day before Mordecai's day. Thus concerning the affairs of Nicanor, and from that time the city having been held by the Hebrews, I also will here end my discourse. And if I have written well and to the point, that is what I myself desired; but if imperfectly and meanly, it is what I could attain to. For as it is hurtful to drink wine alone, and also water alone, while wine mixed with water is pleasant and delighteth the taste: even so speech finely framed delighteth the ears of them that read the story. And here shall be the end.

Here ends the Second Book of Maccabees.

Here ends the book of Maccabees.

(Right column:)
He was steadfast in faith, not yielding to the enemy. And already the enemy had hoped to prevail against them, trusting in wondrous aid: the king said that he would subdue the people through their own names and authorities. The counselors of the Maccabees encouraged their own people, saying that the promises of the warriors would be fulfilled. He said in the name of the Lord: now, O Lord, let your soldiers prevail. And the record shows that he strove against those who pursued him, and the spirit of the Maccabees inspired those who were weakened. And he proclaimed that the Lord of all would receive glory. And the enemies were cast down, and their proud boasts were brought to nothing. And so the glory of the Lord was made manifest to all nations, and those who had trusted in the strength of arms were humbled, and those who called upon the Lord were exalted.

And the armies were gathered and the commanders arrayed for battle. And the men were strengthened in spirit and encouraged by the words of the leaders. And all together they fought bravely and drove out those who had oppressed them. And the commanders of the enemy forces fled, and their camps were taken. And the people gave thanks to the Lord and glorified his name, for he had given them victory over their enemies. And all the people rejoiced and praised the Lord, for he had shown his mercy to Israel.

Here ends the second book of Maccabees.

Letter

Here begins the letter of the blessed Jerome, presbyter, to Pope Damasus, concerning the four Evangelists.

To the most blessed Pope Damasus, Jerome. You compel me to undertake a new work from the old: to examine, as it were, from scattered copies of the Scriptures spread throughout the whole world as though from an arbiter's seat, which among them agree with the Greek truth. This is a pious labor but a dangerous presumption: to judge the ancient texts, which themselves must be judged by all; to dare to change the language of old age and drag the whole world back to the beginnings of childhood. For what learned or unlearned man, when he takes a volume in his hands and notices that what he reads differs from the flavor he once imbibed, will not immediately burst out crying that I am a forger, accusing me of sacrilege, for daring to add, change, or correct anything in the ancient books? Against this hostility a twofold consolation sustains me: both that you, the highest priest, command it to be done, and that what varies cannot be true, as the testimony of detractors themselves confirms. For if faith is to be placed in Latin copies, let our opponents answer which ones — since there are almost as many copies as there are manuscripts. But if truth is to be sought from a greater number, why do we not return to the Greek original to correct what has been poorly edited by careless translators, or carelessly emended by presumptuous incompetents, or added or altered by drowsy copyists? And yet I am speaking of the Old Testament: which, having been translated into Greek by the seventy elders, has come down to us at third hand. I do not inquire what Aquila thinks, what Symmachus thinks, or why Theodotion stands midway between the old and the new. Let that translation stand as authentic which the apostles themselves approved. Now I speak of the New Testament, which is undoubtedly Greek, except for the apostle Matthew, who first published his Gospel in Judea in Hebrew letters. Since this differs in our language and leads along various streams and byways, it must be sought from one source. I pass over those copies which Lucian and Hesychius claimed as their own — a vain contention of a few men — by which neither in the Old Testament after the seventy interpreters was it permitted to emend anything, nor in the New did their emendation profit, since the Scripture translated beforehand into the languages of many nations shows those additions to be false. Therefore this little work, as full as it is pleasing, promises only the four Gospels, in this order: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John — corrected by comparison with old Greek manuscripts, yet in such a way that, lest they depart too far from the custom of Latin reading, we have directed our pen to change only those things which seemed to distort the meaning, leaving the rest as it was. The canons also, which Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, following Ammonius of Alexandria, arranged into ten numbers, we have expressed as they appear in the Greek. So that if anyone wishes to know carefully what things in the Gospels are the same, or similar, or unique to each, he may discern them by these distinctions. A great error has crept into our manuscripts: for when one evangelist said more on the same matter, others, thinking it too little, added to it; or when one expressed the same sense differently, a reader who had first read one of the four corrected the others accordingly — whence it has come about that among us all things are mixed together, and in Mark more things from Luke and

Matthew.

The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham begot Isaac; and Isaac begot Jacob; and Jacob begot Judas and his brethren; and Judas begot Phares and Zara of Thamar; and Phares begot Esrom; and Esrom begot Aram; and Aram begot Aminadab; and Aminadab begot Naasson; and Naasson begot Salmon; and Salmon begot Booz of Rahab; and Booz begot Obed of Ruth; and Obed begot Jesse; and Jesse begot David the king; and David the king begot Solomon of her that had been the wife of Urias; and Solomon begot Roboam; and Roboam begot Abia; and Abia begot Asa; and Asa begot Josaphat; and Josaphat begot Joram; and Joram begot Ozias; and Ozias begot Joatham; and Joatham begot Achaz; and Achaz begot Ezechias; and Ezechias begot Manasses; and Manasses begot Amon; and Amon begot Josias; and Josias begot Jechonias and his brethren, about the time they were carried away to Babylon. And after the carrying away of Babylon, Jechonias begot Salathiel; and Salathiel begot Zorobabel; and Zorobabel begot Abiud; and Abiud begot Eliakim; and Eliakim begot Azor; and Azor begot Sadoc; and Sadoc begot Achim; and Achim begot Eliud; and Eliud begot Eleazar; and Eleazar begot Matthan; and Matthan begot Jacob; and Jacob begot Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ. So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations; and from the carrying away into Babylon unto Christ are fourteen generations. Now the birth of Jesus Christ was in this manner. When his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Spirit. And Joseph her husband, being a just man and not willing to put her to shame, was minded to put her away privately. But while he thought on these things, behold, the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying: Joseph, son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit. And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins. Now all this was done that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying: Behold, a virgin shall be with child and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is God with us. And Joseph, rising from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took unto him his wife. And he knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son, and he called his name Jesus. Chapter 2.

Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, wise men came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he that is born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east and are come to worship him. And when Herod the king had heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where Christ should be born. And they said to him: In Bethlehem of Judea. For so it is written by the prophet: And thou Bethlehem, the land of Judah, art not the least among the princes of Judah; for out of thee shall come a ruler that shall govern my people Israel. Then Herod, privately calling the wise men, learned carefully from them the time of the star which

Matthew.

He washes his hands when he eats bread. But he answered and said to them: Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, saying: Honor your father and your mother: and whoever curses father or mother, let him die. But you say: Whoever shall say to his father or mother, whatever gift you might have received from me, he need not honor his father or mother: and you have made the commandment of God of no effect because of your tradition. Hypocrites: well did Isaiah prophesy of you, saying: This people honors me with their lips: but their heart is far from me. But in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men. And he called the multitudes to him and said to them: Hear and understand. Not that which goes into the mouth defiles a man: but that which comes out of the mouth, this defiles a man. Then his disciples came and said to him: Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying? But he answered and said: Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up. Let them alone: they are blind leaders of the blind. And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch. Then Peter answered and said to him: Explain this parable to us. And he said: Are you also still without understanding? Do you not yet understand that whatever enters in at the mouth goes into the belly, and is cast out into the sewer? But those things which proceed out of the mouth come from the heart: and they defile a man. For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts: murders: adulteries: fornications: thefts: false witness: blasphemies. These are the things which defile a man. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a man. And departing from there, Jesus withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold,

a woman of Canaan came out from those borders and cried out to him, saying: Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David: my daughter is grievously afflicted by a demon. But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and urged him, saying: Send her away, for she cries out after us. But he answered and said: I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Then she came and worshiped him, saying: Lord, help me. But he answered and said: It is not good to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs. And she said: Yes, Lord: yet even the dogs eat the crumbs which fall from their master's table. Then Jesus answered and said to her: O woman, great is your faith: let it be to you as you wish. And her daughter was healed from that very hour. And departing from there, Jesus came near the Sea of Galilee: and he went up on the mountain and sat down there. Then great multitudes came to him, having with them those who were lame, blind, mute, maimed, and many others: and they laid them down at his feet, and he healed them: so that the multitude marveled when they saw the mute speaking, the lame walking, and the blind seeing: and they glorified the God of Israel. But Jesus called his disciples to him and said: I have compassion on the multitude, because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way. And his disciples said to him: Where could we get enough bread in the wilderness to fill such a great multitude? Jesus said to them: How many loaves do you have? And they said: Seven. And a few small fish. And he commanded the multitude to sit down on the ground. And he took the seven loaves and the fish: and giving thanks, he broke them and gave them to his disciples: and the disciples gave them to the multitude. And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over of the fragments

Matthew.

And it came to pass that when Jesus had finished these sayings, he departed from Galilee and came into the coasts of Judea beyond the Jordan. And great multitudes followed him, and he healed them there. Then the Pharisees came to him, tempting him and saying: Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for any cause? And he answered and said to them: Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said: For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. So they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no man put asunder. They said to him: Why then did Moses command to give a bill of divorce and to put her away? He said to them: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to put away your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. And I say to you, that whoever shall put away his wife, except for fornication, and shall marry another, commits adultery; and he who marries her who is put away commits adultery. His disciples said to him: If the case of a man with his wife is so, it is not expedient to marry. He said to them: Not all men can receive this saying, but they to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were born so from their mother's womb; and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men; and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it. Then were little children brought to him that he should lay his hands on them and pray. And the disciples rebuked them. But Jesus said: Permit the little children, and do not forbid them to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven. And when he had laid his hands upon them, he departed thence. And behold, one came and said to him: Good master, what good thing shall I do that I may have eternal life? He said to him: Why do you ask me about what is good? One is good: God. But if you will enter into life, keep the commandments. He said to him: Which? And Jesus said: You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. The young man said to him: All these things I have kept; what do I still lack? Jesus said to him: If you will be perfect, go and sell what you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. But when the young man heard this saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. And Jesus said to his disciples: Truly I say to you that a rich man shall with difficulty enter the kingdom of heaven. And again I say to you: It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God. When his disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying: Who then can be saved? And Jesus, looking on them, said to them: With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible. Then Peter answered and said to him: Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what therefore shall we have? And Jesus said to them: Truly I say to you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his glory, you shall also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall inherit eternal life. But many that are first shall be last, and the last shall be first. Chapter 20. The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning

Matthew.

Early in the morning he went out to hire workers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the workers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. Going out about the third hour, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and said to them: Go also into my vineyard, and I will give you what is just. And they went. Again he went out about the sixth and ninth hour, and did likewise. About the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing, and said to them: Why do you stand here idle all day? They said to him: Because no one has hired us. He said to them: Go also into my vineyard. When evening came, the lord of the vineyard said to his steward: Call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last to the first. When those who had come about the eleventh hour arrived, each received a denarius. When the first came, they thought they would receive more, but each of them also received a denarius. And receiving it, they murmured against the master of the house, saying: These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the heat. But he answered one of them: Friend, I do no wrong to you. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I wish to give to this last one even as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? Is your eye evil because I am good? So the last will be first, and the first last. For many are called, but few are chosen. And Jesus going up to Jerusalem took the twelve disciples aside privately and said to them: Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death, and will deliver him to the Gentiles to be mocked and scourged and crucified, and on the third day he will rise again. Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, worshipping and asking something of him. He said to her: What do you wish? She said to him: Command that these my two sons may sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom. Jesus answered and said: You do not know what you ask. Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink? They said to him: We can. He said to them: Indeed you shall drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father. And the ten, hearing this, were indignant at the two brothers. But Jesus called them to him and said: You know that the princes of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them. It shall not be so among you; but whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be your servant. And whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your slave. Just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. And as they were leaving Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, two blind men sitting by the roadside heard that Jesus was passing by, and cried out: Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David! The crowd rebuked them to be silent. But they cried out all the more: Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David! And Jesus stopped and called them and said: What do you wish that I should do for you? Lord, that our eyes may be opened. And Jesus, moved with compassion, touched their eyes. And immediately they saw, and followed him. Chapter 21.
And when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent

Prologue                    Mark.

And they reported to the chief priests all the things that had happened. And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a large sum of money to the soldiers, saying: Say that his disciples came by night and stole him away while we slept. And if this comes to the governor's ears, we will persuade him and keep you out of trouble. So they took the money and did as they were instructed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this very day. Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had directed them. And when they saw him they worshipped him, but some doubted. And Jesus came and spoke to them saying: All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. Here ends the Gospel according to Matthew. Here begins the prologue to the Gospel according to Mark.

Mark the evangelist, chosen of God, and a companion in baptism of the Son, and in divine word a disciple — serving among the priests of Israel, a Levite by birth, converted to the faith of Christ — wrote the Gospel in Italy: showing in it what was owed to Christ from his own lineage. For at the beginning of the Gospel he establishes through the voice of prophetic proclamation the order of Levitical election: so that, preaching the predestined John, son of Zachary, sent forth by the announcement of an angel — not only the Word made flesh but the body of the Lord animated in all things through the word of the divine voice — at the

beginning of the evangelical proclamation he might show: so that whoever reads this might know the origin of your flesh in God, and might recognize that the dwelling of Jesus coming must be known in the flesh: and might find in himself the word of the voice which he proclaims in harmonies. And indeed, beginning from the aforesaid Gospel's work, entering from the baptism of the Lord to preach God, he did not labor to speak of the nativity of the flesh which he had seen in the former accounts: but pressing on through the whole setting of the desert, they find those fasting at the temptation of the devil — the gathering of beasts — and the ministry of angels: so that instructing us in each thing individually, compressing it briefly — he would not withhold either the authority of the accomplished deed or the fullness of the ministering work. And further, they say that he cut off his thumb after faith so that he would be considered unfit for the priesthood: but the election, agreeing entirely with faith, was able to stand predestined: so that not even thus would he fail in the work of the word, though he had once feared it by reason of lineage. For he was bishop of Alexandria. For whom it was necessary to know each thing and to arrange the Gospel as spoken in himself: and to acknowledge in himself the discipline of the law: and to understand the divine nature of the Lord in the flesh. Which things we seek first to know. Then having inquired, we desired to know, having the reward of exhortation: because the one who plants and the one who waters are one: but God is the one who gives the increase. Here ends the prologue. Here begins the Gospel according to Mark. Chapter 1.

The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God: As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. John was in the desert baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. And there went out to him all

Mark.

The whole region of Judea and all the people of Jerusalem went out to him and were baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins. John was clothed with camel's hair and wore a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. He preached, saying: One mightier than I is coming after me, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. And it came to pass in those days that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened and the Spirit like a dove descending and remaining upon him. And a voice came from the heavens: You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased. And at once the Spirit drove him out into the desert. He was in the desert for forty days and forty nights, being tempted by Satan, and he was with the wild beasts, and angels ministered to him. After John was handed over, Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of God and saying: The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is at hand. Repent and believe in the gospel. And passing along by the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his brother casting their nets into the sea, for they were fishermen. And Jesus said to them: Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men. And immediately leaving their nets they followed him. Going on a little farther, he saw James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, who were in a boat mending their nets. He immediately called them. And leaving their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men, they followed him. And they came to Capernaum, and immediately on the sabbath he entered the synagogue and began to teach them.

And they were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority and not as the scribes. And in their synagogue there was a man with an unclean spirit, and he cried out: What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are — the Holy One of God. And Jesus rebuked him, saying: Be silent and come out of him! And the unclean spirit, convulsing him and crying out with a loud voice, came out of him. And they were all amazed, so that they questioned among themselves, saying: What is this? What is this new teaching? For with authority he commands even the unclean spirits and they obey him. And at once his fame spread everywhere throughout all the region of Galilee. And immediately, leaving the synagogue, they came to the house of Simon and Andrew with James and John. Now Simon's mother-in-law lay sick with a fever, and immediately they told him about her. And he came and took her by the hand and lifted her up, and immediately the fever left her, and she began to serve them. And that evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick and those who were possessed by demons. The whole city was gathered at the door. And he healed many who were sick with various diseases, and he cast out many demons, and he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him. And rising very early before dawn, he went out to a deserted place, and there he prayed. And Simon and those who were with him pursued him, and when they found him they said to him: Everyone is looking for you. And he said to them: Let us go on to the neighboring towns and cities so that I may preach there also, for that is why I came. And he was preaching in their synagogues throughout all of Galilee and casting out demons. And a leper came to him, pleading with him, and kneeling down said: If you will, you can make me

Mark.

to cleanse. But Jesus, having pity on him, stretched out his hand and touching him said to him: I will. Be clean. And when he had spoken, immediately the leprosy departed from him and he was made clean. And he strictly charged him and forthwith sent him away, saying to him: See that you tell no one, but go, show yourself to the chief priest and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them. But he, going out, began to publish and spread abroad the word, so that Jesus could no longer openly enter into the city, but was outside in desert places, and they came to him from all sides. Chapter 2.

And again he entered into Capernaum after some days, and it was heard that he was in the house, and many came together so that there was no room, not even at the door, and he spoke the word to them. And they came to him bringing a paralytic who was carried by four men. And when they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they uncovered the roof where he was, and breaking it open they let down the mat on which the paralytic lay. And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic: Son, your sins are forgiven. Now there were some of the scribes sitting there and reasoning in their hearts: Why does this man speak thus? He blasphemes. Who can forgive sins but God alone? And immediately Jesus, knowing in his spirit that they so reasoned within themselves, said to them: Why do you reason about these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, Your sins are forgiven, or to say, Rise, take up your mat and walk? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, he said to the paralytic: I say to you, rise, take up your mat and go to your house. And immediately he rose and taking up his mat went out before them all, so that they were all amazed and glorified God, saying:

we never saw anything like this. And he went out again beside the sea, and all the crowd came to him and he taught them. And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him: Follow me. And rising, he followed him. And as he sat at table in his house, many tax collectors and sinners were reclining with Jesus and his disciples, for there were many who followed him. And the scribes and Pharisees, seeing that he ate with tax collectors and sinners, said to his disciples: Why does your teacher eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? When Jesus heard this, he said to them: Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners. Now John's disciples and the Pharisees were fasting, and they came and said to him: Why do John's disciples and the disciples of the Pharisees fast, but your disciples do not fast? And Jesus said to them: Can the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? As long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast. The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days. No one sews a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; otherwise the new patch tears away from the old, and a worse tear is made. And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wine bursts the skins, and the wine is lost and so are the skins. But new wine is for new wineskins. And it came to pass that on the Sabbath he was walking through the grainfields, and his disciples began to make their way plucking the ears of grain. And the Pharisees said to him: Look, why are they doing on the Sabbath what is not lawful? And he said to them: Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry,

Mark.

my brother and my sister and my mother. Chapter 3.
And he began again to teach by the sea: and a great multitude was gathered to him, so that he entered into a boat and sat in the sea: and all the multitude was by the sea on the land: and he taught them many things in parables, and said to them in his doctrine: Hear. Behold, a sower went out to sow. And while he sowed, some fell by the way side, and the birds of the air came and ate it up. And other fell upon stony ground, where it had not much earth: and immediately it sprang up, because it had no depth of earth: and when the sun rose it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered away. And other fell among thorns: and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no fruit. And other fell on good ground: and brought forth fruit that sprang up and increased, and yielded some thirty, some sixty, and some a hundred. And he said: He that has ears to hear, let him hear. And when he was alone, those who were around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them: To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God: but to those who are outside, all things are done in parables: that seeing they may see and not perceive: and hearing they may hear and not understand: lest at any time they should be converted and their sins forgiven them. And he said to them: Do you not know this parable? And how then will you understand all parables? He who sows, sows the word. And these are those by the way side, where the word is sown: and as soon as they have heard, Satan comes and takes away the word that was sown in their hearts. And these likewise are those who are sown on stony ground: who, when they have heard the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but are temporal: then when tribulation and persecution arise on account of the word, they are immediately scandalized. And there are others who are sown among thorns: these are those who hear the word: and the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things entering in choke the word, and it is made fruitless. And those who are sown upon good ground are those who hear the word and receive it: and bring forth fruit, some thirty, some sixty, and some a hundred. And he said to them: Does a lamp come in to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? Is it not to be set on a candlestick? For there is nothing hidden that shall not be made manifest: neither was anything kept secret but that it should come to light. If any man has ears to hear, let him hear. And he said to them: Take heed what you hear. With what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you. For he that has, to him shall be given: and he that has not, even what he has shall be taken away from him. And he said: So is the kingdom of God: as if a man should cast seed into the earth and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up while he does not know. For the earth brings forth fruit of herself: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when the fruit is brought forth, immediately he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come. And he said: To what shall we liken the kingdom of God? Or with what parable shall we compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed: which when it is sown in the earth, is less than all the seeds that are in the earth: and when it is sown, it grows up and becomes greater than all herbs, and puts forth large branches, so that the birds of the air can dwell under its shadow. And with many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it: and without parables he did not speak to them. And separately he explained all things to his disciples. And he said to them that same day when evening had come: Let us cross over

Mark.

and James and Andrew. Tell us when shall these things be, and what shall be the sign when all these things shall begin to be fulfilled? And Jesus answering began to say to them: Take heed lest any man deceive you. For many shall come in my name saying I am he, and shall deceive many. And when you shall hear of wars and rumors of wars, fear not. For such things must needs be, but the end is not yet. For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there shall be earthquakes in places, and famines. These things are the beginning of sorrows. But take heed to yourselves. For they shall deliver you up to councils, and in the synagogues you shall be beaten, and you shall stand before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony unto them. And the gospel must first be published among all nations. And when they shall lead you and deliver you up, be not thoughtful beforehand what you shall speak: but whatsoever shall be given you in that hour, speak that. For it is not you that speak, but the Holy Spirit. And the brother shall betray his brother unto death, and the father his son: and children shall rise up against parents, and shall work their death. And you shall be hated by all men for my name's sake. But he that shall endure unto the end, he shall be saved. And when you shall see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not: he that readeth let him understand. Then let them that are in Judea flee to the mountains: and let him that is on the housetop not go down into the house, nor enter therein to take anything out of his house: and let him that shall be in the field not turn back to take up his garment. And woe to them that are with child and that give suck in those days. But pray that these things happen not in winter. For in those days shall be such tribulations as were not from the beginning of creation which God created until now, neither shall be. And unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh should be saved: but for the sake of the elect which he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days.

And then if any man shall say to you: Lo, here is Christ; lo, he is there; believe him not. For there will rise up false Christs and false prophets, and they shall show signs and wonders, to seduce if it were possible even the elect. Take you heed therefore: behold I have foretold you all things. But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light. And the stars of heaven shall be falling down, and the powers that are in heaven shall be moved. And then shall they see the Son of man coming in the clouds, with great power and glory. And then shall he send his angels, and shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the uttermost part of the earth to the uttermost part of heaven. Now of the fig tree learn a parable. When the branch thereof is now tender and the leaves are come forth, you know that summer is very near. So you also when you shall see these things come to pass, know that it is very nigh, even at the doors. Amen I say to you that this generation shall not pass until all these things be done. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away. But of that day or hour no man knoweth, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father. Take heed, watch and pray. For you know not when the time is. Even as a man who going into a far country left his house and gave authority to his servants over every work, and commanded the porter to watch. Watch ye therefore, for you know not when the lord of the house cometh: at even, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning: lest coming on a sudden, he find you sleeping. And what I say to you, I say to all: Watch.

Now the feast of the Passover and of unleavened bread was after two days: and the chief priests and the scribes sought how they might by some wile lay hold on him and kill him. For they said: Not on the festival day, lest there should be a tumult among the people. And when he was in Bethania in the house of Simon

Mark.

he began to curse and swear: "I do not know this man of whom you speak." And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered the word that Jesus had said to him: "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." And he began to weep. Chapter [15].

And immediately in the morning the chief priests, with the elders and scribes and the whole council, held a consultation; and they bound Jesus and led him away and handed him over to Pilate. And Pilate asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered and said to him, "You say so." And the chief priests accused him of many things.
